title: Decision in the Making
text:
Preface: A Decision Is Already in the Making
At 3:17 p.m., the chair of a hiring committee asks for a vote. Five hands rise for one candidate, two for another. The decision appears to happen at that moment.
The committee has reasons. Its members have read the applications, conducted interviews, and discussed what the organization needs. Each can explain why one candidate seems stronger. The result is recorded, an offer is made, and the search is closed.
To understand that vote, however, we would need to arrive much earlier. We would need to hear how the position was defined, see which applications were read first, and notice when an impressive candidate became the standard against which the others were judged. We would need to ask why one interview story kept returning to the discussion while a quieter record of achievement received little attention. When a senior member praised a candidate, did anyone change their mind—or decide to keep a doubt to themselves?
Even a familiar word could matter. The committee agreed that it wanted the best fit, but one member meant competence, another meant shared values, and another meant someone easy to work with. An apparently shared criterion concealed different judgments.
This imagined committee gives us the central question of the book: what has shaped a choice before the moment when someone appears to make it?
crumbs: Preface: A Decision Is Already in the Making

title: Decision in the Making
text:
Follow the decision upstream
A visible choice is one point in a longer process. Something attracts attention and is given meaning. Possible actions come to mind, their consequences are anticipated, and those consequences are judged worth pursuing or avoiding. A choice then has to be carried out. What follows may teach us something useful, although a result can also strengthen a mistaken explanation.
The map below names these functions so that we can examine them separately. Consider the committee again. Predicting which candidate will perform reliably is different from deciding how much reliability matters relative to creativity. Constructing an additional option—reopening the search, for example—is different from comparing the two candidates already under discussion.






Figure 1: A map for examining how a decision forms. The functions can overlap, repeat, or be skipped; feedback can revise earlier judgments. People, institutions, and the surrounding design can influence the whole process. This is the book’s teaching model, not a fixed sequence of psychological stages.



These functions rarely wait politely for one another. Predicting the consequences of an option may reveal that it is infeasible, suggest a better version, or prompt us to imagine another option. What we value affects what we notice, and what we expect can affect how we interpret an ambiguous answer. A decision becomes easier to understand when we can trace those connections.
It also becomes easier to improve. A rational benchmark helps us make the alternatives, beliefs, and values explicit. It gives us a way to ask whether a disagreement concerns what will happen, what matters, or what can be done. The benchmark provides a standard for evaluating a choice; explaining how the choice actually forms requires evidence about human behavior.
crumbs: Preface: A Decision Is Already in the Making

title: Decision in the Making
text:
From labels to causes
Imagine that the committee’s first favorite eventually wins. We might call the result an anchoring effect, a preference for familiarity, or conformity to the chair. None of those labels, by itself, tells us what happened. The candidate might also have been the strongest applicant.
To distinguish the explanations, we would need observations that bear on them. What did members think before they discussed the candidates? Which evidence changed their judgments? Did the criteria shift to favor the early preference? These questions connect a possible mechanism to something we could examine.
The chapters use this approach throughout. Intuition can make effective use of experience, and habits can make useful actions easier to perform. A shortcut becomes troublesome when the cue it relies on is a poor guide in the current setting. A vivid success story, for example, may draw attention away from the outcomes of many comparable cases. The useful question is when to trust the shortcut and how to check it.
The same discipline applies after a decision. Suppose the new hire performs exceptionally well. That is welcome news, but it does not prove that every step of the selection process was sound. An unsuccessful hire would not establish that every step was mistaken either. Learning requires a record of what was believed before the outcome became known, when uncertainty was still visible.
crumbs: Preface: A Decision Is Already in the Making

title: Decision in the Making
section: What is a good decision ultimately for?
text:
What is a good decision ultimately for?
A job offer can look attractive during recruitment and feel quite different on an ordinary Tuesday. A purchase can promise lasting pleasure and soon fade into the background. A difficult commitment may be unpleasant at first while contributing to something a person deeply values.
The book therefore follows choices into the lives that result from them. We will distinguish anticipated feelings from lived experience, and both from a person’s judgment that life is going well. Income, health, relationships, autonomy, and meaning can matter in different ways. Improving one does not automatically settle a conflict among them.
Asking what makes a decision better is part of the analysis. A design that increases purchases may serve the seller while making buyers worse off. A successful negotiation may still produce an agreement that is difficult to carry out. Before evaluating a result, we need to know whose objective it serves and which consequences count.
crumbs: Preface: A Decision Is Already in the Making

title: Decision in the Making
text:
When other minds enter
The hiring committee is already a social setting, and few consequential choices remain within one mind for long. Another person’s action can change what is possible for us; their judgment can become evidence for ours. Cooperation, competition, norms, and market prices all depend on these connections.
The book follows an expanding journey: choice, influence, and agreement. We begin with individual judgment, examine what changes when choices depend on other people, and then turn to deliberate persuasion, communication, and negotiation.
A recommendation reaches an audience that already has beliefs and concerns. To make a persuasive case, we need to understand what listeners are trying to judge and what evidence could reasonably change their minds. A story can help them imagine a consequence, but its vividness does not establish that the consequence is likely.
Conversation lets the audience answer back. When the committee’s members use the word fit differently, a question may do more than another argument. They can explain, check what they have understood, and revise the shared account. Negotiation adds a joint choice: parties with different interests and alternatives seek an arrangement they can accept and implement.
crumbs: Preface: A Decision Is Already in the Making

title: Decision in the Making
text:
The environment gets a vote
Return to the committee room. The chair could ask everyone to record a judgment before discussion. The group could agree on criteria before meeting candidates, compare the same evidence for each person, and preserve its forecasts for later review. Those changes would alter the conditions under which the next decision forms.
The final part of the book examines this practical work. We can redesign a repeated behavior, make a choice easier to understand and carry out, or change how an organization gathers and evaluates evidence. Each change needs a clear purpose and an observable test. A process that sounds sensible may still fail in practice.
That ambition carries responsibility. The same knowledge can help people pursue their goals or make them easier to exploit. A default may remove an obstacle to a considered intention, while an obscure cancellation process may prevent someone from acting on it. We will keep asking whose goal a design serves, who bears its costs, and whether affected people can understand, question, or leave it.
crumbs: Preface: A Decision Is Already in the Making

title: Decision in the Making
text:
Evidence, ethics, and responsibility
Behavioral science offers findings with different levels of support. A classroom demonstration can reveal a possibility without telling us how common it is. A study can identify a difference without settling its mechanism. A result that repeats in one setting may change in another.
The chapters will name those boundaries where they matter to the explanation. We will separate examples from evidence, examine competing accounts, and consider what later research has changed. The early evidence guide explains how to read these distinctions; the research appendices develop them for readers who want to design or evaluate studies.
The purpose is to make confidence answerable to evidence. Scientific caution should help us decide what follows from a finding and what remains to be learned.
crumbs: Preface: A Decision Is Already in the Making

title: Decision in the Making
text:
Notice. Test. Ask. Design. Learn.
This book grew from teaching behavioral economics and decision, persuasion, and negotiation. Students wanted to understand why a sensible recommendation could fail, why a well-intended conversation could create distance, and why people could overlook a useful agreement. They also wanted something they could do differently next time.
You will therefore be invited to make predictions, examine cases, compare explanations, and try small changes. Some exercises produce a forecast; others produce a better question, a conversation plan, or a record that can be checked later. The aim is to leave each chapter with a distinction you can use.
Think again of the moment before the committee votes. The outcome is still uncertain, but there is time to ask what fit means, hear a quiet reservation, or examine an alternative. Better judgment often begins in such moments, while the path can still change.
The decision is already in the making.
crumbs: Preface: A Decision Is Already in the Making

title: How to Use This Book
text:
Reading layers
You can read this book from beginning to end or enter through a decision you want to understand. It is written for advanced undergraduate and master’s students, and for professionals who want evidence they can use. The main explanations stand on their own; optional notes provide additional theory, methods, and applications.
Start with the chapter’s opening situation and follow the main argument. Research Lens boxes and optional research notes develop formal models, measurement, or debates that you can return to later. An Applied Module extends the ideas into a particular domain.
A Practice Lab asks you to produce something: a forecast, a question, a decision record, a message, or a proposed change. Choose a manageable example and make the output specific enough to inspect. You can use a fictional case when a personal one would be sensitive.
An Evidence Boundary explains a limit that changes what we can conclude. Keep it with the finding it qualifies. Knowing that a study measured stated intentions, for example, matters if you are deciding whether an intervention will change behavior.
crumbs: How to Use This Book

title: How to Use This Book
text:
A recurring chapter rhythm
Chapters introduce a problem, develop an explanation, examine evidence, and give you a way to apply what you have learned. Before reading a result, pause when invited to make a prediction. Afterward, ask what you would now do differently and why. The chapter need not persuade you of every interpretation for that comparison to be useful.
crumbs: How to Use This Book

title: How to Use This Book
text:
Use one recurring ethical audit
When you propose a message, intervention, or agreement, ask whose objective it serves, who benefits, and who bears the cost. Consider whether the people affected can understand the arrangement, refuse it, or seek correction. Unequal power can make apparent consent difficult to interpret.
Finally, decide how you would discover that the proposal is causing harm. Appendix C collects the full ethical audit alongside the practical tools.

title: How to Use This Book
section: Find your place in the book
text:
Find your place in the book
The preface’s decision map distinguishes functions that are easy to confuse. Each part opens with a shorter map of its own questions, and chapter notes connect particular mechanisms to the wider process. These are reading aids; human thought can move back and forth among the functions.
Four terms retain consistent meanings:



Table 2: Vocabulary for following the decision process.









Term
Meaning in this book




Interpret
Work out what an observation, action, or message means in context.


Predict
Anticipate the consequences of an option, including uncertainty.


Expectation
A belief about what will happen; in some settings, that belief can also help change the outcome.


Value
Assess how desirable or otherwise important a predicted consequence is.






Chapter 4 also introduces the technical use of prediction in theories of perception and distinguishes it from forecasting future consequences.
crumbs: How to Use This Book

title: How to Use This Book
text:
Use the recurring cases cumulatively
Several cases return as the analysis develops. A hiring decision lets us examine evidence, intuition, and group judgment. Supplier and employment negotiations let us carry the same facts from preparation into agreement design. A difficult workplace conversation connects interpretation to communication and repair.
When a familiar case returns, look for the new question it helps answer. The fictional situations illustrate possible mechanisms; the surrounding studies provide the evidence. How to Read the Evidence in This Book explains that distinction.

text:
Version and link policy
The version date identifies the current build. Some linked resources and applications change over time; the surrounding text supplies the central explanation so that a broken link need not interrupt your reading. Corrections are most useful when they identify the passage and the evidence that would change it.

title: How to Read the Evidence in This Book
text:
Begin with the claim
Imagine a training provider advertising a programme that “raises productivity by 20%.” That number is difficult to use until we know what was compared. Did participants improve relative to their own earlier performance, or relative to people who did not receive the training? Were they randomly assigned? Did the study measure actual work, a test score, or participants’ impressions?
The following questions help turn a memorable result into a claim we can evaluate.
A descriptive claim reports what happened in a sample. A predictive claim says an observation helps forecast another outcome. A causal claim says that changing something produces a difference. A mechanistic claim goes further by identifying how the difference arises. A claim of generality says that the result should extend to other people or settings.
The training participants might improve because of the programme, because unusually motivated people enrolled, or because a temporary slump ended. An association between attendance and improvement would not separate those explanations. Even a credible causal effect would leave questions about why the programme worked and whether it would work elsewhere.
crumbs: How to Read the Evidence in This Book

title: How to Read the Evidence in This Book
section: Read the boundary with the finding
text:
Read the boundary with the finding
A useful account of evidence tells you the supported claim, its important limit, a plausible alternative explanation, and what further observation would change confidence. You will find these elements in the chapter discussions and evidence boxes.
For the training example, a limit such as “the outcome was a short knowledge test” changes the practical implication. It would give us a reason to examine learning, while leaving workplace performance to be tested. The qualification belongs beside the finding because it changes what the finding means.
crumbs: How to Read the Evidence in This Book

title: How to Read the Evidence in This Book
text:
Separate size from certainty
Ask how large the estimated difference is in meaningful units, how uncertain the estimate is, and whether the range of plausible effects would matter for the decision. A 20% relative increase could be large or small in absolute terms, depending on the starting level and the outcome being measured.
A p-value is not an effect size or the probability that a theory is true. A statistically significant result can be too small to matter in practice, while an imprecisely estimated effect may still include important possibilities. Magnitude, uncertainty, and practical relevance need separate attention.
crumbs: How to Read the Evidence in This Book

title: How to Read the Evidence in This Book
text:
Ask what was measured
Trust, happiness, attention, and similar constructs are inferred from observations such as answers, choices, response times, or physiological measures. Each measure captures some aspects more directly than others.
A person who rejects an unequal offer might dislike inequality, want to punish the proposer, or be concerned about reputation. The rejection alone does not identify the motive. A convincing explanation needs a comparison that helps distinguish the alternatives, rather than a new label for the same observation.
crumbs: How to Read the Evidence in This Book

title: How to Read the Evidence in This Book
text:
Distinguish an illustration from evidence
Fictional cases and classroom demonstrations help make an idea concrete. They show how something could happen. A study investigates a specified comparison; replications examine whether the result survives new samples or implementations. Field studies examine behavior in everyday or organizational settings and may be observational or experimental. Formal models make assumptions and their implications explicit.
A meta-analysis combines studies but inherits difficulties in the available literature, including selective publication and differences in measurement. No source type answers every question. Look for the evidence that bears on the particular claim.
crumbs: How to Read the Evidence in This Book

title: How to Read the Evidence in This Book
section: Treat replication as information, not a verdict
text:
Treat replication as information, not a verdict
A failed replication may weaken confidence in an original finding, reveal a boundary, or expose a difference in measurement or implementation. Those possibilities need evidence of their own. A successful replication strengthens support within the conditions tested; it does not make the result universal.
Low precision, flexible analysis, and selective publication can make a literature look more convincing than it is. Preregistration, transparent reporting, accessible data and code, and independent replication help readers examine these problems. Appendix F’s evidence-status map applies this approach to prominent behavioral findings.
crumbs: How to Read the Evidence in This Book

title: How to Read the Evidence in This Book
text:
Ask whether the finding travels
Return to the training claim. Results from volunteers may differ from results among employees required to attend; a short course may work differently when instructors, incentives, or opportunities to practise change. The outcome and follow-up period matter too.
Generalization becomes more informative when we specify which differences should matter and test them. “It depends” is the beginning of an explanation only when we can say what it depends on.
crumbs: How to Read the Evidence in This Book

title: How to Read the Evidence in This Book
text:
A six-question evidence audit
For any claim you might use, ask:

What exactly is being claimed? Description, prediction, causation, mechanism, or generality?
What is the comparison? Compared with what, for whom, and over what period?
How large and uncertain is the estimate? Consider the units and the range of plausible values.
What else could explain the observation? Identify a competing account.
Where might the finding change? Consider the population, task, and setting.
What evidence would change my confidence? Make the belief open to revision.

You do not need to become a methods specialist before reading the book. Keep these questions nearby, and return to them when a result surprises you or seems useful. Appendices E and F develop the research methods behind them.
crumbs: How to Read the Evidence in This Book

title: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape
text:
Questions to carry forward
A hiring committee is about to vote. Everyone has read the applications, yet the discussion turns on different things: one member remembers an impressive interview, another worries about reliability, and a third keeps returning to the candidate they liked first. Before asking who should get the job, we need to understand how these judgments took shape.
This part begins with a standard for a good decision: identify the feasible alternatives, consider their consequences, and clarify what matters. It then follows the actual process, from the evidence that attracts attention to the interpretation, expectations, and values that make one option seem preferable. The hiring case develops along the way, while a choice between job offers shows how to construct alternatives and investigate an uncertainty that could change the decision.
The distinction between predicting an outcome and valuing it will be useful throughout the book. Two people can agree about what is likely to happen and still reasonably prefer different actions.
Once we can see how a judgment forms, we can ask how well it handles uncertainty. Part II follows the shortcuts that help us judge quickly—and the checks that reveal when they mislead.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape

title: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape
text:
What has shaped the choice before the vote begins?
Are we disagreeing about what will happen, what matters, or what is possible?
What should we record now so that the outcome can teach us later?

title: 1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are
text:
One decision, two questions
A rational benchmark is not a psychological portrait
Return to the hiring committee in the preface. At 3:17 p.m., the chair asks for a vote. Two candidates remain. The visible decision is a name. The first question is straightforward:
A defensible process would identify the feasible candidates and any other feasible course of action, such as extending the search, collecting a work sample, redesigning the role, or making a conditional offer. It would predict the consequences of each alternative using job-relevant evidence. It would clarify what the organization values: immediate performance, learning, leadership, reliability, diversity of expertise, retention, or some combination. It would then choose the feasible alternative expected to produce the most valued consequences.
Now ask a different question:
One candidate may have become the early favorite. A vivid story may receive more attention than a reliable but unremarkable indicator. The word fit may mean one thing to the chair and another to the future supervisor. A prestigious employer may be treated as evidence without anyone stating what it predicts. A confident senior colleague may speak first, causing junior members to revise or conceal their judgments. The option of extending the search may never enter the discussion. By the time the vote is called, much of the decision may already have been made.
These are not two versions of the same question. The first asks for a standard. The second asks for a causal explanation. Decision science needs both, and it needs a third question that connects them.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape

title: 1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are
text:
How should the committee decide?




How will the committee actually decide?









NoteCore Idea



A sound decision needs a standard for judging the options and an account of how people actually judge them. Rational choice helps clarify what is feasible, what may happen, and what matters. Behavioral evidence shows how attention, context, and experience shape those ingredients before anyone announces a choice.

title: 1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are
text:
Learning goals
After reading this chapter, you should be able to:

Distinguish normative, descriptive, and prescriptive questions about the same decision.
State the rational-choice benchmark without double-counting constraints or treating the choice rule as another substantive input.
Explain why context-sensitive choice challenges a thin rational model as a stand-alone description without treating every contextual effect as irrational.
Map a visible choice onto the process through which it was already being made.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape
1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are

title: 1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are
text:
Three questions of decision science
Normative, descriptive, and prescriptive are not three kinds of people or three mutually exclusive theories. They are three questions we can ask about the same decision.



Table 1.1: Three questions of decision science










Perspective
Central question
Standard of success




Normative
How should the decision be made under stated assumptions?
Coherence, evidence-responsive beliefs, legitimate objectives, and fit between means and ends.


Descriptive
How are judgments and choices actually formed?
Empirical accuracy about attention, interpretation, option construction, prediction, valuation, action, and learning.


Prescriptive
How can the actual process be improved?
Better calibration, consistency, fairness, implementation, contestability, and learning, given real human capacities and environments.






For the hiring committee, these questions lead to different work. It must agree on relevant evidence and legitimate objectives, investigate how prestige or hierarchy influences the discussion, and design a procedure that makes those influences open to examination. Recording judgments before discussion, for example, could reveal disagreements that an immediate public vote would conceal.
An intervention succeeds only if it improves something worth improving. More agreement or faster voting would not by themselves establish a better hiring decision.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape
1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are

title: 1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are
section: How a decision should be made
text:
How a decision should be made
A rational-choice model offers a deliberately thin answer to the normative question. In its most basic form, the decision-maker faces a set of feasible alternatives, ranks them, and chooses a highest-ranked alternative. For decisions whose consequences are uncertain, it is useful to unpack that ranking into three substantive inputs (von Neumann & Morgenstern, 1944; Edwards, 1954).

Feasible alternatives: What courses of action can actually be taken?
Beliefs or predictions about consequences: What may follow from each alternative, with what likelihood, timing, and uncertainty?
Values or preferences over consequences: How desirable, undesirable, important, fair, meaningful, or unacceptable would those consequences be?

The beliefs describe what may follow; the values say how much those consequences matter. Together they support a ranking, from which the decision-maker selects a highest-ranked feasible alternative. The diagram makes these relationships visible and adds feedback from experience.






Figure 1.1: A normative decision process built around the rational-choice benchmark. Information about alternatives supports prediction; prediction informs valuation; valuation supports choice; and outcomes can provide feedback for later judgment.




Judgment, prediction, valuation, and choice
Judgment includes assessing what may happen (prediction) and how desirable it would be (valuation). Choice selects an alternative, while implementation turns that commitment into action. The diagram compresses this last step: a choice alone does not produce an outcome, and observing an outcome does not guarantee learning.
Information also differs from feasibility. The committee may never hear about a candidate it could hire, or may consider someone who cannot accept. Constraints such as budget, law, and time determine what can actually be done; they are already reflected in the feasible set. Chapter 2 shows how to distinguish these limits from assumptions that can be challenged.
The formal conditions for coherent rankings, including transitivity, belong in Appendix A. Risky Decision-Making develops expected utility, one representation of consequence-based choice under risk.
The benchmark is powerful because it separates disagreements that ordinary language often hides. Two colleagues may agree about what matters but disagree about the probability of success. They may agree about the forecast but value the consequences differently. They may agree about both while recognizing different alternatives as feasible. Words such as best, fit, safe, and risky can conceal all three disagreements.
The model does not require selfishness. Values may include family welfare, dignity, fairness, environmental consequences, loyalty, moral duties, future generations, or the interests of other affected people. Nor does it require emotional coldness. Emotion can provide information about what matters. Rational choice also does not supply a complete moral theory. A choice may consistently advance one person’s objectives while violating another person’s rights. Legitimate objectives, affected parties, and procedural justice therefore cannot simply be hidden inside an unexplained score.
Most importantly, the model is a benchmark, not yet a psychological portrait. It tells us how the ingredients of a coherent consequence-based choice should relate once the alternatives, beliefs, and values have been specified. It does not tell us how alternatives become visible, which evidence receives attention, how that evidence is interpreted, or why beliefs and values change with context. The six examples that follow test those descriptive assumptions.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape
1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are

title: 1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are
section: From a normative benchmark to descriptive predictions
text:
From a normative benchmark to descriptive predictions
A normative model generates descriptive predictions only after we add assumptions about stability. Suppose that two presentations leave the feasible alternatives, predicted consequences, values, and action costs unchanged. A thin rational-choice account then predicts that the choice should also remain unchanged.
For example, expressing the same outcome as survival or mortality should not reverse preference when the descriptions are understood as equivalent. Adding an inferior option should not improve the attributes of an existing one. Yet a default may change the effort needed to act, and an internal state may change what someone currently values. Those cases require different explanations.
The examples below ask where the model succeeds, where its predictions fail, and where it leaves out part of the decision. They do not all provide equally strong evidence, or test the same assumption.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape
1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are

title: 1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are
text:
Six ways context enters choice

Representation and comparison

1. The same treatment data, framed through survival or mortality
McNeil, Pauker, Sox, and Tversky (1982) presented information about surgery and radiation therapy for lung cancer to ambulatory patients with chronic illnesses, graduate students, and physicians. Different groups received outcome data framed in terms of survival or mortality. The cumulative probabilities and time horizons were complementary, yet surgery was relatively more attractive in the survival frame.
A thin rational model treats the descriptions as different ways of presenting the same consequences. If the event, denominator, horizon, and implications are understood as equivalent, preference should not change merely because one description foregrounds living and another foregrounds dying. The observed shift is therefore a comparatively direct challenge to description invariance.
The boundary matters. Participants imagined the treatment decision; the study did not observe signed consent by patients facing an immediate diagnosis. Nor does it show that every positive frame increases risk taking. The more precise result is that complementary descriptions can produce different representations of the same outcome data, and those representations can alter treatment preference. Framing develops the mechanism and the ethical response.


2. The subscription option nobody chose
A well-known classroom demonstration presented three subscription options: web-only access, print-only access, and print plus web access. The print-only option cost the same as the combined offer and was therefore dominated by it. Ariely (2008) reported that nobody in the classroom group chose the print-only option, yet its presence shifted choices toward the combined offer. When the dominated option was removed, web-only access became much more popular.
The exact counts came from a classroom demonstration reported in a trade book, not from customer sales at The Economist. The stronger scientific foundation is the attraction-effect literature. Adding an asymmetrically dominated alternative can increase the share choosing an existing target, contrary to regularity in standard menu-independent models (Huber et al., 1982).
The decoy does not improve the target’s objective attributes. It changes the comparison. The effect is neither universal nor fixed in size; it depends on the alternatives, attribute structure, comprehension, task, and population. Even so, it shows that value is not always retrieved from stable preferences and applied to a menu. The menu can help construct the comparison through which value becomes visible. When Context Rewrites Comparison develops the evidence and mechanism.



The path from intention to action

3. Organ donation and the consequence of doing nothing
An organ-donation form can require people to opt in, presume participation unless they opt out, or require an active choice. Johnson and Goldstein (2003) found large differences in stated agreement across online experimental defaults. Formal freedom to select either response remained, but the consequence of doing nothing did not.
This case is not a pure invariance test between costless equivalents. A default can alter effort, perceived recommendation, normality, responsibility, anticipated regret, and the outcome of postponement. It may therefore change the decision-relevant environment rather than merely relabel it.
The outcome must also be named precisely. Stated agreement is not registration; registration is not a recovered organ; and recovered organs are not completed transplants. A longitudinal analysis of five countries that changed from opt-in to opt-out found no average increase in deceased donation after the policy switch, emphasizing the importance of clinical capacity, public trust, family involvement, and implementation (Dallacker et al., 2024). Choice Architecture treats a default as one component of a system.






NoteTwo suggestive cases, with weaker evidence






4. A right-pointing arrow and a more visible action path
In 2012, Google changed text advertisements on its Display Network by adding a clickable right-pointing arrow while also changing typography, spacing, and layout. The advertised hotel or product did not become objectively better because the arrow appeared, but the route from seeing the offer to clicking it became more salient. Google reported higher clicks after the redesign (Land & Yuan, 2012).
This example does not identify an independent arrow effect or a violation of rational choice. The public report describes a bundled corporate redesign: the arrow, typography, spacing, and layout changed together, and the report disclosed neither a separate arrow effect nor an effect size, profit result, or measure of informed user welfare.
Its narrower lesson is nevertheless useful. A preference can exist without becoming action. Attention, visibility, friction, and affordance lie between evaluating an option and implementing it. A model that predicts clicks solely from the value of the advertised product omits the interface through which intention becomes behavior. Choice Architecture returns to the case as a design problem.


5. Mars publicity and Mars-bar accessibility
News reports in 1997 linked rising sales of Mars bars to intense publicity around NASA’s Pathfinder mission. The bar’s name came from its creator’s family name, not the planet, so the story offers an intuitive accessibility hypothesis: repeated references to Mars may have made the product name easier to retrieve.
The account is not a controlled study. Mars said sales had been rising for about a year, the available report does not provide a usable time series or comparison group, and other market changes could have contributed (Grant, 1997). Berger and Fitzsimons (2008) later used the story to motivate experiments on environmental cues, accessibility, product evaluation, and choice, but those experiments do not retroactively identify the cause of the 1997 sales pattern.
The case belongs here as a lesson in both decision-making and causal inference. A product can become easier to recall without changing its attributes. That accessibility may influence the consideration set or make evaluation easier. But an association that fits a mechanism is not yet evidence that the mechanism caused the outcome. Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease supplies the experimentally grounded concepts.







When an active motive changes the message

6. The same museum, a different active motive
Griskevicius and colleagues (2009) independently manipulated an induced state—fear, romantic desire, or a neutral condition—and the appeal used in advertisements for a museum or Las Vegas. Appeals based on behavioral social proof—many people visit—or distinctiveness—stand out from the crowd—changed in effectiveness across the induced states. Fear made behavioral social proof relatively more persuasive and distinctiveness less persuasive; romantic desire produced the opposite pattern in the reported evaluations.
The venue did not change, but responses depended on the factorial interaction between an induced motivational state and the appeal. The outcome was a persuasion or product-desirability index, not actual museum attendance. The student sample, short induction, and task constrain generalization, and the evolutionary-functional explanation is not uniquely established against every goal-congruence or learned-association account.
The experiment nevertheless illustrates why an option has no fixed value outside the model through which it is interpreted. The same venue can promise safety, belonging, novelty, or distinction depending on the person’s active concerns. A thin model can represent this by changing values, but it does not predict when and how those values will change. Valuation develops state-dependent value.

text:
What the six examples establish—and what they do not



Table 1.2: Six examples with calibrated evidential status










Example
What changed—and why it matters
Evidence boundary




Lung-cancer treatment frame
Complementary survival and mortality descriptions shifted treatment preference; representation can alter valuation.
Controlled framing study; hypothetical treatment choice, not signed consent.


Subscription decoy
A dominated option shifted choice toward the target; the comparison set can construct relative value.
Attraction effect has experimental support; exact classroom counts were not market sales.


Organ-donation default
Stated agreement changed with the default; inaction, effort, recommendation, and responsibility enter choice.
Stated consent is not transplantation; policy effects depend on the wider system.


Advertising redesign
Clicks reportedly increased after a bundled redesign; visibility and affordance affect implementation.
Corporate report; the arrow was not isolated and no effect size or welfare measure was reported.


Mars publicity
Sales reportedly rose during Mars publicity; accessibility may influence consideration and evaluation.
Anecdote with serious alternative explanations.


Museum message
Message effectiveness changed across induced states; active motives shape interpretation and valuation.
Factorial advertising experiment; ratings, not attendance; mechanism not uniquely identified.






Some contextual changes alter real features of a decision, such as effort, the consequence of inaction, or current goals. Others change the representation of otherwise equivalent options. Explaining either requires more than naming the eventual preference.
A model that takes alternatives, beliefs, and values as given can represent a choice once those inputs have been specified. Its harder task is to predict how the inputs will arise. Adding a new preference after every unexpected result may explain the past without predicting the next decision. Bounded-rationality research made this process problem central (Simon, 1955).

title: 1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are
text:
How decisions are actually made
When people explain a decision, they usually begin near the end: “I chose the consulting job because it had better prospects”; “We hired her because she was the strongest candidate”; “I bought the product because it offered the best value.” These explanations may contain genuine reasons. They are rarely the whole causal story.
Long before the committee votes, members have selected evidence, interpreted it, considered some candidates more seriously than others, and formed expectations about working together. Discussion can change both those expectations and the importance attached to them. Even after a choice, an unavailable candidate or an unclear offer can prevent the intended action.
The next diagram opens the earlier loop to show these influences. It also shows why an outcome must be interpreted before it can inform another decision.






Figure 1.2: An evidence-informed functional synthesis of how decisions are actually made. External context shapes presented information and the decision-maker’s internal state and model. Within judgment, selection and interpretation interact with prediction and valuation. Judgment supports choice and action; outcomes provide feedback that may update, reinforce, or fail to correct the internal model.



Figure 1.2 is a functional teaching synthesis, not a claim that every decision follows fixed, conscious, sequential stages or that the complete diagram has been validated as one universal psychological model. The functions may overlap, recur, become compressed through practice, or be distributed across people and technologies. The arrows show possible dependencies and routes of influence.
The map includes two easily overlooked tasks. People must construct options, because the first visible menu is rarely complete. They must also turn choice into action, which depends on effort, authority, and opportunity. Prediction and valuation can interact throughout: learning what an alternative offers may change its appeal, while recognizing a priority can change what evidence people seek.
Chapter 2 turns this account into practical work: expand the feasible set, identify what commitment would give up, and test the assumptions on which a recommendation depends (Milkman et al., 2009).

title: 1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are
text:
Outcome is not process
A good decision can produce a bad outcome, and a poor decision can produce a favorable one. Uncertainty separates process quality from result quality.
An investor may buy after one enthusiastic post and make money. Another may diversify on defensible evidence and lose during an unexpected market shock. A surgeon can recommend the treatment best supported at the time and still encounter a rare complication. Outcome bias judges the earlier decision mainly by its result; hindsight bias makes the result seem more predictable after it occurs (Baron & Hershey, 1988; Fischhoff, 1975).
Feedback therefore does not automatically create learning. A useful review reconstructs what was known, which alternatives were considered, what was predicted, what mattered, and what could have changed the decision. A dated record protects the earlier judgment from a narrator who already knows the ending. The Narrator After Choice develops that problem; Decision Hygiene turns it into organizational practice.

title: 1  How Decisions Should Be Made—and How They Actually Are
text:
One architecture across the book
The same questions extend beyond individual choice. Persuasion changes what another person notices or believes; communication makes interpretations open to checking; negotiation lets people construct a path they could not take alone. Throughout, we will ask whose decision is being changed, toward whose objective, and with what opportunity to question or revise it.

Take it forward
Return to the chair at 3:17 p.m. A better final question might be: “Before we vote, what are we predicting about each candidate, and where do our judgments differ?” The answer would reveal more than a show of hands. It would expose the assumptions that need attention while there is still time to change the decision.

title: 2  Building a Better Decision: Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness
text:
Learning goals
The best calculation cannot rescue a menu that omitted the best feasible path
Two job offers are open on a student’s laptop. The consulting firm promises structured training and a familiar name; the sustainability start-up offers early responsibility and work she cares about. She starts a comparison table, then stops at “work–life balance.” Neither employer has told her what an ordinary week actually looks like.
The missing information matters, but so does a question she has not yet asked: must she choose either offer exactly as written? A better decision may begin by changing the menu.
After reading this chapter, you should be able to:

title: 2  Building a Better Decision: Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness
section: A better decision begins before comparison
text:
A better decision begins before comparison
The student may be able to negotiate workload, request another conversation, or agree on a later start date. None of these possibilities appears in a table labeled only “consulting” and “start-up.” Comparison becomes useful after the alternatives have been examined.






Figure 2.1: A practical sequence for better decisions: expand the feasible set, name the best forgone option, ask what information could change the choice, and stress-test the ranking.



These questions can send the student back to an earlier step. A forecast may reveal a new option, and a priority may reveal a term worth negotiating. The diagram is a guide for inquiry, not a required sequence of calculations.

2  Building a Better Decision: Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness

title: 2  Building a Better Decision: Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness
section: Define the decision before solving it
text:
Define the decision before solving it
A useful decision statement specifies the commitment being considered, the decision-maker, the relevant horizon, and the conditions under which the choice can be revised. Compare:

Should I accept the start-up job?

with:

By Friday, should I accept the start-up offer as written, negotiate its terms, request time for one further conversation, continue the search, or decline, given my financial runway, family location, learning goals, and tolerance for employment risk over the next two years?

The second statement does not guarantee a better answer. It makes the decision boundary inspectable. It reveals alternatives, time, affected values, and the possibility that the offer itself can be changed.
Before analysis, ask:

What commitment is being made now?
Who has authority to make it?
Whose consequences legitimately matter?
What is the relevant time horizon?
Which parts are reversible, and at what cost?
What decision will occur automatically if nobody acts?

These questions prevent a broad life problem from being compressed into a misleading yes-or-no choice.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape
2  Building a Better Decision: Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness

title: 2  Building a Better Decision: Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness
text:
Construct the feasible set
A feasible alternative is a course of action that can actually be taken given relevant limits of money, time, law, authority, technology, health, capability, and commitment. Those limits define feasibility; they are not a separate fourth component added after the alternatives have been listed.
The practical difficulty is that people often confuse three sets:

The imaginable set: everything one can describe, including options that are impossible or impermissible.
The feasible set: the alternatives that can genuinely be implemented.
The consideration set: the alternatives noticed, recalled, or taken seriously, some of which may still need a feasibility check.

People commonly consider only part of what is feasible, while also entertaining options that turn out to be unavailable. A consistent ranking cannot recover a good alternative that never entered the comparison.

Distinguish real constraints from assumed constraints
A visa condition may rule out one location; a deadline imposed by an employer may be negotiable. The student needs to find out which kind of limit she faces. Asking for a later start date changes nothing if the employer cannot accommodate it, but the request may reveal flexibility that the original offer concealed.
Ask: What would have to change for this option to become feasible, and who could change it? The answer might identify a negotiation, permission, investment, or redesign. It might also confirm that the boundary is fixed.


Generate alternatives deliberately
When the visible menu is too narrow, use a small set of generative moves:

Maintain: Keep the status quo or continue the current path.
Delay: Preserve the option while waiting for a defined event or date.
Learn: Gather information, run a test, seek a second opinion, or conduct a pilot.
Negotiate: Change price, timing, scope, responsibilities, safeguards, or exit terms.
Combine: Create a package or hybrid from parts of existing alternatives.
Stage: Begin with a limited, reversible commitment and expand only if conditions are met.
Search: Reopen the market or generate alternatives outside the current menu.
Exit: Stop, decline, or abandon the project.

Option generation is part of rationality, not a decorative act of creativity. Careful comparison cannot rescue a choice set that excludes the best feasible path.
More choice is not automatically better. Choice overload is not universal, but it becomes more likely when alternatives are complex, preferences are uncertain, the task is difficult, or the chooser is trying to minimize effort (Iyengar & Lepper, 2000; Scheibehenne et al., 2010; Chernev et al., 2015). The aim is a set broad enough to escape tunnel vision and structured enough to remain actionable.
A useful stopping question is:

Do we have at least one meaningfully different alternative, not merely a slightly altered version of the current favorite?

2  Building a Better Decision: Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness

title: 2  Building a Better Decision: Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness
text:
Name the opportunity cost
Accepting one job can mean giving up another. Opportunity cost is the value of the best feasible alternative forgone, including the consequences of that complete path. It is neither just the money paid nor the sum of every benefit in every unchosen life. The same reasoning applies to a meeting that displaces focused work or a project that uses capital needed elsewhere.
Opportunity cost depends on the alternative set. Discovering a better feasible option raises the cost of accepting every proposal already on the table. Conversely, if the apparent alternative is not actually feasible, it should not be used to exaggerate the sacrifice.
Research on opportunity-cost neglect shows that people do not always generate the displaced alternative spontaneously. Frederick et al. (2009) demonstrated this with a minimal change in how a hypothetical purchase was described. One hundred and fifty students imagined deciding whether to buy a desirable DVD for $14.99. When the alternative was simply “not buy,” 75% chose the DVD. When that same alternative added the reminder “Keep the $14.99 for other purchases,” the purchase rate fell to 55%. The objective options had not changed; the reminder made an otherwise implicit use of the money easier to represent.
The result does not imply that opportunity costs matter only when someone else states them, or that declining a purchase is necessarily the better decision. Some people generate alternatives spontaneously, and decision quality depends on whether the represented alternative is feasible and valuable. A later meta-analysis of 39 experiments found a robust but considerably smaller average effect than the original studies reported (Maguire et al., 2023). The defensible conclusion is therefore narrower: making a forgone alternative salient can improve awareness of the trade-off and can change choice, but it does not guarantee a better choice.
Before commitment, ask:

If I choose this, what is the best feasible path I will no longer be able to take?

Naming that path often clarifies the decision more than adding another score to the favored option.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape
2  Building a Better Decision: Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness

title: 2  Building a Better Decision: Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness
text:
Separate predictions from values
A consequence-based decision combines two distinct judgments:

Prediction: What is likely to happen if this alternative is chosen?
Valuation: How desirable or undesirable would that consequence be?

The distinction sounds obvious but is often lost in ordinary discussion. “The candidate is the best fit” may combine a prediction about performance, a value placed on similarity, a feeling of interpersonal ease, and an unstated view of what the organization should become. “The project is too risky” may combine the probability of failure, the size of the loss, the ability to recover, and the speaker’s tolerance for uncertainty.
Separating predictions from values helps diagnose disagreement. If two people disagree about the probability of success, more relevant evidence may help. If they agree about the forecast but value the outcome differently, more data may not resolve the conflict. They need to discuss priorities, rights, trade-offs, or authority.

Make predictions inspectable
For each alternative, write the consequential forecast, its horizon, a plausible range, and the evidence supporting it. “The start-up will offer faster learning” becomes more useful when the student specifies what she expects to learn in the first year, from whom, and what would make that expectation wrong. Comparable past cases can provide a reference class against which to check the forecast.
The purpose is to make an expectation testable. Confidence and a detailed story cannot substitute for evidence about what usually happens in comparable circumstances.


Make values and trade-offs inspectable
Important decisions usually involve several objectives. A job can affect income, learning, autonomy, health, location, family time, mission, relationships, and future options. A public decision may affect different groups unequally. Some consequences can be traded off; others may be unacceptable even when an aggregate score is high. Multiattribute decision analysis can help make these objectives and trade-offs explicit (Keeney & Raiffa, 1976).
The student should explain what “learning” means before assigning it a weight. Is it valuable in itself, or mainly because it opens future opportunities? Counting both without checking their overlap can exaggerate the advantage. Health may instead be a threshold: an option is unacceptable if its expected demands exceed what she can sustain.
A decision table helps people discuss these judgments. A weight such as “health: 30 percent” is hard to interpret until the relevant range and trade-off are specified, and uncertainty should remain visible in the entries.



Table 2.1: A prediction–value table for comparing alternatives










Alternative
Prediction: consequences, evidence, and uncertainty
Valuation, thresholds, and safeguards




Option A
What is expected to happen, when, and across what plausible range? What evidence and causal assumption support the forecast?
Which consequences matter, to whom, and why? What must be true before committing?


Option B
What is expected to happen, when, and across what plausible range? What evidence and causal assumption support the forecast?
Which consequences matter, to whom, and why? What must be true before committing?


Status quo or delay
What follows if no new action is taken? Is inaction really neutral?
What is preserved, lost, or postponed? When will the decision be reopened?






The table should preserve uncertainty rather than hiding it. If one option looks best only because every uncertain input has been entered at its most favorable value, the apparent precision is misleading.

title: 2  Building a Better Decision: Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness
section: Gather information only when it can change action
text:
Gather information only when it can change action
Information has instrumental value when it can improve action enough to justify its costs. Those costs include money, delay, attention, privacy, processing, false reassurance, and strategic exposure.
To assess a proposed question or test, list its plausible answers and the action that would follow each. Then compare the expected benefit of acting on the answer with the cost of obtaining and using it. The table gives examples of this reasoning.
If every plausible result leaves action unchanged, the inquiry may still serve curiosity, reassurance, or documentation. It has little instrumental value for that particular decision.



Table 2.2: A decision-branch test for information










Question or test
Result that could change action
Likely decision value




Reference check on role-critical behavior
Credible evidence changes the ranking, safeguards, or contract terms.
Potentially high when the choice is close and the source is informative.


Small pilot before an irreversible launch
A pre-stated threshold triggers scale-up, revision, delay, or stopping.
Often high when the pilot is cheap, representative, and tied to a decision rule.


Diagnostic test when treatment would be identical either way
No plausible result changes treatment.
Low for this treatment decision, though it may serve another purpose.


Negotiation question about timing
A real difference reveals a feasible trade or package.
Potentially high when the answer is credible and contractible.






The technical appendix formalizes the expected value of information. For now, the student can ask the employers about ordinary working hours and decide in advance which answers would change the offer she accepts or the terms she requests.

2  Building a Better Decision: Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness

title: 2  Building a Better Decision: Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness
text:
Stress-test the recommendation
A robust recommendation remains preferred across specified, plausible changes in the assumptions. A fragile recommendation reverses when a small credible change is made. Neither label is absolute: the assessment depends on which uncertainties were included and how widely they were varied. Sensitivity analysis examines these changes.
Sensitivity analysis asks:

Which assumption contributes most to the recommendation?
How far would that assumption have to move before the preferred option changes?
Is that threshold inside or outside the plausible range?
Are the assumptions correlated?
What happens under a jointly unfavorable scenario?
Can the decision be staged or made reversible if the ranking is fragile?

Suppose the start-up is preferred only if it survives for three years, workload remains below a certain level, and rapid learning receives a very high value. The decision should not be reported simply as “the start-up scores 82 and consulting scores 78.” The useful conclusion is conditional:

The start-up is preferred if its survival probability is above the stated threshold and if early autonomy is valued more than near-term income by at least the specified trade-off. Otherwise, consulting is preferred.

This form of conclusion identifies what should be investigated, negotiated, protected, or monitored.
Fragility does not always justify more analysis. When information is expensive or unavailable, a reversible choice may be better than another forecast. A pilot, probation period, staged investment, contingency clause, or exit option can reduce the cost of being wrong.
crumbs: Part I. How a Choice Takes Shape
2  Building a Better Decision: Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness

title: 2  Building a Better Decision: Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness
text:
Use proportionate analysis
Bounded rationality recognizes that search, attention, time, memory, and computation are scarce (Simon, 1955, 1956). People often satisfice: they search until an alternative meets an aspiration level rather than proving global optimality. That can be procedurally rational when further search costs more than it is likely to improve the decision.
The appropriate depth of analysis depends on the decision.



Table 2.3: When to use more or less decision structure










Decision feature
Usually warrants less structure
Usually warrants more structure




Stakes
Low
High


Familiarity
Repeated and well learned
Novel


Reversibility
Easy and inexpensive to reverse
Irreversible or costly to reverse


Feedback
Fast, clear, and diagnostic
Delayed, noisy, or absent


Interdependence
Mostly individual
Depends strategically on other people


Distributional effects
Limited and private
Affects rights, fairness, or many stakeholders


Uncertainty
Narrow and well understood
Wide, ambiguous, or model-dependent






Low-stakes, familiar, reversible choices can rely on routines, trained intuition, or simple rules. High-stakes, novel, irreversible, strategically interdependent, or low-feedback choices deserve more explicit structure. Rationality should guide proportionate deliberation, not turn life into continuous calculation. Fast and Frugal Thinking asks when compressed judgment is well trained; Risky Decision-Making develops the expected-utility detail needed when uncertain consequences must be combined.

2  Building a Better Decision: Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness

title: 2  Building a Better Decision: Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness
section: Produce a decision recommendation, not merely a score
text:
Produce a decision recommendation, not merely a score
By Friday, the student’s recommendation should explain more than which offer scored highest. Suppose the start-up is preferred because she values early responsibility, can absorb a limited period without income, and expects to receive close supervision. The supervision forecast now becomes a question worth checking before commitment. If that support is absent, the recommendation may reverse.
The record should also name the best alternative forgone. If consulting is the next-best feasible path, its complete value is the opportunity cost of accepting the start-up; structured training and income are parts of that value, not separate alternatives to add together.
A short recommendation can therefore state the chosen path, its main reasons, the assumptions that could reverse it, and the safeguards needed to proceed. A workload agreement and a scheduled review may make the choice easier to live with even when uncertainty remains. Use the practice below to create this record for a real decision.

title: 2  Building a Better Decision: Alternatives, Opportunity Cost, Information, and Robustness
text:
Practice Lab
Prepare a one-page decision record for a consequential decision.

Rewrite the decision so that the commitment, decision-maker, horizon, and automatic outcome of inaction are explicit.
List the visible alternatives, then add at least one option created through delay, learning, negotiation, combination, staging, search, or exit.
Mark which alternatives are imaginable, feasible, and seriously considered.
State the best feasible alternative forgone by the current favorite.
Separate the three most important predictions from the three most important values.
Identify one piece of information and write the action that would follow each plausible result. Remove the information request if no branch changes action.
State the assumption most capable of reversing the recommendation and the threshold at which it would do so.
Specify one implementation safeguard and one review point.

title: 3  Attention: What Becomes Evidence?
section: Inattentional blindness: what attention leaves out
text:
Inattentional blindness: what attention leaves out
In Simons and Chabris’s (1999) study, participants who were counting passes often failed to notice an unexpected person crossing the scene, including a person in a gorilla suit. The object was available to vision while the counting task occupied attention. This is inattentional blindness: failing to notice an unexpected object or event while engaged in another task (Mack & Rock, 1998).
Expertise does not remove this limit. Drew, Võ, and Wolfe (2013) inserted a large gorilla image into lung scans that 24 radiologists inspected for nodules. Eighty-three percent did not report it; most of those who missed it had looked at its location. The study shows that trained search can coexist with failure to report a conspicuous, unexpected item. It does not estimate how often radiologists miss clinically relevant abnormalities.
The useful question is therefore how a search task shapes awareness. A person can attend carefully to the assigned target and still miss something consequential outside that target.

3  Attention: What Becomes Evidence?

title: 3  Attention: What Becomes Evidence?
text:
Top-down goals and bottom-up capture
Attention selects and prioritizes information rather than illuminating everything equally. Goals, expectations, and the properties of incoming signals all influence this selection (Broadbent, 1958; Desimone & Duncan, 1995; Kahneman, 1973; Treisman, 1964).
Some selection is top-down: guided by goals, plans, and expectations. If you are searching for your friend in a crowd, your mind is tuned to face shape, height, clothing, or gait. If a radiologist is searching for nodules, the visual system is tuned to nodules. If a negotiator is searching for price concessions, price becomes more visible than timing, warranty, risk-sharing, or relationship value.
Other shifts are bottom-up: striking changes in the environment, such as sudden movement or a loud sound, draw attention. Capture also depends on the task and the observer; salience is not an irresistible command. A phone notification, a flashing advertisement, a crying baby, a sharp tone, or an angry face can capture attention before conscious choice. Corbetta and Shulman (2002) distinguish between networks involved in goal-directed attention and those involved in stimulus-driven reorienting. In real life, attention reflects the interaction between what we are trying to do and what the world pulls from us.
A negotiator searching only for price concessions may give little attention to delivery timing or risk sharing. Those other terms can be available in the conversation and still receive too little consideration to influence the agreement.

3  Attention: What Becomes Evidence?

title: 3  Attention: What Becomes Evidence?
text:
Attention under divided demand
Holding one task in mind leaves less capacity for some competing tasks. Attention, working memory, and control constrain how much information people can use at once (Baddeley, 1992; Cowan, 2001; Marois & Ivanoff, 2005). These limits are most directly demonstrated by comparing performance under single and divided demands.






NoteResearch note: two very different information rates





Zheng and Meister (2025) compare estimates of sensory acquisition on the order of \(10^9\) bits per second with deliberate behavioral throughput near 10 bits per second across selected tasks. The contrast raises a question about how rich sensory signals support much slower observable responses. It does not measure the total content of consciousness or identify attention as the cause of a numerical loss: the estimates concern different stages, tasks, and definitions of information.






Figure 3.1: Sensory acquisition and deliberate behavior have very different estimated information rates. These are broad orders of magnitude from Zheng and Meister (2025), not quantities that can be subtracted to calculate “lost bits.”



The brain’s energy use is a separate issue. Its substantial resting demand does not mean a difficult thought consumes a proportionately large extra amount of whole-brain energy; tasks redistribute activity within an already active system (Attwell & Laughlin, 2001; Raichle & Gusnard, 2002).



The classroom provides a more direct test of divided demand.
Students who divide attention between class and digital distractions often learn less. Junco and Cotten (2012) found that multitasking with technology was associated with poorer academic performance. Sana, Weston, and Cepeda (2013) found that laptop multitasking harmed not only the multitasker’s learning but also the learning of nearby students who could see the screen. Gingerich and Lineweaver (2014) experimentally varied classroom texting and found poorer comprehension under texting demands. The experimental comparisons support a causal claim about the tested tasks, while the association with academic performance alone does not.
Drivers using phones suffer similar limits. Strayer and Johnston (2001) showed that cell phone conversations can impair driving performance, and Strayer, Drews, and Johnston (2003) found that hands-free conversation does not eliminate the attentional cost. The problem is not merely holding a device. It is the diversion of attention from the driving environment.
The same question can be asked of a team. A meeting devoted to quarterly revenue may leave burnout or customer confusion out of discussion, even when the relevant reports are available. This is an application of the selection problem, rather than proof that organizational attention operates like one person’s visual system.

title: 3  Attention: What Becomes Evidence?
text:
Change blindness
Change blindness shows a related problem. People often fail to notice changes in a scene when the change occurs during a brief interruption, eye movement, or visual disruption. Rensink, O’Regan, and Clark (1997) demonstrated that large changes can go unnoticed when attention is not directed to the changing feature. Simons and Levin (1998) famously showed that people giving directions to a stranger often failed to notice when the stranger was replaced by a different person during a brief interruption.






NoteWatch and test: what did your model preserve?



Open the change-blindness demonstration. Before replaying it, write down the details you believe remained stable. On the second viewing, track one category only—people, objects, colour, or position. The contrast between the two viewings shows why “look more carefully” is weaker advice than assigning a search target.


A change therefore has to be detected against what the observer encoded and retained. “Look carefully” gives less guidance than a specific search target, but every target also has a cost: it can draw attention away from something else. A second pass or an independent observer may help when the missed category matters; neither guarantees complete detection.

title: 3  Attention: What Becomes Evidence?
section: Available information is not complete information
text:
Available information is not complete information






Figure 3.2: Attention selects and prioritizes information for conscious report and deliberate use; it does not determine whether unattended information is processed at all.



Attention filters information that a sensory or measurement system first makes available. That initial sample is already partial. Jakob von Uexküll called an organism’s species-specific perceptual world its Umwelt (von Uexküll, 1934/2010). Bees can use ultraviolet-sensitive vision, pit-bearing snakes detect radiant heating, some elephant calls contain infrasonic components, and migratory birds use geomagnetic cues (Chittka & Menzel, 1992; Gracheva et al., 2010; Payne et al., 1986; Wiltschko & Wiltschko, 2005). These studies establish sensory access or behavior, not what another species experiences subjectively.






Figure 3.3: Different sensory systems make different physical cues available. The examples establish detection or behavior, not subjective experience; sensory access also does not determine which available cue receives attention.



The decision lesson is epistemic humility. People easily confuse what is available with what is complete. We can see a confident presenter but not long-run reliability, a rising price but not fundamental value, attendance but not attention, and the visible cost of prevention but not the harm it averts. Instruments, records, and models can extend perception, but they still need to be attended to and interpreted. The practical question is therefore: What consequential information is absent from the current sensory, metric, or reporting system?

title: 3  Attention: What Becomes Evidence?
text:
Designing better attention
A team cannot make every item equally prominent. It can make a deliberate choice about what should receive attention and test whether the design improves detection. Four practical moves follow from that reasoning:

Protect focus. Remove avoidable capture and reserve focused intervals for high-stakes encoding or comparison.
Assign the search. Give people distinct roles for evidence, anomalies, risks, stakeholders, assumptions, and implementation rather than expecting everyone to notice everything.
Change the question and representation. A hiring question about who impressed the committee highlights charisma; a criterion-specific evidence table highlights job-relevant performance. Dashboards and decision aids should place delayed effects, base rates, and opportunity costs beside vivid immediate outcomes.
Create a second pass. Use a diagnostic timeout, premortem, or independent review before closure, then connect feedback to the original observation or forecast (Gawande, 2009; Klein, 2007).

These moves treat attention as an environment and process problem, not merely a personal virtue.

Attention architecture: the organization chooses what can be seen
Meetings and dashboards allocate attention before any participant begins to reason. Five design choices deserve an explicit audit:



Table 3.1: Attention architecture before deliberation










Design choice
What it makes visible
Failure when unmanaged




Agenda
Which issue counts as the decision problem
The team optimizes the wrong problem.


Metrics
What is counted and compared
Important unmeasured consequences disappear.


Roles
What each person is expected and permitted to notice
Dissent, anomalies, and stakeholder harms remain silent.


Time pressure
Which cues can win quickly
Emotion and salience outrun slower evidence.


Representation
Which trade-offs are easy to inspect together
Delayed, probabilistic, or cross-functional effects remain abstract.






Suppose a project meeting begins with one question: “How do we cut costs?” The team notices supplier prices, headcount, and time spent. Customer trust, safety margin, learning value, and implementation risk become the meeting’s invisible gorilla. The question is not neutral; it defines the search target. A redesigned agenda might ask first, “Which value must this project preserve?” and then examine cost reductions alongside service, risk, learning, and implementation consequences.






NoteWatch and test: directed attention in a story



In this short scene from Focus, track how one person deliberately constructs the other person’s field of attention. After viewing, list the cues that were present, the cues that became psychologically prominent, and the decision that prominence supported. The clip is linked for analysis; no film frame is reproduced here.

Failure
Mechanism

Assign an anomaly role or run a deliberate second scan.

Change the question, representation, or speaking order.

Competing tasks interrupt encoding and compete for limited capacity.
