title: 12  Framing: When the Same Facts Become Different Decisions
text:
Ethical framing
Responsible framing preserves accurate information, shows material trade-offs, and makes room for another valid account. It should distinguish evidence from recommendation: a communicator can advocate a choice while making clear which values support it.
For numerical claims, check the event, denominator, time horizon, baseline, and comparison. For causal claims, check what is assumed about responsibility. For a proposed choice, make refusal and other feasible options visible. These checks are more useful than a claim that one preferred wording is perfectly neutral.
Framing is particularly sensitive in medicine. Patients need information in ways they can understand and use. Gigerenzer and Edwards (2003) argued that health statistics should often be presented in transparent formats such as natural frequencies rather than confusing relative risks. A treatment that reduces risk from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000 can be described as a 50% relative risk reduction or an absolute reduction of 1 in 1,000. Both are true. They do not feel the same. Ethical risk communication should include absolute risks, baselines, and comparisons.
The same care applies in management. A label such as “rightsizing” should not obscure job losses, and calling a workload a “stretch goal” does not establish that it is sustainable. Use language that lets the people affected understand the consequences and challenge the assumptions.



Table 12.1: Framing mechanisms and safeguards










Frame type
What changes
Safeguard




Attribute frame
Which side of an equivalent description is focal.
Present both logically equivalent forms.


Risky-choice frame
Whether outcomes are coded as gains or losses.
Make the reference point explicit.


Goal frame
Whether action pursues benefit or avoids cost.
Match the frame to accurate stakes and efficacy.


Question frame
Which alternatives and causes enter search.
Ask a second question from another stakeholder’s perspective.


Causal frame
Who or what appears responsible.
Test competing mechanisms before assigning blame.

title: 12  Framing: When the Same Facts Become Different Decisions
text:
Practice Lab
Take one consequential decision statement. Produce a paired-frame brief that reports gains and losses, absolute and relative quantities, final states and changes, and individual and system consequences. For each pair, mark what becomes visible and what recedes. End with the version you would show a decision-maker and explain why it preserves relevant choice rather than steering toward your preferred answer.

title: 12  Framing: When the Same Facts Become Different Decisions
text:
Take it forward
Before presenting a recommendation, write the strongest valid complementary description. Check that its denominator, horizon, and facts match the first version. If the preference changes, investigate which consequence or value the original wording made too easy to overlook.

title: 13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease
text:
Learning goals
What comes readily to mind—and what moves smoothly through it—can feel more relevant, likable, and true than the evidence warrants
A manager opens a meeting by saying, “We need to understand why the launch failed.” The group searches for mistakes, blame, and broken plans. Now change one sentence: “We need to understand what the launch taught us about the market.” The facts have not changed, but different concepts are ready to organize them.
Later, one explanation is repeated in three meetings: “Customers were not ready.” It becomes easier to retrieve, easier to say, and easier to understand. That ease can reflect genuine learning. It can also arise because the organization has repeated one story while neglecting alternatives such as poor positioning, weak onboarding, or an unreliable product.
The meeting opening is a frame: it organizes the current problem. Hearing it may also make related concepts more accessible for a later judgment, a possible priming effect. Repetition can increase processing fluency, the ease with which the explanation is handled. These mechanisms need to be distinguished before assigning a cause to a change in judgment.

13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease

title: 13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease
text:
Distinguish semantic and affective accessibility from familiarity and processing fluency.
Explain how repetition can increase liking and perceived truth without adding evidence.
Redesign a message so that clarity improves comprehension without borrowing credibility from ease.

13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease

title: 13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease
text:
Accessibility: memory prepares an answer
Human memory is not a set of isolated folders. Concepts are linked. “Doctor” is connected to nurse, hospital, illness, medicine, care, authority, and perhaps anxiety. “Negotiation” may connect to battle, compromise, money, fairness, or problem-solving, depending on experience. When one concept becomes active, related concepts become easier to retrieve.
Classic semantic-priming experiments show this basic mechanism. People recognize nurse faster after doctor than after an unrelated word because the related concept has become accessible (Meyer & Schvaneveldt, 1971). Timing and task can also recruit expectations and strategic processing, but the basic facilitation of related material is robust (Neely, 1977).
This is an efficient property of memory. If a person hears airport, it is useful for luggage, passport, gate, and delay to become ready. The problem begins when accessibility is treated as diagnosticity. A recently seen illness may be easier for a physician to diagnose even when another illness is more prevalent. A dramatic cybersecurity incident can dominate a risk meeting even when a quieter operational failure has a larger expected cost. A familiar candidate profile can come to mind as the image of leadership even when it does not predict the role’s outcomes.






Figure 13.1: An earlier cue can make a meaning more accessible, which may influence how the next input is understood. The input itself remains a separate source of evidence.



Accessibility differs from framing. A frame organizes the information in the decision itself—for example, survival rather than mortality. A prime changes the mental context from which that information is encountered—for example, a frightening medical story heard before the statistic. Accessibility also differs from a default, which changes what happens when no action is taken. Precise names matter because the mechanism identifies the correction.
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease

title: 13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease
text:
Accessible concepts interpret ambiguity
Priming matters most when the next event can support more than one interpretation. Bank can mean a financial institution or a riverbank. A short email can be efficient or rude. A supplier’s hesitation can signal rejection, capacity limits, or a request for reassurance. Accessibility gives one interpretation a head start.
Higgins, Rholes, and Jones (1977) exposed participants to words associated with positive traits such as adventurous or negative traits such as reckless. Participants later evaluated the same ambiguously described person. The accessible trait influenced whether the behavior appeared admirable or irresponsible. Srull and Wyer (1979) similarly found that accessible hostility concepts could influence later impressions of an ambiguous target.
A professional application is a hypothesis to test, not an automatic extension of the laboratory result. Discussing a previous employee’s passivity might influence how a committee interprets a careful answer; discussing reckless overconfidence might favor a different reading. To investigate, compare equivalent answers under different introductions instead of inferring priming from one impression.
The aim is not to replace every negative cue with a positive one. It is to give plausible interpretations access to the same evidence and ask which account it supports.
Accessibility can carry affect as well as meaning, and affective-priming tasks have sometimes shifted immediate evaluation in specified laboratory conditions (Fazio et al., 1986; Murphy & Zajonc, 1993). Chapters 6 and 9 distinguish feelings about an option from feelings carried into it. Here the narrower implication is order sensitivity: when an ambiguous target follows an emotional cue, use independent ratings, counterbalancing, a break, or delayed review before treating the evaluation as evidence about the target.
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease

title: 13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease
text:
Familiarity and cognitive ease
Accessibility concerns what is ready. Processing fluency concerns how easily information is perceived, understood, retrieved, or pronounced. Cognitive ease is the subjective feeling of smooth processing. A repeated statement, familiar face, clear sentence, expected image, or easily compared option can all feel fluent (Alter & Oppenheimer, 2009; Reber et al., 2004).






Figure 13.2: Repetition, clarity, familiarity, and pronounceability can alter processing ease. Depending on the task and how that feeling is attributed, ease can influence perceived truth, liking, confidence, or risk and safety judgments; it does not establish any of them.



Figure 13.2 is a teaching synthesis of several fluency literatures, not a claim that one common pathway always produces all four judgments (Alter & Oppenheimer, 2009; Reber et al., 2004). Ease is a useful metacognitive signal. A clear explanation is easier to use than a confused one. A familiar route has often worked before. A readable warning is more actionable than an unreadable one. But ease has multiple causes. A claim can be fluent because it is understood, because it fits prior belief, because its complexity has been hidden, or simply because it has been repeated. Safety inferences are especially context-specific: easy pronunciation has affected risk judgments in some tasks (Song & Schwarz, 2009), but fluency is not a general safety detector.
That ambiguity produces a common attribution error: “This is easy to process” becomes “This is true,” “safe,” “good,” or “well supported.” People rarely report the source of the judgment as font, repetition, rhyme, or familiarity. They report that the conclusion “just makes sense.”
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease

title: 13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease
section: Repetition can become liking and truth
text:
Repetition can become liking and truth
Repeated exposure can increase liking for initially neutral stimuli, a pattern known as the mere-exposure effect (Zajonc, 1968; Bornstein, 1989). Familiarity often signals that an object has been encountered without harm, so a modest preference for the familiar can be adaptive. It can also be manufactured through advertising, repeated visibility, and algorithmic exposure. The effect is not universal: repetition can create boredom or reactance, especially when the stimulus is unpleasant or exposure feels coercive.
Repetition also increases perceived truth. In the illusory-truth effect, repeated statements are later judged more truthful than new statements even when repetition adds no evidence (Hasher et al., 1977; Dechêne et al., 2010). Familiarity can outlast source memory. A person remembers having heard the claim but forgets that it came from a rumor, satire, a low-quality website, or a hypothetical example (Begg et al., 1992; Johnson et al., 1993).
Prior knowledge helps, but it does not always eliminate the effect. Fazio and colleagues (2015) found that repetition could increase perceived truth even for statements participants should have known were false. The finding does not imply helplessness. It shows why source checking and independent evidence must be separate steps rather than feelings retrieved with the claim.
A correction may need to repeat a false claim so that readers know what is being corrected. The illusory-truth effect does not imply that doing so normally backfires: experiments testing that concern found little evidence of a familiarity backfire effect (Ecker et al., 2020). Make the correction explicit, explain the error, and provide an accurate alternative account where the misconception leaves a causal gap (Lewandowsky et al., 2012).
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease

title: 13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease
text:
Clarity without borrowed credibility
Fluency changes more than truth and liking. Easy-to-pronounce names have sometimes been judged less risky, rhyming aphorisms more accurate, and unnecessarily complex prose less intelligent (McGlone & Tofighbakhsh, 2000; Oppenheimer, 2006; Song & Schwarz, 2009). These effects should not become recipes for manipulation. They show that presentation can alter evaluation when substantive evidence is weak or difficult to access.
The right lesson is double-sided. Improve clarity because comprehension is a prerequisite for informed choice. Define terms, organize comparisons, use readable text, express risk in natural frequencies where helpful, and remove unnecessary jargon. Do not treat clarity as validation. A fluent slogan can hide an omitted trade-off, a smooth speaker can carry weak evidence, and an attractive chart can make an unsupported claim feel complete.
Difficulty is equally ambiguous. A challenging comparison, retrieval test, premortem, or requirement to state a rival model can create useful effort. A blurry slide, dense disclosure, confusing cancellation path, or unfamiliar acronym usually creates strain without insight. Some early work suggested that perceptual disfluency could reduce intuitive errors, but results are not a general license to make information hard to read (Alter et al., 2007; Eitel & Kühl, 2016).
Use a simple test: Does the difficulty expose the structure the reader must understand, or does it obstruct access to that structure? Productive difficulty asks for a meaningful judgment. Pointless strain taxes the reader before judgment can begin.
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease

title: 13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease
text:
The risk of the familiar
Familiarity can be a valid cue. A colleague who has repeatedly kept commitments deserves more trust than a stranger with no record. A route that has worked through many conditions is informative. A supplier’s history can reduce uncertainty. The mistake is not using familiarity; it is failing to ask what produced it and whether the environment has changed.
Organizations often confuse the comfort of an old system with evidence of its quality. A familiar process has low learning cost, known workarounds, and an established language. A new process feels slower because people must build skill. Early disfluency can therefore be mistaken for failure. The relevant comparison is not the old system at mature fluency against the new system on its first day. It is performance after a fair learning period, including error, effort, welfare, and adaptability.
The reverse error is equally possible. Leaders sometimes dismiss every objection as “resistance to change.” A new system may create genuine burden, shift power, hide work, or solve the wrong problem. Improvement during a fair trial is consistent with a learning cost, but does not identify familiarity as the sole cause. Changes in training, support, or the system itself may contribute.
Run a familiarity audit with four questions:

What repeated experience makes this option feel safe or true?
Did that experience provide outcome feedback, or only repeated exposure?
Has the environment changed enough to break the learned relationship?
What comparison after a fair trial would separate reliability from mere familiarity?

This audit applies to a trusted supplier, a standard interview, an investment in the employer’s industry, a familiar policy slogan, or an inherited meeting routine. Familiarity is evidence when it summarizes relevant feedback. It is inertia when exposure has replaced evaluation.
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease

title: 13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease
text:
Make accurate information fluent
A useful message makes its central claim memorable without stripping away the conditions that make it true. Lead with the conclusion, show the comparison and uncertainty, and provide the source for readers who need to examine it.
For a fictional pilot, “completion rose from 62 to 74 percent over three months; the comparison was not randomized” is more informative than “the pilot worked.” Both the result and its limit can travel with the sentence. These invented numbers illustrate a reporting format; they are not a study result.
Teaching benefits from stable terms for recurring distinctions, provided each return does new work. A reminder should help readers solve the next problem, rather than restate an entire previous explanation.
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease

title: 13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease
text:
Evidence Boundary



Table 13.1: Evidence tiers for accessibility and ease










Claim
Evidential position
Responsible interpretation




Semantic and perceptual accessibility
Robust across many laboratory paradigms
Recent activation can change processing speed and interpretation.


Affective accessibility
Supported in specified tasks
Prior valence can tilt immediate evaluation; effects depend on task and context.


Repetition, familiarity, and illusory truth
Substantial, replicated literatures
Familiarity can influence liking and truth judgments without adding evidence.


Large automatic behavioral effects from subtle social primes
Many prominent claims are contested or difficult to replicate
Do not describe priming as mind control or assume a portable effect size.


Disfluency as debiasing
Mixed and mechanism-dependent
Difficulty helps only when it directs effort to relevant reasoning.






The boundary is conceptual as well as empirical. A prime can make an idea accessible without producing behavior. A fluent claim can feel true without changing action. An observed action does not reveal which pathway operated. Motivation, incentives, constraints, identity, and competing cues can dominate or reverse the effect. The responsible claim specifies the cue, pathway, outcome, population, and comparison.






CautionEvidence Boundary: concealed cues are not mind control




Masked-priming studies briefly present cues while limiting conscious report, allowing narrow tests of processing without ordinary awareness (Forster & Davis, 1984; Marcel, 1983). They do not show that hidden messages can implant complex goals, override preferences, or force purchases. The practical boundary is ethical as well as empirical: a visible reminder that supports a person’s stated goal is different from concealed influence designed to defeat reflection.
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease

title: 13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease
text:
Designing an evidence-aligned message
Start with a short workplace message: “The new review system is simple, fair, and proven.” It is fluent, but each adjective hides a claim. The following fictional redesign illustrates what a message would need to substantiate; its pilot claims are invented for the exercise:

The new review system uses the same four job-relevant criteria for every employee. In a three-month pilot, managers completed reviews faster and employee understanding improved; disagreement about ratings did not disappear. The pilot report and appeal process are linked here. We will review error patterns after the first cycle.

The revision is still readable. It identifies a procedure, reported outcomes, a limit, and a review route. A real message would also need the actual comparison and evidence supporting those claims. Clarity carries the evidence rather than substituting for it.
For any important message, run four checks:

Accessibility: Which interpretation does the opening make ready, and which plausible rival recedes?
Source: Is the claim familiar because independent evidence supports it or because one source repeated it?
Ease: Does the design clarify the underlying structure or hide uncertainty and trade-offs?
Agency: Would the influence remain defensible if the audience understood how it worked and could question or refuse it?

The ethical objective is not a neutral environment—no environment is neutral. It is an environment in which task-relevant meanings are accessible, accurate information is easy to use, counterevidence can enter, and the reader does not have to confuse fluency with truth.

13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease

title: 13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease
text:
Practice Lab
Select one message used in a meeting, course, website, policy, or campaign. Produce a before-and-after redesign. Annotate the original for concepts made accessible, sources of familiarity, and sources of processing ease or strain. The revision must preserve every substantive qualification while improving clarity. Add one independent source check, one rival interpretation, and one measure that would reveal whether comprehension improved without increasing unwarranted belief.

13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease

title: 13  Accessibility, Familiarity, and Ease
text:
Take it forward
At the next meeting, ask who first concluded that “customers were not ready” and what evidence supported it. Repetition may have made the phrase easier to say without making it better supported. Keep the explanation readable, but let a documented comparison decide how much confidence it deserves.

title: 14  Base Rates, Conditional Probability, and Bayesian Updating
text:
Learning goals
A plausible story becomes a probability only after the event, denominator, and competing explanations are specified
A candidate passes a screening test that is described as “80 percent accurate.” How confident should the hiring committee be that the candidate will meet the performance standard? The number sounds decisive, but it does not yet answer the question. Eighty percent of what? How common are strong performers in the applicant pool? How often does the screen pass a weaker candidate? Was the test validated on a comparable population and outcome?
The committee’s target is \(P(\text{strong performance}\mid\text{positive screen})\). A report may instead provide \(P(\text{positive screen}\mid\text{strong performance})\). Those quantities reverse the conditioning and use different denominators. The distinction is the spine of this chapter: before calculating, specify the event, comparison set, and process that produced the evidence.

title: 14  Base Rates, Conditional Probability, and Bayesian Updating
section: Worked update: the same screen in two applicant pools
text:
Worked update: the same screen in two applicant pools
Return to the hiring screen. Suppose, for teaching purposes, that 20% of applicants in a broad pool would meet a clearly defined performance standard, the screen passes 80% of those future strong performers, and it also passes 30% of the others. Among 10,000 applicants:

2,000 would meet the standard; 1,600 pass the screen.
8,000 would not; 2,400 nevertheless pass.
Of 4,000 positive screens, 1,600 are true positives.

Under those assumptions, \(P(\text{strong performance}\mid\text{positive screen})=1{,}600/4{,}000=0.40\). The screen can be meaningfully informative—it raises the probability from 20% to 40%—without making a positive result decisive.
Now place the same screen in a carefully preselected pool where 50% would meet the standard. If its sensitivity and false-positive rate transport unchanged, then among 10,000 applicants it produces 4,000 true positives and 1,500 false positives, so the posterior is about 72.7%. Nothing about the assumed test characteristics changed; the starting population did. This is why an “80% sensitivity” claim cannot travel on its own: the receiving population and the transportability of both error rates are part of its meaning.
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
14  Base Rates, Conditional Probability, and Bayesian Updating

title: 14  Base Rates, Conditional Probability, and Bayesian Updating
text:
Probability begins with a model
The screen example works by dividing a common population into cases. Probability notation makes the same logic available for other decisions. A sample space \(\Omega\) lists the elementary outcomes allowed by a model. An event \(A\) is a subset of those outcomes. A probability measure assigns numbers satisfying
\[
0\le P(A)\le 1, \qquad P(\Omega)=1,
\]
and adds probabilities for mutually exclusive events. The notation cannot choose a good model for us. Calling a coin fair, successive observations independent, or an applicant pool comparable to the validation sample are substantive assumptions.

Complement: preserve the event boundary
If \(A^c\) means “not \(A\),” then
\[
P(A^c)=1-P(A).
\]
If a project has a 0.70 probability of finishing by Friday, it has a 0.30 probability of not finishing by Friday under the same model. “Not finished by Friday” is not the same event as “the project fails.” A complement works only when the time horizon and outcome definition remain fixed.


AND: use the conditional branch
For events \(A\) and \(B\),
\[
P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B\mid A).
\]
If the events are independent, \(P(B\mid A)=P(B)\). Independence is not the same as mutual exclusivity. Rain and traffic delay can occur together and may be dependent. Two cards drawn without replacement are dependent because the first draw changes the deck.


OR: restore the overlap
For “\(A\) or \(B\) or both,”
\[
P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B).
\]
The subtraction prevents double counting. A project can be delayed by a supplier problem, a software problem, or both. Adding the separate probabilities as though the routes were disjoint exaggerates total risk; considering only the most vivid route understates it.
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
14  Base Rates, Conditional Probability, and Bayesian Updating

title: 14  Base Rates, Conditional Probability, and Bayesian Updating
text:
Conditional direction matters
Provided \(P(B)>0\),
\[
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}.
\]
“How often does the test turn positive among people with the condition?” is not “How often do people with a positive test have the condition?” The first conditions on the condition; the second conditions on the positive tests.
The same reversal appears in court. A one-in-a-million probability of a DNA profile among unrelated people is not a one-in-a-million probability that a matched defendant is innocent. The latter depends on how the suspect was selected, how many people were compared, laboratory error, relatedness, the prior probability of different sources, and the rest of the case (Thompson & Schumann, 1987).
Conditional probability also makes independence explicit. Events are independent when learning one does not change the probability of the other. Zero correlation is not generally equivalent to independence: it rules out one linear relationship, not every probabilistic dependence.
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
14  Base Rates, Conditional Probability, and Bayesian Updating

title: 14  Base Rates, Conditional Probability, and Bayesian Updating
text:
Bayes’ rule restores the alternatives
If \(A\) and \(A^c\) partition the cases, total probability rebuilds the denominator:
\[
P(B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)+P(B\mid A^c)P(A^c).
\]
Bayes’ rule then reverses the conditioning without reversing the evidence:
\[
P(A\mid B)=
\frac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}
{P(B\mid A)P(A)+P(B\mid A^c)P(A^c)}.
\]
The prior \(P(A)\) gives the starting probability, which is a prevalence in this screening example. The likelihood \(P(B\mid A)\) asks how probable the evidence would be if \(A\) held. The competing likelihood \(P(B\mid A^c)\) asks how often the same evidence appears without \(A\). The posterior is the probability after incorporating the evidence (Bayes, 1763).
Bayes’ rule cannot rescue a poor hypothesis set. Missing alternatives, selected samples, changing environments, weak measurements, and uncertain parameters remain problems. A posterior is precise only conditional on the model and inputs that produced it.
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
14  Base Rates, Conditional Probability, and Bayesian Updating

title: 14  Base Rates, Conditional Probability, and Bayesian Updating
text:
Natural frequencies make Bayes visible
For a second hypothetical example, suppose 1 percent of a population has a disease. A test is positive for 90 percent of people who have it and for 9 percent of people who do not. A person tests positive. The tempting answer is 90 percent, but that is \(P(+\mid D)\) rather than \(P(D\mid +)\).
Imagine 10,000 people:

100 have the disease; 90 test positive.
9,900 do not; 891 test positive.
Of 981 positive tests, 90 are true positives.

Therefore,
\[
P(D\mid +)=\frac{90}{90+891}=\frac{90}{981}\approx 0.0917.
\]






Figure 14.1: A positive result can come from either group. In this hypothetical population, the much larger group without disease supplies most of the positive tests.



Natural frequencies preserve the nested sets and denominator, often making Bayesian reasoning more transparent than isolated percentages (Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, 1995). They do not solve measurement error or transportability; they make the assumed structure visible.
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
14  Base Rates, Conditional Probability, and Bayesian Updating

title: 14  Base Rates, Conditional Probability, and Bayesian Updating
text:
Reference classes are judgment calls
A base rate is only as useful as its reference class. Should a start-up be compared with all new firms, firms in the same sector, firms at the same funding stage, or firms with similarly experienced founders? A narrow class may be more relevant but noisier. A broad class is more stable but less tailored.
Base-rate neglect is more likely when individuating detail feels causal and the statistic feels incidental (Bar-Hillel, 1980). The outside view therefore begins with comparable cases before explaining why the focal case differs (Kahneman & Lovallo, 1993). A defensible analysis reports several nested classes, shows whether the conclusion changes, and identifies which differences are genuinely diagnostic. “This case is unique” is a hypothesis, not a denominator.
Return to hiring. The base rate should concern future performance under the organization’s role, support, and criterion—not an undefined pool of “talent.” The screen’s sensitivity and false-positive rate must come from a comparable applicant population. If the criterion rewards manager similarity rather than job output, the posterior can be mathematically correct and substantively wrong.







NoteResearch Lens: conjunction, disjunction, and dilution



The resemblance chapter showed why a coherent story can feel probable. Probability supplies a non-negotiable set relation:
\[
P(A\cap B)\le P(A), \qquad P(A\cup B)\ge P(A).
\]
Adding a condition makes the event a subset. “A bank teller active in a social movement” cannot be more probable than “a bank teller,” however well the detail matches the description (Tversky & Kahneman, 1983). By contrast, adding alternative routes expands a union. The probability that a project is delayed by at least one of several causes cannot be smaller than the probability of any single route, though overlaps must be handled rather than simply added.
More detail is not always more information. Weakly diagnostic detail can dilute attention to stronger evidence. Sivanathan and Kakkar (2017) found that adding minor side effects to serious drug side effects could reduce perceived overall severity. The ethical response is not to hide minor effects. It is to group evidence by severity, probability, and decision relevance so completeness does not destroy structure.








TipCheck your denominator



For each prompt, write the target conditional before answering.

Seventy percent of successful trainees used a practice platform. What additional quantities are needed to estimate the probability of success among platform users?
Ten percent of projects suffer supplier delay and 12% suffer software delay. What must be known before adding the percentages?
A screen validated in experienced applicants is applied to entry-level applicants. Which part of the Bayesian model may no longer transport?

A complete answer names the conditioning event, denominator, relevant overlap or alternative, and at least one assumption about how the evidence was generated.

title: 14  Base Rates, Conditional Probability, and Bayesian Updating
text:
Practice Lab
Take one positive test, screening result, warning signal, or performance indicator. Produce a one-page Bayesian audit using a population of 10,000. State the target conditional probability, choose and defend two plausible reference classes, show true positives and false positives under each, and identify one omitted alternative or measurement problem. The observable output is the two natural-frequency trees and a decision rule that states what action changes at which posterior range.

title: 14  Base Rates, Conditional Probability, and Bayesian Updating
text:
Take it forward
The committee can now replace “the screen is 80 percent accurate” with a meaningful account: who was screened, how often each kind of applicant passed, and what a positive result implies in this pool. Before using a striking percentage, identify its denominator and the alternative route by which the same evidence could appear.

title: 15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration
text:
Learning goals
A pattern becomes evidence only after we ask how much variation the process could produce on its own
A branch manager arrives after the worst quarter in the company’s history. Three months later, sales have recovered and headquarters praises the rescue. Perhaps the manager changed something that mattered. But a branch selected because it had an exceptionally bad quarter may also improve when temporary setbacks pass. How much of the recovery should count as evidence of good management?
The same question appears in smaller decisions: whether two successful hires validate an interview method, whether a winning streak reveals skill, or whether a missed deadline was foreseeable. We need to learn what variation alone can produce before deciding what a striking result means.

title: 15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration
text:
Explain why small samples, streaks, and clusters can look more informative than they are.
Diagnose regression to the mean without dismissing real change or causal effects.
Distinguish overestimation, overplacement, and overprecision, then record and score forecasts for calibration and resolution.

15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration

title: 15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration
text:
Which sequence looks random?
A fair coin will be tossed six times. Rank these exact sequences from most to least likely:

H H H H H H
H H H T T T
H T H T H T

The first looks designed, while the third looks comfortably random. Yet every specified sequence has probability
\[
\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^6=\frac{1}{64}.
\]
The intuition answers a different question: Which sequence resembles my prototype of randomness? Alternation looks random; a run looks meaningful. Probability asks which event was specified before the tosses and how many elementary outcomes it contains.
The distinction also explains why “three heads and three tails in any order” is more likely than “all heads or all tails.” The first category contains \(\binom{6}{3}=20\) exact sequences; the second contains two. Each exact outcome remains equally likely. Categories differ because they collect different numbers of outcomes.
Randomness is clumpier than intuition expects. When many sequences, people, schools, funds, products, or locations are observed, some will display striking runs and clusters even when the underlying process is unchanged. A pattern invites explanation; a statistical model asks how surprising that pattern was given all the opportunities for one to appear.
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration

title: 15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration
text:
Small samples swing widely
People often expect a small sample to resemble its population too closely, a tendency Tversky and Kahneman (1971) called belief in the law of small numbers. After three successful hires, an interview panel may feel it has found a reliable method. Yet three outcomes can change dramatically with the next appointment, especially if applicants and jobs vary. The question is how much confidence that sample can support.
For an independent Bernoulli event with probability \(p\), the standard error of the sample proportion is
\[
SE(\hat p)=\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}.
\]
When \(p=0.5\), the standard error is about 0.158 for \(n=10\) and 0.050 for \(n=100\). The population did not become steadier; the estimate did. Small samples produce more extreme proportions because each observation carries more weight.
Selection magnifies the problem. The branch reached headquarters’ agenda because its quarter was unusually bad, just as a fund enters a performance ranking because its returns were unusually good. In both cases, temporary variation has helped select the evidence we are about to explain.
The correction is not “wait for a large sample” in every setting. Some decisions cannot wait and some populations are inherently small. Report uncertainty, pool comparable evidence cautiously, use hierarchical or shrinkage estimates where appropriate, and identify which conclusion depends on one or two observations. A small sample can provide information; it cannot provide the stability of a large one by force of narrative.
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration

title: 15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration
text:
Streaks require a process model
After five reds at roulette, black may feel due. Under independent fair spins, it is not. The wheel has no memory. The gambler’s fallacy treats short-run balancing as a physical correction because the sequence is expected to look representative quickly (Clotfelter & Cook, 1993).
The opposite intuition appears after success: a basketball player who has made several shots seems more likely to make the next. That hot-hand belief could misread random clustering, or it could reflect genuine state dependence through confidence, fatigue, strategy, defense, learning, or shot selection.
Gilovich, Vallone, and Tversky (1985) famously argued that observers saw more hot-hand dependence than basketball data supported. Later work identified a finite-sample bias in common comparisons of success following success and showed that some earlier tests understated streakiness (Miller & Sanjurjo, 2018). The correction is not to replace “hot hands are illusions” with “hot hands are real.” It is to specify and test the process:

What would independent outcomes produce?
Was the streak pattern chosen before or after examining the data?
Did opportunities, difficulty, strategy, or selection change during the run?
Does the pattern replicate with a statistic suited to the sampling process?
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration

title: 15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration
section: Clusters and the search for causes
text:
Clusters and the search for causes
Searching more units, periods, or subgroups gives chance more opportunities to produce an impressive cluster (Nickerson, 2002).
This does not make clusters meaningless. A disease cluster may reveal a local exposure; a manufacturing cluster may reveal a faulty machine; a set of related forecast errors may reveal a missing variable. The test needs a denominator that includes the number of units, periods, outcomes, subgroups, and models searched. It also needs a mechanism or independent replication that was not selected by the same extreme pattern.
A useful sequence is:
Describe → compare with chance → specify a mechanism → predict new observations → replicate.
Stopping after description rewards the most surprising pattern. Jumping directly to a favored mechanism invites confirmation. A new prediction forces the proposed cause to do work outside the data that suggested it.
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration

title: 15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration
text:
Regression to the mean
Suppose observed performance is
\[
Y=\theta+\varepsilon,
\]
where \(\theta\) is a persistent component and \(\varepsilon\) is temporary noise. Selecting an unusually high \(Y\) selects cases with high persistent ability, favorable noise, or both. When the next noise term is less extreme, performance tends to move toward average even if the underlying ability does not change.
For two standardized measures with correlation \(r\), a simple linear prediction is
\[
\widehat z_2=r z_1.
\]
If a measure two standard deviations above average has test–retest correlation \(r=0.40\), the best linear prediction under that model is 0.8 standard deviations above average. The predicted person remains above average; the extreme observation is shrunk because part of it was unreliable.
The flight-instructor example illustrates the attribution trap. Praise follows unusually good performance and criticism follows unusually poor performance. The next attempt often looks worse after praise and better after criticism. An instructor may conclude that criticism improves performance and praise harms it, although part of both movements reflects regression (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973).
Regression does not show that an intervention had no effect. It shows why before–after change among units selected for extreme outcomes does not identify the effect by itself. Use comparison groups, repeated pre-periods, credible counterfactuals, and uncertainty intervals. A real treatment effect and regression can occur together.






Figure 15.1: A fixed-seed teaching simulation draws 50 observations from \(z_1,\varepsilon\sim N(0,1)\) and \(z_2=0.40z_1+\sqrt{0.84}\varepsilon\) (seed 50273; displayed sample \(r\approx0.40\)). The model’s conditional mean is \(E[z_2\mid z_1]=0.40z_1\): \(z_1=+2\) predicts \(z_2=+0.8\). Regression describes conditional averages; an individual outcome need not reverse, and before–after movement does not identify an intervention effect.



Return to the branch manager. The recovery is real, but attributing all of it to the rescue plan would confuse improvement with evidence of its cause. Compare the branch with similarly troubled branches, examine several earlier periods, and identify which changes the manager actually introduced. That makes room for a managerial effect while accounting for the recovery that might have happened anyway.
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration

title: 15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration
text:
Confidence must face a distribution
Confidence is not one quantity. Moore and Healy (2008) distinguish three patterns:

Overestimation: believing one’s performance or ability is better than it is.
Overplacement: believing one ranks above other people.
Overprecision: expressing more certainty than the evidence supports.

Each requires a different comparison, as Table 15.1 shows. Asking a confident person to “think harder” supplies none of them.
The familiar Dunning–Kruger pattern requires the same discipline. Kruger and Dunning (1999) reported larger self-assessment errors among lower performers in several tasks and proposed that some skills needed for good performance also help people recognize good performance. But a quartile plot alone does not identify that mechanism. Measurement error, regression to the mean, scale boundaries, task difficulty, and general self-enhancement can produce part of the pattern; later work suggests that any distinctive metacognitive component may be smaller and more task-specific than the popular slogan implies (Gignac & Zajenkowski, 2020). Measure performance and confidence separately. Do not diagnose a person’s metacognition from one rank comparison.
The planning fallacy is a related forecast error: people often construct an inside-view story of the steps that should occur while underweighting delays observed in similar projects (Buehler et al., 1994; Kahneman & Tversky, 1979). It can produce optimistic point estimates, intervals that are too narrow, or both. The outside view begins with a reference class and then adjusts only for differences that are genuinely predictive (Kahneman & Lovallo, 1993; Lovallo & Kahneman, 2003).
Suppose a city team proposes an 18-month rail-project schedule. Before hearing why this project is special, obtain the completion-time distribution for comparable projects. Then require each departure from that range to name a causal difference and evidence that the difference changed outcomes elsewhere. The inside view remains useful because it reveals mechanisms and dependencies; the outside view prevents an elegant plan from erasing how projects actually unfold.



Table 15.1: Different confidence problems require different feedback










Confidence problem
Comparison required
Observable correction




Overestimation
Forecast versus measured performance
Record the estimate and outcome on the same scale.


Overplacement
Self versus a defined comparison distribution
Specify the population and criterion before ranking.


Overprecision
Stated interval or probability versus repeated coverage
Widen or update ranges when outcomes fall outside too often.


Planning fallacy
Inside plan versus comparable completed cases
Start from the reference-class distribution; justify each adjustment.












NoteResearch Lens: information protocols change probability puzzles





Monty Hall and the two-child problem are useful only when the information protocol is explicit. In the standard Monty Hall protocol, a knowledgeable host always reveals a goat behind an unchosen door and always offers a switch; if either goat door could be opened, assume the host chooses between them uniformly at random. Switching then wins with probability \(2/3\) (Selvin, 1975). If the host instead opens doors or offers a switch selectively, the evidence changes. Likewise, “at least one child is a boy,” “the older child is a boy,” and a parent volunteering “I have a boy” arise from different sampling rules. The transferable question is not the puzzle answer but: How was this information generated?






Figure 15.2: The standard Monty Hall protocol keeps the information-generating rule visible. The initial choice has probability one-third, the two unchosen doors carry two-thirds together, and a knowledgeable host must reveal a goat before offering a switch, using a random tie-break when either goat door is available. The remaining unchosen door retains the two-thirds branch; a different host rule can change the inference.
crumbs: Part II. Judgment Under Uncertainty
15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration

title: 15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration
text:
Calibration makes confidence answerable
A forecaster is calibrated when events assigned 70 percent occur about 70 percent of the time, events assigned 20 percent occur about 20 percent of the time, and so forth. Calibration is a property of repeated forecasts, not one dramatic success.
Accuracy also requires resolution or discrimination. A forecaster who assigns 50 percent to everything may be calibrated in a balanced environment but contributes little separation. Useful forecasts move away from the base rate when evidence warrants it and remain calibrated across those movements.
For a binary event with forecast \(p\) and outcome \(o\in\{0,1\}\), the Brier score is
\[
BS=(p-o)^2.
\]
Lower is better. A 0.70 forecast scores 0.09 if the event occurs and 0.49 if it does not. Across forecasts, average the scores. The scoring convention for multicategory forecasts must be stated because scales can differ (Brier, 1950; Murphy, 1973).
Forecasting research suggests that performance can improve through habits rather than clairvoyance: define the event precisely, start from reference classes, decompose the problem, update in small increments, seek disconfirming information, aggregate independent views, and obtain feedback (Mellers et al., 2014). Numeric probabilities also reveal false agreement. Two colleagues may both say “likely” while one means 55 percent and the other 90 percent.



Table 15.2: A minimal forecast ledger









Field
Example




Event and resolution rule
“The supplier passes acceptance testing by 30 September, documented by a signed report.”


Probability and date
0.65 on 1 June


Reference classes
Comparable suppliers; this supplier’s last ten deliveries


Main evidence
Prototype passed; staffing remains incomplete


Alternative pathways
Certification, integration, staffing, or scope delay


Update triggers
Test failure, staff appointment, scope change


Outcome and score
Enter after resolution; preserve the original forecast






The record matters because memory rounds forecasts toward outcomes. “We knew it might fail” can describe almost any vague prior statement. A dated number, event definition, and update rule allow learning to survive hindsight.

title: 15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration
section: From a project story to a forecast system
text:
From a project story to a forecast system
A project team assigns 15 percent to supplier delay, 10 percent to regulatory delay, and 20 percent to software delay. Adding them gives 45 percent only if the events are mutually exclusive. They are not: supplier delay can cause software delay, and regulatory change can affect both.
The team should draw an event tree or build a small simulation with conditional pathways, then compare the combined estimate with the empirical delay rate for similar projects. The inside model explains mechanisms; the outside view checks whether the combined answer is plausible. If the inside model gives 18 percent while comparable projects miss the date 55 percent of the time, the discrepancy is evidence. It requires investigation, not automatic rejection of the base rate.
Record one forecast for the final date and separate forecasts for leading mechanisms. Update when relevant evidence arrives, including an unexpected development; record why the new information changes the forecast. After resolution, score the forecasts and examine whether errors came from the base rate, dependence assumptions, missing pathways, or unjustified confidence. One project cannot establish calibration, but it can begin the ledger.






CautionEvidence Boundary



An unusual pattern is not automatically noise, and regression is not an explanation for every reversal. Chance models need justified assumptions; genuine dependence and causal change require tests that can distinguish them from selection and ordinary variation.

title: 15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration
text:
Practice Lab
Choose one event that will resolve within four weeks. Produce a complete forecast ledger: an unambiguous event and resolution source, a numerical probability, two reference classes, an inside-view mechanism, one argument against, and a dated update trigger. For a quantity such as cost or completion time, add the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles and explain every adjustment away from the outside-view distribution. When the date arrives, enter the outcome and score without revising the original entry. The observable output is the preserved ledger plus a diagnosis of whether any error came from sampling, model, or confidence.

title: 15  Samples, Randomness, Regression, and Calibration
text:
Take it forward
The next time a spectacular success or failure reaches the meeting agenda, ask what led that case to be selected and what a comparable case would be expected to do next. Then write down the prediction before the next quarter arrives. That simple record gives the organization a chance to learn something more durable than a story about its latest result.

title: Part III. Risk, Time, and Well-Being
text:
Questions to carry forward
Imagine choosing between a secure job and a new venture. A forecast can help you estimate the chance of success, but it cannot decide how much security, independence, or possible regret matters to you. Even after the choice, everyday spending and routines will influence what the decision becomes.
This part connects uncertain outcomes to the lives in which they occur. It starts with the comparison of risky options and shows why a gain or loss depends partly on the point from which it is judged. It then asks how learning from experience differs from reading probabilities, why future plans can lose their appeal when action is due, and how mental accounts shape the use of money.
The habit chapter brings these questions into an ordinary afternoon, when a student keeps checking his phone while trying to write. The final chapter widens the lens: a decision that looks attractive in advance may contribute differently to daily experience, satisfaction, relationships, and meaning.
Many of those consequences depend on other people. Part IV examines choices whose outcomes are shaped by what others believe, value, and do.

text:
Learning goals
Probability describes what may happen. Choice still requires a theory of what those outcomes mean to the decision-maker.
A small organization receives a quote for cyber insurance. The premium seems expensive beside the average annual loss in its spreadsheet, and the finance team considers declining it. Then someone asks what would happen if an attack arrived next month: could the organization restore its systems, keep paying staff, and continue serving clients? An average loss and an affordable loss are different things.

title: 16  Risky Decision-Making: A Probability Is Not Yet a Feeling
section: Opening puzzle: the same expected value, a different choice
text:
Opening puzzle: the same expected value, a different choice
Choose between:

Option S: €50 for certain.
Option G: a 50% chance of €100 and a 50% chance of €0.

Both have expected monetary value €50. Many people nevertheless choose the sure €50. Now imagine that the gamble determines whether you can pay rent. The sure amount may become much more attractive. Imagine instead that both amounts are entertainment money and the gamble itself is enjoyable. The gamble may become more attractive.
Expected money leaves out what the money would make possible. To evaluate the insurance quote, we need a way to express that difference.

title: 16  Risky Decision-Making: A Probability Is Not Yet a Feeling
text:
Risk, uncertainty, and ambiguity
In a textbook lottery, outcomes and probabilities are specified: a coin gives a 50% chance of each result. This is risk in the narrow decision-theory sense. In many real decisions, the probabilities are estimated, disputed, or partly unknown. This broader uncertainty includes model error, missing outcomes, changing environments, and ambiguous evidence.
Ambiguity describes uncertainty about the probability model itself. A jar with a known 30 red and 60 black balls is risky; a jar with 30 red and 60 balls of unknown black–yellow composition introduces ambiguity. A precise-looking spreadsheet can still be ambiguous if the probability estimates rest on one historical period or an untested causal model.
The categories are useful, but the boundary is not natural law. Even “known” probabilities depend on a trusted randomization mechanism, and real-world risks often combine sampling variation with model uncertainty.

title: 16  Risky Decision-Making: A Probability Is Not Yet a Feeling
text:
Expected value: the monetary benchmark
For outcomes \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) with probabilities \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\), expected monetary value is
\[
EV(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i x_i.
\]
Expected value is a probability-weighted average, not the outcome most likely to occur and not a guarantee. A 1% chance of €10,000 and a 99% chance of zero has expected value €100, although €100 is never paid.
Expected value is powerful when outcomes are repeatable, stakes are small relative to resources, and money is the relevant consequence. A casino can rely on a small expected advantage across millions of plays. One household facing one chance of ruin cannot automatically treat the same average as adequate.
The benchmark also exposes missing costs. A gamble that pays €100 with probability one-half and zero otherwise does not have expected net value €50 if entry costs €60. The expected net value is −€10.

title: 16  Risky Decision-Making: A Probability Is Not Yet a Feeling
section: Expected utility: value over final consequences
text:
Expected utility: value over final consequences
Expected utility theory evaluates a lottery over final wealth or consequences:
\[
EU(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i u(W+x_i),
\]
where \(W\) is initial wealth and \(u(\cdot)\) represents preferences over final wealth. The theory does not say that people consciously calculate a utility function. It states conditions under which consistent choices can be represented as if they maximize expected utility (von Neumann & Morgenstern, 1944).
The independence axiom is central. If lottery \(A\) is preferred to lottery \(B\), mixing both with the same third lottery \(C\) in the same proportion should preserve the ranking. Common components should cancel. The Allais pattern below shows why this attractive requirement is descriptively fragile.

Curvature and attitudes toward a mean-preserving risk

A linear utility function implies risk neutrality: utility of the expected value equals expected utility.
A concave utility function implies weak risk aversion: \(u(E[X])\geq E[u(X)]\). The inequality is strict for a nondegenerate lottery when utility is strictly concave over its outcomes.
A convex utility function implies weak risk seeking over that range: \(u(E[X])\leq E[u(X)]\), with a strict inequality under the corresponding strict-convexity conditions.

Curvature is local. A function can be concave over one wealth range and different elsewhere. Observing one safe choice does not establish a stable trait across stakes, domains, or reference points.






Figure 16.1: A 50–50 lottery paying 0 or 100 has expected value 50. Under the illustrative utility function u(x)=square root of x, expected utility is 5, the certainty equivalent is 25, and the risk premium is 25. A companion panel separates known risk from ambiguous probabilities and reminds the reader to evaluate process before outcome.





Certainty equivalents and risk premia
For payoff changes \(x_i\) around initial wealth \(W\), the certainty-equivalent payoff \(c\) solves
\[
u(W+c)=\sum_i p_i u(W+x_i).
\]
The risk premium is
\[
\pi=E[x]-c.
\]
For the compact opening example, normalize initial wealth to zero and treat 0 and 100 as final-wealth outcomes. Let \(u(w)=\sqrt{w}\). Then
\[
EU=0.5\sqrt{0}+0.5\sqrt{100}=5.
\]
Because \(\sqrt{25}=5\), the certainty-equivalent final wealth is 25. Expected final wealth is 50, so the risk premium is 25. Under this utility function and normalization, the decision-maker is indifferent between the lottery and final wealth of 25 for certain.
This is an illustration, not an estimate of anyone’s utility. If the outcomes are changes around wealth, then wealth must enter the calculation. Treating gains and losses as if utility were defined only over the change can produce different predictions—the issue that motivates prospect theory in the next chapter.


Insurance: expected loss is not the whole premium
Insurance exchanges an uncertain loss for a certain premium. Under concave utility, a person may pay more than the actuarially fair expected loss to remove variability. The difference can reflect a risk premium, but real insurance decisions also include insurer costs, exclusions, deductibles, counterparty risk, liquidity, legal requirements, and protection against ruin.
The key comparison is not “premium versus expected loss” alone. It is final wealth and feasible action in each state. Insurance can be valuable because a rare loss would be unaffordable even when its expected amount is modest.


Why do people buy insurance and lottery tickets?
A globally concave utility function over money cannot explain paying for an unfavorable monetary gamble. Yet a lottery ticket may also buy entertainment and anticipation, while insurance protects against an unaffordable loss. Separate mental accounts, misunderstanding, or extra weight on tiny probabilities offer other explanations. Buying both products challenges a simple account of monetary risk preference without identifying which alternative is right.

title: 16  Risky Decision-Making: A Probability Is Not Yet a Feeling
section: The Allais pattern: certainty does not cancel cleanly
text:
The Allais pattern: certainty does not cancel cleanly
Consider two pairs of choices, with monetary units scaled to “millions.”
Pair 1

\(A\): 1 for certain.
\(B\): 89% chance of 1, 10% chance of 5, and 1% chance of 0.

Pair 2

\(C\): 11% chance of 1 and 89% chance of 0.
\(D\): 10% chance of 5 and 90% chance of 0.

Many people prefer \(A\) to \(B\) but \(D\) to \(C\) (Allais, 1953). In Pair 1, certainty is attractive. In Pair 2, neither option is certain, so the larger prize becomes attractive.
Under expected utility and independence, the pattern is inconsistent. If \(A\succ B\), subtracting the common 89% chance of receiving 1 implies \(C\succ D\). Choosing \(A\) and \(D\) gives special weight to the move from 99% to 100% or to the presentation of certainty.
The Allais pattern identifies a violated axiom; it does not prove that every participant used the same psychology. Certainty, regret, misunderstanding, probability weighting, and response noise can contribute. Prospect theory offers one systematic account in the next chapter.

title: 16  Risky Decision-Making: A Probability Is Not Yet a Feeling
section: The Ellsberg urn: risk is not ambiguity
text:
The Ellsberg urn: risk is not ambiguity
An urn contains 90 balls:

exactly 30 are red;
the remaining 60 are black or yellow in an unknown proportion.

First choose a bet that pays if red is drawn or a bet that pays if black is drawn. Many choose red because its probability is known to be \(1/3\).
Now choose a bet that pays if red or yellow is drawn or a bet that pays if black or yellow is drawn. Many choose black-or-yellow because its probability is known to be \(2/3\).
Preferring red to black suggests \(P(R)>P(B)\). Preferring black-or-yellow to red-or-yellow suggests \(P(B)>P(R)\). No single additive subjective probability can support both comparisons when the payoff is otherwise identical (Ellsberg, 1961).
This pattern is called ambiguity aversion, but it has boundaries. People may seek ambiguity when they feel competent, suspect favorable hidden information, enjoy exploration, or believe the known option was selected against them. Comparative ignorance matters: an ambiguous option can become less attractive when placed beside a transparent one. The practical response is to separate:

variability given a model;
uncertainty about parameters;
uncertainty about the model and missing outcomes;
the decision-maker’s trust in the source.

Collapsing all four into one probability hides the reason for caution.







TipProcess check: risk does not rewrite decision quality



The distinction between process and outcome matters whenever uncertainty can obscure the quality of a choice (Baron & Hershey, 1988): a calibrated choice can lose, while a reckless choice can be rescued by luck. Preserve the probabilities, alternatives, constraints, and reasons available before the uncertainty resolves; otherwise one realized path becomes a false measure of ex ante judgment.

title: 16  Risky Decision-Making: A Probability Is Not Yet a Feeling
section: Worked application: should we insure this exposure?
text:
Worked application: should we insure this exposure?
Return to the insurance quote. Instead of voting on whether the premium “feels high,” the team can organize its discussion around four questions:

Exposure: list final consequences—restoration cost, interrupted service, legal liability, reputation, and possible ruin—not only the insurer’s payout.
Probability: use base rates for comparable organizations, internal controls, and uncertainty ranges. Separate known event frequency from model uncertainty.
Contract: read deductibles, exclusions, caps, reporting duties, and insurer credit risk. “Coverage” is not a binary state.
Capacity: compare the uninsured worst credible loss with liquid reserves and the ability to continue operating.

The team may discover that it can absorb minor incidents but cannot finance a major interruption, or that the quoted policy excludes the loss it most needs covered. Either finding changes the decision in a way that the average annual loss alone cannot. Record the recommendation and its assumptions now, so that a quiet year does not automatically make buying insurance look foolish.

Extension: one project or a portfolio?
A firm considers ten independent projects. Each costs €40,000 and has a 30% chance of returning €200,000, otherwise zero. One project has expected net value
\[
0.30(200{,}000)-40{,}000=20{,}000.
\]
Positive expected value does not make one project safe: it still loses the full investment 70% of the time. A diversified portfolio can reduce idiosyncratic variation if the outcomes are genuinely independent, but common market shocks can make the projects move together. The decision therefore needs both project-level EV and a dependence model at portfolio level.
The mental-accounting chapter later shows why decision-makers often evaluate each gain and loss in isolation. Here the benchmark is already clear: the unit of evaluation changes the risk.

title: 16  Risky Decision-Making: A Probability Is Not Yet a Feeling
section: Ethics: who receives the expected benefit, and who bears the tail?
text:
Ethics: who receives the expected benefit, and who bears the tail?
An organization can accept a positive expected-value project while shifting catastrophic losses onto employees, customers, taxpayers, or future stakeholders. Expected value does not settle distribution, rights, consent, or ruin.
For the insurance decision, identify whose losses the policy covers and whose remain exposed. A policy that protects the organization’s balance sheet may leave clients carrying the cost of interrupted service. Those people’s capacity to bear the harm, and their ability to understand and refuse the exposure, belong in the decision alongside the premium.

text:
Practice Lab
Build a one-page risk register for a real insurance or project decision. Report final-state consequences, probabilities or ranges, dependencies, affected parties, expected value where meaningful, one capacity-to-bear-loss constraint, and one ambiguity the point estimates hide. Conclude with a recommendation, a review date, and an observable condition that would reverse it. The output is the completed register—not a description of what one might contain.

title: 16  Risky Decision-Making: A Probability Is Not Yet a Feeling
text:
Optional research and application notes






NoteApplication box: the single-period newsvendor





A retailer orders once before uncertain demand \(D\) is known. Each unit sells for \(p\), costs \(c\), and has salvage value \(s\), with \(p>c>s\). Ordering one unit too few sacrifices the margin
\[
C_u=p-c,
\]
whereas ordering one unit too many creates the net overage cost
\[
C_o=c-s.
\]
For risk-neutral expected-profit maximization with a known continuous demand distribution \(F\), the optimal order satisfies the critical-fractile rule
\[
F(Q^*)=\frac{C_u}{C_u+C_o}=\frac{p-c}{p-s}.
\]
For discrete demand, choose the smallest quantity whose cumulative probability reaches the fractile. Shortage penalties, disposal costs, capacity constraints, ambiguity, and risk preferences change the rule.
Experiments often find pull-to-center ordering: too much relative to the optimum when the optimal fractile is low and too little when it is high. Schweitzer and Cachon’s (2000) experiments were consistent with anchoring and insufficient adjustment or a preference to reduce ex post inventory error; their pattern did not uniquely support prospect theory. Demand chasing, asymmetric attention to leftover and missed-sales losses, misunderstanding, and loss aversion in other specifications remain candidate mechanisms that require separate tests. Pull-to-center alone identifies none of them.









NoteOptional theory lens: the St Petersburg puzzle





Consider a game in which a fair coin is tossed until the first head. If the first head occurs on toss \(n\), the game pays \(2^n\) monetary units. The probability of that outcome is \(2^{-n}\). Its expected monetary value is
\[
EV=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^{-n}2^n
=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1
=\infty.
\]
Yet few people would pay an enormous entry price. Bernoulli’s solution was to distinguish money from the utility of money: an additional unit matters less when one already has more (Bernoulli, 1738/1954). If utility grows slowly enough—for example, logarithmically—the expected utility can be finite even when expected money is infinite.
The puzzle does not prove diminishing marginal utility: finite wealth, bounded liability, mistrust, transaction costs, or a limit on tosses can also change willingness to pay. Expected value depends on a realizable contract.









NoteResearch Lens: every elicitation task measures a bundle





Risk preference is not observed directly. A task presents options, and a model maps choices back to a parameter. Different tasks change comprehension, probability format, reference point, response mode, and noise.



Table 16.1: Common risk-elicitation methods and what travels with them











Method
What the participant does
What it can reveal
Main identification limits




Certainty equivalent
States or selects a sure amount equal to a lottery
A point or interval of indifference
Open responses invite rounding, anchoring, strategic answers, and misunderstanding


Multiple price list
Chooses between safer and riskier lotteries as probabilities or payoffs change
A switching interval for curvature under a model
Multiple switching, row-order effects, compound lotteries, and assumed functional form


Ordered lotteries
Chooses one lottery from a menu with changing mean and variance
Coarse ranking of risk taking
Mean and variance change together; few categories; loss and probability weighting remain confounded


Investment task
Allocates an endowment between a safe and risky asset
Continuous risky share
Portfolio framing, endowment, beliefs, and scale affect the share


Bomb risk elicitation task
Chooses exposure to more reward-bearing boxes while one hidden box destroys earnings
A continuous stopping point
Sequential interface, loss salience, probability knowledge, and task-specific emotion






Holt and Laury’s (2002) multiple-price-list design, Eckel and Grossman’s (2008) ordered gambles, and the bomb task of Crosetto and Filippin (2013) are all useful. They are not interchangeable rulers. Reviews and direct comparisons find that classifications can vary substantially across elicitation methods (Charness et al., 2013; Pedroni et al., 2017).

Identification requires more than a choice
A safe choice might reflect concave utility, distrust of the probabilities, a liquidity constraint, or misunderstanding of the task. Estimating a “risk-aversion coefficient” holds some of these possibilities fixed. Report the task, stakes, probability format, model, error structure, and population so readers can see what the parameter identifies.











NoteResearch Lens: a positive arithmetic average can conceal multiplicative collapse





Suppose a deliberately extreme gamble risks all current wealth in every round. It multiplies wealth by 1.8 with probability one half and by 0.4 with probability one half, independently across 52 rounds. The one-round arithmetic mean return is +10%, so expected terminal wealth from €10,000 is
\[
10{,}000[0.5(1.8)+0.5(0.4)]^{52}
=10{,}000(1.10)^{52}
\approx €1{,}420{,}429.
\]
Yet 26 gains and 26 losses—the median and modal number of gains—produce
\[
10{,}000(1.8)^{26}(0.4)^{26}
=10{,}000(0.72)^{26}
\approx €1.95.
\]
The expected terminal value is pulled upward by rare paths with many gains, while the median or typical compounded outcome nearly exhausts the initial wealth; the geometric mean return per round is \(\sqrt{0.72}-1\approx-15.1\%\). Drawdown is different again because it depends on the order of gains and losses. Literal ruin has probability zero in this toy model because neither multiplier is zero, but the probability of crossing a practical solvency threshold can be high and must be defined explicitly. Arithmetic return, expected wealth, median compounded wealth, drawdown, and ruin are therefore different risk questions.

Schweitzer, M. E., & Cachon, G. P. (2000). Decision bias in the newsvendor problem with a known demand distribution: Experimental evidence. Management Science, 46(3), 404–420.


von Neumann, J., & Morgenstern, O. (1944). Theory of games and economic behavior. Princeton University Press.

title: 17  Prospect Theory: Gains and Losses Begin at a Reference Point
text:
Opening puzzle: 200 saved or 400 lost?
Expected utility asks where wealth ends. Prospect theory asks how the outcome is represented—as a gain or a loss, with what distance from a reference point, and with what decision weight.
Imagine an outbreak expected to kill 600 people. Choose between:
Now choose between:
Programs A and C describe the same final number of lives. Programs B and D describe the same probability distribution. Yet in Tversky and Kahneman’s (1981) separate samples, 72% selected A in the gain frame, whereas 78% selected D in the loss frame.
The first frame makes lives saved feel like gains and supports the sure option. The second makes deaths feel like losses and supports the gamble that might avoid the loss. This result does not mean wording always reverses preference, or that all respondents reasoned identically. It creates the question prospect theory was built to answer: why can equivalent final states produce different risk attitudes when represented as gains and losses?

title: 17  Prospect Theory: Gains and Losses Begin at a Reference Point
text:
Program A: 200 people will be saved.
Program B: a one-third chance that 600 will be saved and a two-thirds chance that nobody will be saved.



Program C: 400 people will die.
Program D: a one-third chance that nobody will die and a two-thirds chance that 600 will die.









NoteCore Idea



An outcome can feel like a gain or a loss depending on what it is compared with. Prospect theory explains how that reference point, sensitivity to gains and losses, and the influence of probabilities can jointly shape a risky choice. Each part must be examined; a preference reversal does not reveal its cause by itself.
