title: 30  Persuasion: Changing Minds Means Updating Models
section: Diagnose the audience before designing the message
text:
Diagnose the audience before designing the message
The barrier matrix becomes useful when the audience can correct it. Ask a few employees to explain the proposed change in their own words, identify their strongest objection, and describe what would make a trial worthwhile. An efficiency argument may miss a concern about professional judgment; moral reframing studies show that the values used to justify a proposal can affect its reception (Feinberg & Willer, 2015). Adapting the explanation should make the real reasons accessible, without concealing the speaker’s aims or the proposal’s costs.
Then distinguish agreement from action. Employees may accept the case for coordination yet lack training time. “Support innovation” leaves that obstacle untouched; “test this workflow for six weeks with two hours of training provided” creates a decision they can evaluate. Chapter 32 develops the message-building routine.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
30  Persuasion: Changing Minds Means Updating Models

title: 30  Persuasion: Changing Minds Means Updating Models
text:
Resistance and reactance
Employees who hear “Only people afraid of accountability oppose this system” now have a further reason to object. Their freedom to disagree has become part of the dispute.
Reactance is motivation to restore a freedom perceived as threatened (Brehm, 1966; Brehm & Brehm, 1981). It is one explanation for resistance, alongside reasonable disagreement, distrust, competing priorities, and practical constraints. Calling every objection reactance would simply repeat the original mistake of ignoring its content.
An autonomy-supportive message can explain a strong recommendation while acknowledging concerns and identifying real choices. Self-determination theory connects the quality of motivation with experiences of autonomy, competence, and relatedness (Deci & Ryan, 2000). That framework offers reasons to provide choice and support; it does not guarantee that a polite message will overcome opposition. Where a decision is mandatory, communicate that limit honestly and specify what remains open to input.
Inoculation theory offers another approach to resistance. McGuire (1964) proposed that people can be made more resistant to persuasion by exposing them to weakened counterarguments and refutations, much like a vaccine exposes the body to a weakened threat. Inoculation messages warn people that they may encounter persuasion attempts, present common misleading arguments, and refute them. Meta-analyses suggest that inoculation can build resistance across domains (Banas & Rains, 2010).
One application is to explain a misleading technique before people encounter it: show how a graph can exaggerate a change, then let the audience inspect another example. Whether this improves later judgment should be tested, rather than inferred from the audience enjoying the exercise.
Corrections also deserve a realistic expectation. A broad effect in which corrections routinely strengthen false beliefs has proved elusive (Wood & Porter, 2019), although a corrected claim can continue to influence reasoning. Clear corrections that offer an alternative explanation can help people replace the account they previously used (Lewandowsky et al., 2012).
Clinical motivational interviewing provides another example of eliciting people’s own reasons for change while respecting autonomy (Miller & Rollnick, 2013). Its conversational stance is instructive here, though a workplace discussion is not automatically an application of the clinical method.
The platform pilot should preserve meaningful choice where possible: teams can compare two workflows, propose safeguards, and examine results before scale-up. Participation does not mean that every organizational decision becomes a referendum. It means that concerns become testable inputs rather than labels such as “resistance to change.”
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
30  Persuasion: Changing Minds Means Updating Models

title: 30  Persuasion: Changing Minds Means Updating Models
text:
Ethical persuasion
An ethical proposal lets the audience inspect the trade-off. It states consequential costs and uncertainty, makes the speaker’s purpose clear, and uses emotion in proportion to the evidence. A vivid account of wasted time is appropriate when it illuminates the problem; invented threats of dismissal would make the decision harder to judge.
Power makes this especially consequential. A manager’s “voluntary” pilot may feel compulsory if refusal threatens promotion. Ethical design therefore requires attention to the actual consequences of saying no, not merely a reassuring phrase in the presentation.
Before using a message, imagine giving the audience the design brief behind it. Could you explain why you chose the messenger, example, evidence, and proposed action? If their effectiveness depends on hiding relevant facts or manufacturing obligation, revise the proposal.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
30  Persuasion: Changing Minds Means Updating Models

title: 30  Persuasion: Changing Minds Means Updating Models
text:
The platform proposal, redesigned
The original message said, in effect, “The evidence shows that this platform is efficient; therefore use it.” The redesigned proposal follows the audience’s model instead of ignoring it.
First, it begins in shared reality: teams are losing time to duplicate files, conflicting versions, and invisible handoffs. Second, it names the concern fairly: a shared system can improve coordination and create surveillance if access rules are vague. Third, it offers evidence matched to the claims: workflow data for duplication, a live demonstration for usability, written governance for data use, and a limited pilot for predicted time savings. Fourth, it makes identity and value explicit: the aim is to protect professional time and judgment, not replace them. Finally, it proposes an actionable and revisable step: two volunteer teams test the system for six weeks against predeclared measures, with training time, an independent feedback channel, and a decision rule for stopping, revising, or scaling.
Ethos, logos, and pathos now support the same update. A trusted project leader and a technical specialist share the message. The causal argument is inspectable. The emotional stakes—avoidable frustration, competent work, and fear of misuse—fit the situation. Motivation and ability are supported by relevance, demonstration, training, and time. Resistance is not treated as a defect; it helps specify the test.
This design may still fail. Employees may reasonably reject the trade-off, the pilot may show little benefit, or governance may remain untrustworthy. Persuasion is not successful merely because the audience agrees. It is successful when a defensible model receives appropriate weight and the audience retains the capacity to judge and refuse.






CautionEvidence Boundary



Research supports the importance of argument quality, credibility, motivation, ability, emotion, and perceived autonomy, but no checklist guarantees persuasion. Peripheral processing is not synonymous with stupidity: source and consensus can be rational cues when they reliably track expertise or independent evidence. Agreement does not establish that a message was true, ethical, or causally effective; coercion, incentives, conformity, and selective exposure can produce the same observable response.

30  Persuasion: Changing Minds Means Updating Models

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
Learning goals
Narrative turns information into simulated meaning
Sara, a fictional team leader, reads an anonymous comment about her meetings: “We wish we could tell you bad news before it becomes an emergency.” She had thought solving problems quietly protected her team. Now she wonders whether her habit of arriving with an answer has made people reluctant to bring her a question.
Compare that scene with the statement “Leaders should encourage upward feedback.” The statement is clear, but the scene gives us something to investigate: why might a capable, well-intentioned leader make it difficult to speak? Following Sara can make the problem easier to imagine. It can also make her explanation feel true before we have tested it.
This chapter asks what a story adds to a message, and when the addition helps people judge well.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
31  Why Stories Move Minds

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
Distinguish a story from information, an example, and a vivid anecdote.
Explain how stories influence attention, simulation, identity, emotion, memory, and resistance.
Diagnose when a story adds decision-relevant meaning, when it adds distortion, and what evidence must accompany it.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
31  Why Stories Move Minds

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
What is a story?
For this chapter, a story follows someone pursuing a goal through events that have consequences. A protagonist, goal, obstacle, stakes, choice, and change are useful things to look for, rather than mandatory ingredients in a scientific definition. Sara wants to protect her team; a comment raises doubts about how she has tried to do it.
An example can clarify a concept without developing an unfolding situation: asking each team member for a concern illustrates upward feedback. An anecdote is a particular case, which may or may not develop into a story. Calling it a story does not make it representative.
Bruner (1986, 1990) distinguished narrative thinking, organized around agents and consequences, from reasoning through categories and general principles. Both can help us understand a problem. Fisher (1984, 1987) likewise distinguished a story’s coherence from its fit with an audience’s experiences and values. These accounts explain why a story may feel meaningful; neither coherence nor familiarity establishes that its causal account is correct.






NoteCraft sources are design aids, not effect evidence



Practitioner writers such as Lisa Cron and Will Storr offer useful craft questions: What does the protagonist want? What changes? Which belief becomes less workable? These syntheses can help construct a message, but they are not substitutes for experimental or observational evidence about narrative effects. This chapter therefore uses them as design vocabulary and relies on communication research when making empirical claims.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
31  Why Stories Move Minds

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
Information is not yet narrative
A report might say, “The team introduced anonymous feedback and monthly check-ins.” To turn that information into a story, we need a person with a reason to care and events that alter the situation.
In our fictional continuation, Sara initially dismisses the comment as unfair. Then she rereads the last month’s meeting notes and finds that nearly every proposed solution was her own. At the next meeting, she waits for colleagues to describe the problem before offering an answer. One raises a delivery risk that has not appeared on the dashboard.
The story makes the tension between helping and taking over visible. It also embeds a hypothesis: Sara’s meeting style discouraged useful information. A reader can now understand that hypothesis, but establishing it would require evidence beyond this invented episode.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
31  Why Stories Move Minds

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
Story as model updating






Figure 31.1: One narrative-design template begins with the audience’s current model, introduces meaningful trouble, and offers a candidate new model, supporting evidence, and a possible action. This author’s template is not a scientific definition of story or a universal persuasion mechanism.



The previous chapter treated a model as an explanation of what is happening and what to expect. A story can make a change in that explanation visible: Sara begins by equating quick solutions with helpful leadership, encounters information that troubles this view, and tries another way of running a meeting.
That sequence is useful for writing, but it is not inevitable. People may ignore contradictory evidence, revise the wrong belief, or change their behavior without changing their view. The five-part writing route in Figure 31.1 is a design template, not a neurological mechanism or a definition of every narrative.
When using it, ask what the protagonist believed, what observation challenged that belief, and what further evidence would justify the proposed change. The final question prevents the turning point from doing the work of a scientific test.

31  Why Stories Move Minds

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
Why facts alone can fail
A direct factual statement may be all a reader needs, especially when the question is clear and the source trusted. A story becomes useful when the reader needs help imagining the situation: why a choice is difficult, whom it affects, or how its consequences could unfold.
For Sara’s colleagues, a rule requiring more participation might sound straightforward. Following her hesitation makes its difficulty understandable without excusing a poor meeting process. We can then examine whether that imagined difficulty resembles the one people actually face.

31  Why Stories Move Minds

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
Four mechanisms of narrative persuasion
Research and theory suggest several overlapping ways stories can affect readers, including absorption in the narrative, identification with a character, and imagining consequences (Green & Brock, 2000; Cohen, 2001; van Laer et al., 2014). The four families below organize our discussion; they are not four independent effects that every story produces.



Table 31.1: Narrative mechanisms, design questions, and risks










Mechanism family
Design question
Risk




Attention and curiosity
What unresolved question earns attention?
Manufactured suspense can hide weak relevance.


Simulation and causal understanding
What mechanism links choice to consequence?
Coherence can be mistaken for causal proof.


Identity and self-reference
Whose goals and constraints can the audience understand?
A single perspective can erase affected others.


Emotion, memory, and reduced resistance
What should matter and remain retrievable?
Feeling can exceed the evidence and bypass scrutiny.

31  Why Stories Move Minds

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
1. Attention and curiosity
A story begins when something important is unresolved. Someone wants something, but the outcome is uncertain. This creates a gap the audience wants to close. Will the protagonist succeed? What will they do? What will happen next? What does this reveal?
Attention matters because people cannot process everything. In an information-rich world, the first persuasive problem is not only accuracy. It is relevance. A message that does not create a reason to attend may disappear before it is judged. A story opening should therefore begin near disruption, not background. “Our organization was founded in 1986 and has always valued innovation” is rarely a strong opening. “On paper, the new system was perfect. In practice, no one used it” creates a question.

Transportation
Narrative transportation refers to mental absorption into a story world. When transported, people devote attention, imagery, and emotion to the unfolding narrative. They are not merely evaluating claims from the outside; they are experiencing a situation from within. Green and Brock’s work made transportation a central concept in narrative persuasion, and later research, including meta-analytic work by van Laer and colleagues, supports its importance.
Transportation matters because persuasion often fails when people remain outside the message, evaluating it defensively. A transported audience temporarily enters the logic of the story. This does not mean they become irrational. It means they process the claim through simulation rather than only detached critique. In teaching, this suggests that opening with a problem situation can be more effective than opening with a definition. The definition becomes meaningful after the learner has entered the problem.
Transportation also creates risk. A compelling story can smuggle assumptions into experience. A political film can make a misleading causal story feel true. A corporate change story can make a strategy feel inevitable while hiding alternatives. Ethical storytellers must ask: What world am I inviting the audience to enter? What assumptions does that world make? Whose perspective is centered? Whose perspective is missing? What will feel true after the story ends?
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
31  Why Stories Move Minds

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
2. Identity and self-reference

Identification
Identification occurs when audience members imaginatively take the perspective of a character, share goals or emotions, and experience events partly from inside the character’s situation. Identification differs from liking. You may identify with a character you do not entirely like because you understand their motives or feel their struggle from within.
Following a character can shift the question from “What do I think of this person?” toward “What would this situation be like from their position?” Sara need not be wholly admirable for readers to understand her wish to appear competent.
A useful character has intelligible reasons and meaningful constraints. Showing why speaking up risks embarrassment, for example, gives an audience more to consider than labeling a colleague timid. Whether that portrayal improves empathy or persuasion remains an empirical question, and another character may experience the same meeting differently.


Self-reference
A reader may connect Sara’s predicament to a meeting they have led or attended. That connection gives the abstract issue a personal reference point. It can also narrow interpretation: a leader who recognizes only their own good intentions may miss how the meeting feels to a junior colleague.
Use identification to expand the perspectives available for judgment. After following Sara, ask what the quiet team member wanted, what made speaking costly, and how the same exchange looked from that seat.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
31  Why Stories Move Minds

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
3. Emotion, memory, and reduced resistance
Stories persuade because they connect information to value. Emotion is not merely decoration added to cognition. It helps prioritize attention, encode memory, guide action, and signal what matters. In a story, emotion arises from stakes: someone wants something, something could be lost, and the outcome is uncertain. Without stakes, there is little reason to care.
A common mistake in academic and managerial communication is to remove all emotion in the name of objectivity. Objectivity is important for evidence, but persuasion requires significance. A story can preserve accuracy while making significance visible. “The project was delayed by six months” is information. The meaning becomes clearer when we understand who was affected: a small supplier that invested in new equipment, expected a contract, lost revenue, laid off workers, and became reluctant to join future innovation partnerships.
Stories can also improve retrieval when their causal and emotional structure organizes otherwise disconnected details. People may remember what someone wanted, what blocked them, what they chose, and what happened. The story can provide a retrieval path for the principle, although vividness may also preserve an unrepresentative case better than the qualifying evidence.

Reduced resistance
Absorption in a story can leave less attention for generating objections. Green and Brock (2000) linked transportation with story-consistent beliefs and evaluations across their experiments. This does not imply that every story persuades, or that a reader who follows a character abandons critical thought.
For a teacher, the opportunity is to let students encounter a difficult choice before discussing the principle. The responsibility is to reopen scrutiny afterward: which assumptions made the ending seem reasonable, and what would happen if they were wrong?
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
31  Why Stories Move Minds

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
4. Simulation and causal understanding
Stories allow audiences to simulate decisions before making them. This is one reason case teaching is powerful. A good case does not simply deliver a conclusion; it places students inside a decision context. They must ask: What do we know? What is uncertain? What are the options? What are the risks? What would I do?
Mental simulation helps people understand causal structure. Instead of passively receiving advice, they rehearse consequences. This makes story especially useful for risk communication, ethics training, leadership development, entrepreneurship, public policy, and negotiation.
An ethics lecture that says, “Conflicts of interest are dangerous” may be less effective than a story in which a researcher accepts a small favor, then a larger favor, and gradually finds it harder to report unfavorable results. The story simulates moral drift. A negotiation lecture that says, “Positions hide interests” may be less effective than a story in which two teams fight over a deadline until they discover that one side needs symbolic reassurance and the other needs operational flexibility.

Causal stories and causal evidence
Stories persuade because they organize causality. They show how one thing led to another: because the protagonist believed X, they did Y; because they did Y, consequence Z followed; because Z happened, the old belief had to be revised. A coherent sequence can help a reader organize scattered evidence, while also making a missing link easy to overlook.
Organizations do something similar after success or failure. They construct stories: the market changed, leadership failed, customers were not ready, the technology was immature, incentives were wrong, or the team lacked discipline. The story determines what the organization learns. If the story is wrong, the organization learns the wrong lesson.
This creates a discipline: distinguish causal story from causal evidence. What mechanism does the story imply? What evidence supports that mechanism? What alternative story could explain the same events? What base rates or comparison cases are missing? What role did luck play? What structural factors are hidden by focusing on one character?






NoteResearch Lens: shared processing is not shared belief



Naturalistic neuroscience has found time-locked similarities in brain activity when people encounter the same films or stories, and speaker–listener coupling has been associated with comprehension (Hasson et al., 2004, 2008; Stephens et al., 2010). These are findings about coordinated processing under shared stimulation. They do not show identical interpretations, emotions, beliefs, or persuasion. Selection and sequence can guide attention without determining what the audience concludes.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
31  Why Stories Move Minds

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
The power—and danger—of one
Stories often persuade through one face, one name, one family, one patient, one customer, one employee. This can be morally important because large numbers can become abstract. A single person can restore emotional reality. In donation experiments, presenting an identifiable person has sometimes elicited more giving than presenting statistical information about need (Small et al., 2007). The response depends on the comparison and setting; it is not a rule that one person always moves an audience more than many.
But the same mechanism can distort judgment. One vivid victim may receive attention while many unseen victims are neglected. A rare disease with a compelling story may attract disproportionate funding. A dramatic crime may shape policy more than widespread harms. A single customer complaint may dominate managerial attention even when broader data point elsewhere.
The ethical challenge is to connect story and scale. A good humanitarian message may begin with one person’s story, then connect it to accurate statistics: this is one person, and the evidence shows how common or rare this pattern is. The story creates attention and care; the statistic creates proportion. Together they support responsible action.






CautionEvidence Boundary



A vivid story can create attention, simulation, identification, emotion, and memory. Those outcomes do not establish that the implied mechanism is correct, the case is representative, or the recommended action works. Narrative should illuminate evidence, not replace base rates, comparison groups, causal identification, affected perspectives, or uncertainty.

31  Why Stories Move Minds

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
Practice Lab
Select one existing message that uses a story—or one abstract claim for which a story has been proposed. Complete a one-page narrative diagnosis:

Decision: What belief or choice should the message help the audience examine?
Narrative job: Which one function is most needed—attention, simulation, identity and self-reference, or emotion and memory?
Form: Is a story necessary, or would a direct statement, example, comparison, or case make the point with less distortion?
Evidence companion: If a story is retained, name the denominator or scale estimate, relevant comparison, evidence for the proposed mechanism, strongest alternative account, and one affected perspective the story leaves out.
Verdict: Retain, replace, or omit the story, and give the reason in one sentence.

The output is the diagnosis, not a polished story. Chapter 32 provides the construction workflow if the verdict is to retain one.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
31  Why Stories Move Minds

title: 31  Why Stories Move Minds
text:
Take it forward
A story can make an unfamiliar problem worth attending to, but its vividness cannot tell us how common the problem is. When you retell a case, carry that distinction with it: explain what the story illustrates and which broader claim still needs evidence.

31  Why Stories Move Minds

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
Learning goals
Use narrative to carry evidence, not to replace it
A restaurant owner receives a pitch for a forecasting assistant. The first slide lists algorithms; the second celebrates the development team. By the third, the owner still cannot tell whether the tool will help decide how much food to prepare tomorrow.
Imagine rebuilding the pitch around that decision. Too much preparation wastes ingredients; too little loses sales. The proposed tool might help, but the owner needs to see how it uses the restaurant’s records, what evidence supports its forecasts, and what trying it would cost.
We will use this fictional pitch to build a message that earns attention and gives the audience enough information to decide. A story is optional; a defensible claim and a clear request are essential.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
Build one message with STORY as the primary workflow; use AND–BUT–THEREFORE only as an optional compression test.
Match the strength of each claim to appropriate evidence, comparison, and uncertainty.
Produce and audit a message that remains accurate, dignified, and genuinely rejectable.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
Design the change

Begin with the audience’s current story
Ask the owner how preparation decisions are currently made and where mistakes become costly. An experienced owner may already forecast informally using bookings, weather, and local events. Beginning with “Restaurants need data-driven decisions” would overlook that knowledge and give the owner a reason to distrust the rest of the pitch.


Hidden resistance and protected identity
Find out what makes trying the tool unattractive. The owner may doubt its accuracy, lack clean records, or worry that staff will treat recommendations as orders. These are different problems. A demonstration can address usability; a pilot may test forecasts; explicit override rules address control. If the proposed product cannot meet an important constraint, improve the proposal before polishing the message.


Protagonist, goal, and stakes
If a story would help, follow a person facing the decision. Picture the owner checking yesterday’s waste against today’s bookings, knowing that a cautious preparation plan could leave popular dishes unavailable. This scene gives the audience a goal and a trade-off. It does not need an invented crisis or a heroic founder.


Conflict, obstacle, and misbelief
The obstacle should make the proposed response worth considering. Perhaps the owner has sales records but cannot readily combine them into a daily forecast. That problem suggests a role for the tool. If the real problem is unreliable deliveries, better demand forecasts may help little.
Do not assume the audience’s current belief is a “misbelief” simply because it conflicts with the proposal. The pitch should reveal a limitation that can be investigated, with room for the investigation to vindicate the current practice.


Turning point, evidence, and change
A useful turning point changes what the audience can see. Comparing a forecast with the owner’s existing estimate may reveal a promising improvement, or it may reveal that the tool adds little. Either result should change what the speaker claims.
In a fictional story, label the episode as imagined. In a factual case, report what was actually observed and what alternatives remain. An illustrative ending cannot establish demand, effectiveness, or savings; those claims need their own evidence.






NoteOptional research note: give curiosity a question





Imagine showing the restaurant owner two days with similar bookings but very different amounts of leftover food. Before presenting the software, ask what might explain the difference. The owner now has something specific to investigate: what did the booking count miss, and could that information improve tomorrow’s preparation?
Loewenstein’s (1994) information-gap account of curiosity explains why a partly understood situation can invite further attention. Curiosity arises when people become aware of a gap between what they know and what they want to know. Simply presenting an unfamiliar subject may leave them without enough understanding to notice a particular gap. A recognizable starting point and an answerable question can give the missing information a place to fit. This is an account of how curiosity can arise, rather than a guarantee that every unanswered question will hold attention.
For this pitch, use the owner’s experience to make the question meaningful, then show how it could be answered. A comparison of forecasts with actual demand might reveal useful information, or show that the owner’s existing judgment performs just as well. Either result resolves something worth knowing. Curiosity helps invite the investigation; it does not establish that the proposed explanation is true. Disclose costs and limitations when they become relevant to the decision, even if withholding them would make the presentation more suspenseful.

32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
section: Build the message with one primary workflow
text:
Build the message with one primary workflow






Figure 32.1: An author’s ethical communication framework braids human meaning with base rates, mechanisms, comparisons, and uncertainty; it is a design aid, not a validated causal model of persuasion.



The following five prompts keep the audience’s decision, explanation, evidence, and requested action together. Use them as a drafting aid, adapting the amount of narrative to the message’s purpose.

32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
The STORY framework
STORY is this book’s practical mnemonic: Shared reality, Trouble, Opportunity, Reasons, and Yes. “Yes” names the decision being requested; a well-informed “no” remains a legitimate outcome.



Table 32.1: STORY as an operational model-update sequence










Letter
Function
Test




S · Shared reality
Start with an accepted goal, behavior, change, or constraint.
Is the opening recognizable without jargon or a claim the audience already rejects?


T · Trouble
Reveal the contradiction that makes the old model fail.
Are the pain, change, and stakes real and proportionate?


O · Opportunity
Explain the better model or mechanism of progress.
Does it resolve this trouble, rather than merely advertise a feature?


R · Reasons
Supply the evidence needed for the pivotal claim, including a relevant comparison and uncertainty.
Can the audience inspect the support, and does it match the claim?


Y · Yes
Ask for a specific decision or next step.
Who does what, by when, at what cost—and can the audience genuinely decline?






For a brief version, try AND–BUT–THEREFORE: the shared situation, the consequential difficulty, and the proposed response. This is an optional compression test. Neither it nor STORY is a validated psychological law, and a message need not force every audience into the same narrative sequence.
For an illustrative restaurant-forecasting pitch, the moves could be: S—independent restaurants already use point-of-sale and ordering tools; T—owners still have to guess daily preparation, so overestimates waste food and underestimates lose sales; O—a forecasting assistant turns existing sales history into preparation recommendations; R—report only verified pilot behavior, comparisons, uncertainty, and limits; Y—invite a defined number of eligible restaurants to a time-bounded pilot with stated success criteria. The sequence is reusable; any traction number must be real, sourced, and appropriate to the claim.
After drafting, read the message from the owner’s position. Is tomorrow’s preparation decision still visible, or has the pitch drifted back to celebrating the software? Keep a statistic when it helps evaluate the proposal, and remove it when it merely makes the slide look authoritative.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
Match evidence to the claim
Evidence does not form one universal ladder. An interview, prototype, behavior record, impact estimate, and cost model answer different questions. A prototype can establish technical feasibility without showing demand. Observed adoption can establish use without showing that the intervention caused a beneficial outcome. A causal effect can be real while the delivery model remains unaffordable. The task is therefore to identify the pivotal claim for the audience’s decision and match it to evidence capable of testing that claim.



Table 32.2: Match the pivotal claim to evidence that can test it











Claim to be tested
Decision question
Evidence that can address it
What that evidence alone does not establish




Need or problem
Does the problem exist, for whom, how often, and with what consequence?
Representative surveys, administrative or behavioral records, systematic observation, interviews with a clear sampling purpose, prevalence and distribution data
That the proposed solution works or that every affected group experiences the same problem


Mechanism
Why should the proposed change produce the predicted result?
Discriminating process measures, mechanism-specific predictions, experiments or comparisons that vary the proposed pathway, triangulated qualitative process evidence
Population-scale effectiveness, durability, or affordability


Feasibility
Can the intervention or product be delivered reliably under the relevant constraints?
Working prototypes, technical tests, operational pilots, failure logs, capacity and safety checks
Demand, beneficial impact, or viable economics


Adoption or behavior
Will eligible users choose, use, return to, pay for, or comply with it under realistic conditions?
Observed uptake, use, retention, purchase, referral, or completion with a stated denominator and comparison period
Why behavior changed or whether use improves welfare


Causal impact
Does the intervention change the intended outcome relative to a credible counterfactual?
Randomized experiments or defensible quasi-experimental and comparative designs, with outcome definitions, uncertainty, attrition, and relevant follow-up
Generalization to every setting, implementation capacity, or net value


Economics
Can the model create and sustain value after relevant costs, risks, and alternatives?
Transparent cost and revenue data, unit economics, sensitivity analysis, opportunity costs, and distribution of gains and losses
Causal or social benefit merely because the activity is financially viable






Not every message needs all six claim types. A policy recommendation may hinge on need, causal impact, distribution, and cost; an early prototype may appropriately make only a feasibility claim. For the Reasons row of STORY, record the pivotal claim, its type, the strongest available evidence, the relevant source or comparison, and what remains unestablished. If the available evidence cannot support the necessary claim, weaken the claim, change the requested action, or collect better evidence.

32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
Fluency: power and danger
A clear layout and familiar language make the pitch easier to inspect. Repetition can also make a claim feel truer through familiarity (Hasher et al., 1977; Fazio et al., 2015), so ease of reading must not become the reason to believe it. Chapter 13 develops this distinction.
For the restaurant owner, show waste in units they can reconstruct—portions or ingredient costs over a stated period—and identify the comparison. Resolve the question that earned attention rather than using suspense to delay an inconvenient limitation.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
The story-evidence braid
Return to the owner preparing food for tomorrow. The scene makes a cost understandable, but only data can show how common that cost is or whether the proposed tool reduces it. Pairing a case with an appropriate denominator and comparison helps keep its emotional force in proportion (Small et al., 2007; Slovic, 2007; Dahlstrom, 2014).
A useful draft can move from the scene to evidence, explain the proposed mechanism, and then return to the decision. If there are no pilot results yet, say so and request a trial. If there are results, show who participated, what was compared, and what remains uncertain. The ending should reflect the evidence available, even when that makes the story less tidy.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
section: Adapt the message without changing its discipline
text:
Adapt the message without changing its discipline
STORY travels across teaching, leadership, health, policy, entrepreneurship, and negotiation because all involve a person or group deciding whether to revise a model. The surface changes; the discipline does not. Start from the stakeholder’s consequential decision, make the trouble specific, state the proposed mechanism, match reasons to claims, and end with an action that can be refused.
In teaching, a case should create the need for a concept and then yield to analysis. In leadership, a change story should acknowledge loss and protect valued identity rather than invent a “burning platform.” In health and policy, a patient or citizen story should be paired with prevalence, effects, alternatives, and uncertainty. In entrepreneurship, the stakeholder—not the product or founder—is usually the protagonist. In negotiation, a short story can explain why an interest matters without pretending that one side’s account is the whole situation.
The message fails when adaptation becomes a new catalogue of tricks. Keep the same questions: What model is being updated? What evidence warrants that update? What action follows? What could the audience still reasonably reject?
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
Ethics and common failure modes

Ethical storytelling
A story inevitably selects details. Check whether that selection hides an affected group, makes a rare event seem common, or turns one person’s success into a claim about what everyone can achieve. The ethical audit below is useful after drafting, when these omissions can be located in actual sentences.


Common mistakes

Speaker-first opening: beginning with the organization, product, or research team before establishing the audience’s decision. Start with shared reality and a consequential stake.
Decorative trouble: adding a dramatic but that changes the subject without exposing why the current model fails. The trouble must make the proposed explanation necessary to consider.
Anecdote as denominator: allowing one vivid case to imply frequency, representativeness, or causal force. Pair the case with the comparison or distribution needed to judge scale.
Evidence dump: presenting impressive numbers that do not test the pivotal claim. State what each item of evidence should change and what it cannot establish.
Inevitable yes: ending as though understanding obliges agreement. Name the decision, costs, alternatives, uncertainty, and a meaningful way to decline, revise, or stop.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
Worked transformations

Worked example: structured hiring
Persuasive goal: convince managers to use structured hiring interviews.
Information-only version: “Structured interviews have higher validity than unstructured interviews. Comparable questions and job-relevant criteria can reduce inconsistent judgment.”
Fictional story version: Maria had hired dozens of people and believed she was good at reading candidates. In one interview, a candidate from a familiar university spoke confidently about teamwork and leadership. Maria felt an immediate connection. Another candidate was quieter, less polished, and from an institution Maria did not know well. The team hired the first candidate. Six months later, performance problems appeared: missed deadlines, poor collaboration, and resistance to feedback. During a later review, Maria reread the interview notes and realized there were almost none. She had recorded impressions, not evidence. When the company introduced structured interviews, she resisted at first. They felt mechanical. But after using the same job-relevant questions and scoring evidence separately, she noticed something uncomfortable: her “intuition” had often been confidence responding to confidence. The structure did not replace her judgment. It gave her judgment something better to work with.
This story begins inside the manager’s existing belief: “I can read people.” It introduces a problem: a confident choice is followed by poor performance. It creates a turning point: rereading the notes reveals the absence of evidence. It offers a new model: structure improves judgment rather than replacing it. The example makes the reason for structure understandable. It does not establish that confidence caused the hiring failure or that structured interviews would have prevented it; those claims require comparative research, discussed in Chapter 41.


Worked example: negotiation deadline
Persuasive goal: explain why a delivery deadline matters without making it sound like an arbitrary demand.
Information-only version: “We need delivery by June 1.”
Fictional story version: Last year, a component arrived four days late. The delay looked small on paper. But the production line had been scheduled tightly, customers had already booked installation dates, and workers were assigned to shifts that depended on the component arriving. By June 5, the line was stopped, customer orders were rescheduled, and the team had to explain a preventable delay. This year, the June 1 date is not a preference; it is the point that keeps the rest of the system from failing. We are willing to discuss price, batch size, or earlier partial delivery, but we need a plan that protects that date.
If these events were real and accurately reported, this story could explain an interest without revealing a reservation value. It humanizes the constraint and opens problem-solving rather than simply asserting a position.

32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
section: Edit for clarity without confusing fluency with truth
text:
Edit for clarity without confusing fluency with truth
Once the message is evidence-aligned, make it easier to process: use concrete verbs, legible comparisons, one governing tension, and a visible denominator. Familiar language can provide an entry point and one meaningful surprise can create attention. These are editing choices, not reasons to believe the claim.
Numbers, images, and metaphors should make magnitude or mechanism inspectable. Ask what each representation reveals, what it hides, and whether the audience could reconstruct the underlying quantity. A memorable metaphor may help organize a claim, but its average persuasive advantage is small and context-dependent (Sopory & Dillard, 2002).
A message worth sharing is not necessarily worth believing. People may pass content on because it expresses identity, creates connection, signals competence, helps someone, or supports collective action (Berger & Milkman, 2012; Falk et al., 2013; Baek et al., 2017). Optimize first for accuracy and inspectability, then for transmission.






CautionEvidence Boundary



STORY and ABT are practical writing tools, not validated psychological laws. A memorable structure cannot rescue false evidence, a hidden conflict of interest, an unrepresentative case, or a recommendation that removes meaningful choice. Fluency, emotional response, agreement, and sharing are message outcomes—not proof that the model is correct.





Table 32.3: Information, example, anecdote, case, and story











Form
What it does
Example
Limitation




Information
States facts, events, features, dates, or numbers.
“The team introduced monthly check-ins.”
May not show why the change was difficult or meaningful.


Example
Clarifies a concept by illustrating it.
“Asking each colleague for a risk illustrates upward feedback.”
May not create tension, cause, stakes, or transformation.


Anecdote
Provides a vivid individual case.
“One customer waited three hours and gave up.”
Can be unrepresentative and can overpower base rates.


Case
Describes a real or hypothetical situation for analysis.
A company adopts a feedback system and engagement rises.
A useful case can remain descriptive; it need not contain an inner transformation.


Story
Shows motivated action under constraint and change through cause and consequence.
Sara resists anonymous feedback, sees that her competence has become a bottleneck, changes her meeting ritual, and creates a habit of honesty.
Can mislead if causality, evidence, or representativeness is distorted.









Table 32.4: An ethical story audit










Principle
Guiding question
Warning sign




Truthfulness
Is the story factual, composite, or fictional, and is that clear?
Invented realism or altered key facts.


Representativeness
Does the case reflect a broader pattern supported by evidence?
Anecdote pretending to be a base rate.


Dignity
Are people more than props, victims, villains, or stereotypes?
Humans reduced to symbols or emotional instruments.


Complexity
Is causality simplified without becoming false?
One villain explains everything.


Transparency
Does the audience know what kind of story this is?
Composite or illustrative stories presented as single real cases.


Evidence alignment
Does the story illuminate evidence rather than replace it?
The story is used to hide weak or missing evidence.


Agency
Does the story expand action possibilities?
Fear, shame, or identity threat without a path forward.


Plurality
Are important missing perspectives acknowledged?
The story prevents the audience from seeing anything else.


Proportion
Does emotional force match the real significance of the issue?
Rare cases presented as common without scale.


Actionability
Does the story point toward a meaningful response?
Distress without a credible path.

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
Practice Lab
Build a one-page STORY brief for one research claim, policy, product, leadership request, or negotiation proposal. The single brief contains five rows: Shared reality, Trouble, Opportunity, Reasons, and Yes. In the Reasons row, identify the pivotal claim, classify it using Table 32.2, give the strongest available evidence and comparison, state the uncertainty, and name what the evidence does not establish. At the bottom, answer three audit questions: Is any case presented as representative without a denominator? Can the audience meaningfully decline or revise the requested action? Which one sentence should be weakened or removed if the evidence is insufficient? Use the completed brief to deliver a 90-second message. Peer feedback identifies one unsupported inferential jump and one concrete repair.

32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message

title: 32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message
text:
Take it forward
Read your draft from the audience’s position. Can a reader identify the problem, inspect the evidence behind the pivotal claim, and understand the next decision? If the story works only while a qualification is hidden, revise the story before polishing the language.
The message is now ready to leave the page, but meaning will not travel intact. Chapter 33 follows what happens when another person interprets, tests, and corrects it.

32  Building an Evidence-Aligned Message

title: 33  Communication: Language Is Not a File Transfer
text:
Begin with a failed email
Words are the visible tip; context and relationship do the hidden work
After a project deadline slips, a manager writes: “We need to discuss accountability. Please come prepared tomorrow.” The manager intends urgency and clearer ownership. One employee reads blame. Another expects layoffs. A third assumes the sentence targets someone else. The next meeting begins defensively before anyone has spoken.
The words were transmitted perfectly. Meaning was not. Each reader combined the sentence with a different history, power relationship, expectation, and fear. Communication therefore cannot be understood as placing a complete meaning into a message and sending it intact. It is joint inference under incomplete information.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
33  Communication: Language Is Not a File Transfer

title: 33  Communication: Language Is Not a File Transfer
text:
NoteCore Idea



Words give another person evidence about what we mean. Their interpretation also depends on context and experience, so a clear intention can still produce a misunderstanding. Communication improves when people can test their interpretations, correct them, and agree on what to do next.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
33  Communication: Language Is Not a File Transfer

title: 33  Communication: Language Is Not a File Transfer
text:
Learning goals

Map how the same utterance can produce different interpretations.
Use grounding and perspective-getting to test a social inference.
Redesign a high-stakes message so its intent, context, action, and repair path are recoverable.


Here, shared reality means a perceived commonality with another person’s inner state about a referent: for example, feeling that both of you understand the same problem in a similar way or attach similar significance to an event (Echterhoff et al., 2009). It does not require identical backgrounds, complete agreement, or one merged perspective. Nor does it establish truth. Two people can share an interpretation that the evidence does not support; grounding makes the interpretation mutually testable, while external evidence must still test the world it describes.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
33  Communication: Language Is Not a File Transfer

title: 33  Communication: Language Is Not a File Transfer
section: Meaning is inferred, tested, and repaired
text:
Meaning is inferred, tested, and repaired






Figure 33.1: An utterance permits several interpretations. Context supplies evidence, while grounding and repair make those interpretations mutually testable. This author’s synthesis follows grounding theory; it does not assume a fixed hidden quantity of meaning waiting to be recovered.



Language turns an intention into a public signal, but meaning is not simply a submerged object with a fixed size that the listener retrieves. The listener infers a working interpretation from words, tone, relationship, history, power, culture, local context, and beliefs about what both parties know. The speaker can then respond to that interpretation, so meaning is partly jointly constructed through grounding and repair. The same “Fine. Let’s discuss this tomorrow” could signal genuine agreement, irritation, overload, caution, a wish to de-escalate, or a threat. Interpretation feels immediate even when the evidence permits several stories.
The design goal is therefore recoverability, not perfect transmission. A recoverable message supplies enough context, makes intent and relational stance visible, names the next action, and invites correction: “I am too tired to give this a fair hearing tonight. I am not dismissing the concern. Could we discuss it at 09:00 tomorrow? If I have misunderstood what is urgent, tell me now.” The message cannot eliminate ambiguity, but it gives the other person a path to repair it.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
33  Communication: Language Is Not a File Transfer

title: 33  Communication: Language Is Not a File Transfer
text:
Communication is coordination and repair






Figure 33.2: Human communication requires grounding: participants check, correct, and repair interpretations until common ground is sufficient for action.



The transmission model of communication is associated with Shannon and Weaver’s mathematical theory of communication (Shannon & Weaver, 1949). In that model, a sender transmits a signal through a channel to a receiver, and noise can interfere. This model is powerful for engineering problems. But human communication is not only signal transmission. It is meaning-making.
The failed email shows the limit of a transmission analogy: the signal arrived intact, yet the employees inferred different intentions. The next task is to discover those differences before acting on them.
Herbert Clark’s work emphasizes common ground: the shared knowledge, assumptions, and context that speakers use to understand one another (Clark, 1996). Communication requires people to coordinate on what they both know, what they assume, and what has already been established. Clark and Brennan (1991) describe grounding as the process of establishing that people have understood each other well enough for the current purpose.
Grounding is why conversation includes signals such as “yes,” “I see,” “wait,” “what do you mean?,” “so you are saying…,” nods, pauses, repetition, examples, and repair. These are not meaningless fillers. They are coordination devices. They help participants check whether meaning is shared.
Grice’s cooperative principle also helps explain communication. Grice (1975) argued that conversation is guided by expectations that speakers provide information that is relevant, truthful, sufficiently informative, and clear. Much meaning comes from these expectations. If someone says, “Some of the students passed,” listeners may infer that not all passed, even though the sentence does not logically say that. If someone asks, “Can you pass the salt?” the literal answer may be “yes,” but the intended meaning is a request.
Human communication depends heavily on implication. People often say less than they mean because they expect listeners to infer. This makes communication efficient, but also fragile. Misunderstanding happens when people do not share the same assumptions.
This is especially clear in email and text communication. Kruger and colleagues (2005) found that people overestimate how well they can communicate tone over email. In one study, senders expected roughly 78% accuracy, receivers expected roughly 90%, yet actual email accuracy was only 56%; adding voice raised actual accuracy to 73.1% but did not eliminate error. The exact numbers belong to that task, not to every message. The portable lesson is the gap: both sides can feel confident while reconstructing different tones. The sender thinks, “How could they not understand?” The receiver thinks, “How could they write such a thing?”






Figure 33.3: In a task involving 29 dyads, senders and receivers forecast high decoding accuracy in both email and voice, while actual accuracy was lower—especially in email (Kruger et al., 2005, Study 2). The estimates describe this task, not a universal channel ranking. The companion schematic contrasts private perspective-taking with perspective-getting through questions and verification (Eyal et al., 2018).



The left panel is not a general ranking of communication channels; it is a calibration result from one sarcasm task. The right panel states the transferable response: use richer evidence when stakes rise, and let the other person correct the model you have formed (Eyal et al., 2018).



Table 33.1: Designing a message for recoverability









If a message is easy to misread, add…
Example




Context
“I am writing after today’s deadline changed.”


Intent
“My aim is to clarify ownership, not assign blame.”


Relational stance
“I value the work and want us to solve this together.”


Next action
“Please mark the two dates you can meet.”


Repair invitation
“If this lands differently from how I intend, call me.”






The manager’s email can now be rewritten: “Yesterday’s delay exposed two handoffs without clear owners. My aim is to repair the workflow, not assign blame. Before tomorrow’s meeting, please mark where you believed ownership changed and one constraint I may not see. We will compare the maps, agree on the next handoff, and record unresolved concerns. If you read this as a performance warning, please tell me; that is not the purpose of this meeting.” The revision does not guarantee trust. It makes the intended model, evidence request, next action, and correction path visible.
At the meeting, “Which handoff did you think you owned?” will reveal more than “Everyone understands now?” A concrete example lets each person check whether the same words imply the same action.



Table 33.2: Grounding failures and repair moves










Failure
Hidden source
Repair move




Same word, different meaning
Different assumptions or professional models.
Ask for an example and define the term in use.


Tone is misread
Text removes vocal and contextual cues.
State intent explicitly and check interpretation.


Mind-reading hardens
An inference is treated as fact.
Name it as a hypothesis and ask the person.


Agreement is assumed
Silence is interpreted as consent.
Invite a summary, private response, or explicit concern.


Perspective-taking projects the self
We imagine what we would feel.
Use perspective-getting: ask, listen, and verify.

33  Communication: Language Is Not a File Transfer

title: 33  Communication: Language Is Not a File Transfer
text:
Mind-reading is a hypothesis
Inferring another person’s beliefs or intentions is often called mentalizing or theory of mind. We need it to cooperate and coordinate, but the apparent immediacy of an interpretation can hide its uncertainty. “She is angry with me” may be a plausible explanation of a curt reply, or the reply may reflect an urgent task we cannot see.
Familiarity helps, but it does not turn inference into telepathy. In a study of romantic couples, partners predicted each other’s judgments of self-worth, abilities, and preferences better than chance, yet expected substantially greater accuracy than they achieved (Eyal & Epley, 2010). Calibration depends on the target, cue, relationship, context, and mental state being judged. The aim is not permanent doubt; it is confidence proportional to evidence.
One major error is egocentric projection: anchoring on one’s own perspective and insufficiently adjusting to another person’s perspective (Epley et al., 2004). We assume that our model of the world is closer to theirs than it really is. “I would not be offended by this feedback, so she should not be offended.” “I understood the email, so they should understand it.” “I enjoy this kind of small talk, so they must too.” “I would want direct advice, so they must want it.”
The communication task is to notice when your own reaction is doing more work than evidence about the other person. Ask what they understood before defending what you intended.
A related error is the false consensus effect: people overestimate how common their own beliefs, preferences, choices, and behaviors are (Ross et al., 1977). If I think an action is ethical, I may assume most reasonable people agree. If I dislike a policy, I may assume most people secretly dislike it too. If I would accept a risk, I may assume others would. False consensus is a population-level version of egocentric projection.
Keep the levels distinct. Egocentric projection is the inferential process by which my own state anchors a judgment about your state; false consensus is one possible population judgment about how widely a view is shared. Both imply a useful diagnostic: my judgment of another person contains information about them, but also about the values, expectations, experiences, and concerns through which I interpreted them.
People can also misjudge how self-serving others’ accounts will be. Kruger and Gilovich (1999) studied such “naïve cynicism” in responsibility judgments. Expecting a colleague to claim all the credit can make their explanation sound strategic before we have examined it.
Another error is the illusion of transparency: people overestimate how visible their internal states are to others (Gilovich et al., 1998). We think our anxiety, gratitude, embarrassment, confusion, or affection is obvious. It often is not. A student assumes the teacher can see they are confused. A manager assumes employees know they appreciate their effort. A friend assumes their hurt feelings are visible. A negotiator assumes the other side can see their constraint. Much conflict arises because people expect others to read emotions that have not been expressed.
The counterpart is the illusion of understanding: overestimating how much of the context in our own mind survived in the message. Likewise, faces, bodies, and brief behavioral samples can contain information without becoming reliable dictionaries of a person’s exact emotion, motive, or truthfulness (Ambady & Rosenthal, 1993; Barrett et al., 2019; DePaulo et al., 2003). Verbal information and direct questions are often more diagnostic than confident interpretation of isolated expressions (Gesn & Ickes, 1999; Hall & Schmid Mast, 2007). If something is important, do not rely on hints, microexpressions, or silence. State it, ask, and verify.
In the deadline case, the employee’s defensiveness may reflect guilt, but it may also reflect an innocent misunderstanding or a history of blame. Treat the inference as a hypothesis that the next exchange can revise.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
33  Communication: Language Is Not a File Transfer

title: 33  Communication: Language Is Not a File Transfer
text:
Ask rather than merely imagine
Perspective-taking means imagining how a situation looks to another person. Perspective-getting means asking them and listening to the answer. Imagination can generate a useful question, but it cannot supply the other person’s answer.
Eyal, Steffel, and Epley (2018) found that people were often more accurate when they asked others for their perspective than when they merely tried to imagine it. This distinction is crucial. Perspective-taking can become confident projection. Perspective-getting corrects it.
For the manager, a useful question is: “When did you learn that the deadline had changed?” That may uncover a missing message rather than reluctance to accept responsibility. Follow with a paraphrase the colleague can correct: “So you were still working toward Friday because the new date was only discussed with the client team?”
Direct answers can also be incomplete, especially when honesty carries a cost. Perspective-getting works best when the question is specific and the response can be given without avoidable pressure; consequential factual claims may still need independent checking.
crumbs: Part V. Persuasion, Communication, and Connection
33  Communication: Language Is Not a File Transfer

title: 33  Communication: Language Is Not a File Transfer
section: Close the loop: utterance to shared-enough meaning
text:
Close the loop: utterance to shared-enough meaning
The manager’s first email treated understanding as private: the sender knew the intended meaning and assumed everyone else would recover it. The revised email treats understanding as a sequence:
Utterance → interpretation → test → correction → shared-enough meaning.
At the meeting, each person first maps where they believed ownership changed. The manager asks for examples rather than motives. Participants reflect what they heard before defending a view. Differences become visible: one handoff was never defined, one deadline changed without reaching operations, and one employee interpreted an ambiguous sentence through a previous experience of blame. The group does not need identical feelings or a single story. It needs enough grounded meaning to assign the next action and enough openness to revise the map when new evidence appears.
This is the boundary between communication and persuasion. Persuasion seeks a warranted change in another person’s model. Communication makes the models mutually testable. Either can support the other, but a communicator has not established shared meaning merely because the other person complied.






CautionEvidence Boundary



Words, body language, facial expression, and silence are informative but noisy. None provides direct access to a person’s hidden state, and confident interpretations can become self-confirming. Grounding can establish shared-enough meaning for a purpose; it cannot prove identical understanding, agreement, sincerity, or future behavior. Ask, reflect, and verify in proportion to the stakes.

title: 33  Communication: Language Is Not a File Transfer
text:
Practice Lab
Choose a recent high-stakes email, message, or instruction. Produce a one-page grounding map with: literal words; intended meaning; at least two plausible interpretations; missing context; power or relationship cues; a perspective-getting question; a reflective summary; a correction invitation; and the shared action required. Rewrite the message so another reader can identify its context, intent, relational stance, next action, and repair path without guessing.

title: 33  Communication: Language Is Not a File Transfer
text:
Take it forward
Choose one interpretation you have been treating as settled in a conversation. Turn it into a question, listen to the answer, and offer a summary the other person can correct. The useful outcome is an understanding both people can work with, even when they still disagree.

title: 34  Connection and Repair: Warm Honesty Makes Truth Usable
text:
Learning goals
Understand accurately, speak with warm honesty, and repair what breaks
A project manager receives a colleague’s section after the client deadline and writes, “This is unacceptable. We need to discuss your reliability.” The colleague replies, “You never told me the client changed the date.”
The manager checks the email thread. The new date was discussed with the client, but the colleague was never copied in. There is still a delivery problem to solve, and now there is an unfair accusation to repair. Explaining the original intention will not do both jobs.
We will follow this fictional exchange through listening, a more accurate account of what happened, and a response that accepts responsibility without losing sight of the work.
