title: 38  Designing Better Agreements
section: Start with a minimum viable agreement
text:
Start with a minimum viable agreement
The chapter uses six required fields as its spine:



Table 38.1: Six fields that turn a package into a minimum viable agreement









Required field
Agreement-design purpose




Owner
Assign the promise to a named role with authority and resources.


Measure
Define the observable event, metric, threshold, and deadline.


Verification source
Name the record, data source, inspection right, and challenge process.


Review date
State when the responsible parties will examine performance and who may approve a revision.


Failure rule
Define cure, escalation, consequence, and treatment of relevant external shocks.


Exit
Define termination rights, transition, surviving duties, and any appeal.






For the supplier’s forecast-and-capacity obligation, the minimum record could look like this:



Table 38.2: A minimum viable agreement for one supplier obligation









Field
Illustrative operating term




Owner
The buyer’s demand-planning lead submits the rolling forecast; the supplier’s account lead confirms available capacity.


Measure
Submission is time-stamped; capacity inside the agreed band is confirmed within two working days.


Verification source
Both parties can inspect the shared forecast, order, and confirmation log.


Review date
Operational leads review the record monthly; designated commercial sponsors approve any change to the band.


Failure rule
A buyer-caused late forecast moves the delivery clock; a supplier-controlled miss after confirmed capacity activates the stated cure and service-credit rule.


Exit
Repeated uncured failure activates the agreed termination and transition process, including treatment of dedicated tooling and surviving duties.






The record is deliberately small. It does not settle every legal question, and legal drafting still requires the relevant expertise and jurisdiction. It does make the operational promise testable before complexity accumulates.






TipAdd an advanced module only for a diagnosed problem






Table 38.3: Route a diagnosed agreement problem to an optional module










Diagnosed problem
Optional module
Use only if…




The parties do not know which issues the other side values most
Multiple equivalent simultaneous offers (MESOs)
The packages are sincere, understandable, and approximately equivalent to the offer-maker


The parties make materially different forecasts
Contingent term
The outcome is measurable, verifiable, sufficiently controllable, and worth the contracting burden


Important information is sensitive or a claim is consequential
Staged disclosure and claim verification
Disclosure is reciprocal or protected and a credible verification path exists


Agenda, authority, communication, or impasse blocks progress
Process or third-party rule
Decision rights, confidentiality, timing, and transfer of control can be specified


A signed agreement may leave mutually beneficial trades unexplored
Protected post-settlement search
The signed agreement remains the fallback and either party may stop without penalty






If no diagnosed problem fits a module, do not add one. Complexity creates interpretation, monitoring, gaming, and enforcement costs of its own.

38  Designing Better Agreements

title: 38  Designing Better Agreements
section: Optional module 1: Reveal priorities through packages
text:
Optional module 1: Reveal priorities through packages
One powerful tool for discovering integrative agreements is the use of multiple equivalent simultaneous offers, or MESOs.
A MESO is a set of two or more offers made at the same time, each designed to be roughly equal in value to the offer-maker but different in how value is allocated across issues. The other side’s reaction can provide clues to its priorities.
The supplier might offer three packages it has privately valued as roughly equivalent:

Capacity package: lower unit price, firm annual minimum, narrow monthly call-off band.
Flexibility package: higher unit price, wider call-off band, quarterly forecast commitment.
Investment package: middle unit price, buyer contribution to dedicated tooling, longer term, and an exit schedule for unrecovered investment.

The buyer can compare these trade-offs without disclosing its reservation value. Its choice gives the supplier a starting point for a more specific question.
A comparison can teach the supplier which trade the buyer prefers, while giving the buyer several workable ways to proceed. Research has found economic and relational benefits from MESOs in studied bargaining settings (Leonardelli et al., 2019), but a preference is still a clue to investigate. If several terms differ, the choice alone cannot identify which term drove it.
Prepare the packages carefully. Approximate equivalence is from the offer-maker’s perspective, not an assurance that the counterpart will regard them as equally attractive. Each must be sincere and understandable; a deliberately unavailable decoy would undermine the exchange.

Turn a package into a diagnostic question
Return to the supplier’s capacity and flexibility packages. Ask which is closer to the buyer’s needs, then ask why. A preference for flexibility might reflect expected demand variation, reluctance to commit cash, or a hidden approval constraint.
A useful next question isolates one trade: “If we widened the call-off band, could you accept a longer forecast commitment?” The answer gives more information than simply treating the first package choice as a stable priority ranking.
crumbs: Part VI. Negotiating Joint Decisions
38  Designing Better Agreements

title: 38  Designing Better Agreements
section: Optional module 2: Use contingent terms when forecasts differ
text:
Optional module 2: Use contingent terms when forecasts differ






Figure 38.1: This author’s prescriptive synthesis shows four agreement-design tools together with the conditions that make each defensible. The figure is a design checklist, not a validated universal sequence or a claim that the tools necessarily improve an agreement.



The conditions in Figure 38.1 are substantive. A MESO is informative only when its packages are sincere, understandable, and approximately equivalent to the offer-maker; a preference is a clue, not proof of a stable priority. A contingent term is useful only when the outcome can be measured and verified, incentives and control are aligned, enforcement is credible, and sabotage and risk-bearing remain acceptable. Post-settlement search protects rather than reopens the signed deal only when the parties explicitly and voluntarily preserve it as the fallback. None of these tools substitutes for comparing the package with each BATNA or testing feasibility, fairness, legality, consent, and implementation.
A contingent contract makes a term depend on a future outcome. Suppose a builder expects early completion while a buyer fears delay. A bonus for finishing early and compensation for specified delays may offer each something it values, provided the possible payments, risks, and incentives are acceptable. Confidence alone does not make the arrangement beneficial.
The main questions concern measurement and control. Define completion so that speed cannot be achieved by omitting quality checks. Specify which delays the builder controls, how external disruptions are treated, who verifies the date, and how a disputed finding can be challenged. A payment tied to a vague “successful launch” simply moves the disagreement into the future.
Contingent terms also create new incentives. A party that controls the measurement or part of the outcome may be able to influence the payment in ways the other did not intend. The contracting and verification burden must be worthwhile relative to a simpler fixed term (Bazerman & Gillespie, 1999).

Apply the logic to supplier capacity
The buyer expects monthly demand to remain within a narrow band. The supplier expects volatile peaks that would require overtime and displaced orders. Arguing about whose forecast is right will not create capacity. A contingent term can allocate the consequence:

The buyer supplies a rolling twelve-week forecast and commits only to the first four weeks.
Volume inside the agreed band receives the base price.
Volume above the band is accepted only when capacity is confirmed and carries a predeclared surge price.
If the buyer’s committed forecast arrives late, the delivery clock moves by the same number of days.
If the supplier confirms capacity and then misses a dependency it controls, service credits apply; repeated failure activates cure and exit rights.

This term turns forecast disagreement into a measurable allocation of responsibility. It still needs definitions: what counts as a forecast, confirmation, surge volume, supplier-controlled delay, external shock, and cure? The agreement should avoid cliffs that reward strategic reporting just above or below a threshold. When parties disagree about the future, let future evidence affect terms only when measurement, control, incentives, and enforcement are credible (Bazerman & Gillespie, 1999).
crumbs: Part VI. Negotiating Joint Decisions
38  Designing Better Agreements

title: 38  Designing Better Agreements
section: Optional module 3: Stage disclosure and verification
text:
Optional module 3: Stage disclosure and verification
Integrative negotiation needs information, but disclosure can create vulnerability. Stage it. Begin with interests and lower-risk priorities that explain a position—“Delivery reliability matters because our customer contract contains penalties”—and ask for comparable information. Use the answer to propose a trade, not to impose the maximum pressure it reveals. Exact reservation values and confidential alternatives remain private unless disclosure produces a clear process, legal, or agreement benefit.
Trust is updated through response. If a disclosed concern is immediately exploited, future disclosure stops. If it generates a reciprocal question, verification path, or useful package, additional openness becomes safer. The goal is neither confession nor blind trust. It is enough validated information to design terms that can be observed and governed.

Ask before inferring
Chapter 33 distinguished perspective-taking from perspective-getting. Imagination can reduce egocentrism and improve strategic thinking, but it can also project one’s own priorities onto the counterpart; direct questions provide new, correctable evidence (Eyal et al., 2018; Galinsky et al., 2008). Ask what a term protects, who must approve it, what risk worries the other side, and what implementation success would look like. Partial or strategic answers remain possible, so verify consequential claims and reward useful disclosure with reciprocity rather than immediate exploitation.


Culture changes the meaning of a move
Culture, profession, organization, and law can change what a move means. Directness can signal efficiency or disrespect; silence can mean refusal, consultation, deference, or thought; a concession can invite reciprocity or threaten face. Cross-cultural negotiation studies support attention to such variation but do not license reading a group average as a counterpart’s personality, and common measures do not predict joint gains uniformly across settings (Brett & Okumura, 1998; Brett et al., 2021).
Return to the Meaning Audit in Culture and Identity. Treat cultural knowledge as a hypothesis and ask how this interaction works:

How is disagreement expressed safely here?
Who must be consulted before a proposal can become a commitment?
Does “yes” mean agreement, acknowledgment, or willingness to continue?
Which terms need explicit definition rather than assumed shared meaning?
Would a public concession, correction, or apology impose an avoidable face cost?

The prescriptive rule is simple: use group-level evidence to generate questions, then test meaning, authority, and consent in the particular interaction (Gunia et al., 2016).


Replace lie detection with claim verification
Negotiation creates incentives to manage information. A person may lie by commission, omit a material fact, answer a different question, or use literally true statements to create a false impression—the practice called paltering (Rogers et al., 2017). But privacy is not automatically deception. A negotiator may decline to reveal a reservation value, private preference, or confidential alternative without making a false claim.
The dangerous response is to become a human lie detector. A meta-analysis of 206 documents involving 24,483 judges found average unaided truth–lie classification of 54 percent: 47 percent of lies were identified as deceptive and 61 percent of truths as truthful (Bond & DePaulo, 2006). Reviews conclude that nonverbal cues to deception are faint and unreliable (Vrij et al., 2019). A pause, gaze shift, nervous movement, polished delivery, or confident tone does not reliably diagnose deceit. Such behavior can also reflect stress, memory search, language, status, culture, or fear of being disbelieved.






Figure 38.2: Beliefs about behavioral “tells” can be much stronger than the observed associations. The observed points reproduce all nine behaviors in the source comparison; student and professional belief estimates were available for seven, but were not reported there for nodding or hand movements. The values describe group-level associations and beliefs—not the diagnostic accuracy of a cue for an individual person. No single behavior proves that someone is lying. Original redraw of Sporer and Schwandt (2007), Figure 1.



This is the same inference problem developed in The Predictive Mind, Beliefs That Defend Themselves, and Communication Is Joint Inference. Suspicion supplies a prior; ambiguous behavior then appears to confirm it. The correction is not greater confidence in reading people. It is a better evidence path.
For every material claim, ask:

What exactly has been asserted, and what has merely been implied?
What record, date, document, authority, reference, test, or independent source could verify it?
Can the claim become a representation, warranty, milestone, inspection right, or contingent term?
What happens if the claim is mistaken rather than deceptive?

Direct questions can reduce deception, but they do not guarantee truth. Schweitzer and Croson (1999) found an overall reduction in deception in their first study; in their second, direct questions particularly reduced omission but could increase lies of commission. Therefore ask a precise question and verify the answer when it matters. Good agreement design makes important claims testable without pretending that every inconsistency reveals intent.

title: 38  Designing Better Agreements
text:
Optional module 4: Negotiate the process
A promising package can fail because the wrong people are in the room or because tentative suggestions are treated as commitments. Agree early on who can approve terms, which information is confidential, and when a proposal becomes binding.
For the supplier discussion, the buyer might say: “Could we first list the issues and compare two complete packages? Our planning leads can test capacity, while the commercial sponsors approve any price or volume commitment.” This allows operational knowledge into the search without confusing expertise with authority.
Record how an impasse will be handled as well. A pause for data, an internal approval, or an outside facilitator solves a different problem from another price concession. Revisit earlier assumptions when new information changes the package’s value; a process diagram should not make agreement feel predetermined.







NoteOptional module: when direct negotiation needs a third party



A third party can repair a process or replace it. These are different interventions. The mediation–arbitration distinction below follows the non-adjudicatory versus adjudicatory allocation of authority used in the UNCITRAL frameworks; the fit and risk columns are the author’s decision aid, not comparative-effect estimates (UNCITRAL, 2022).



Table 38.4: Author decision aid: mediation assists party choice; arbitration transfers decision authority












Process
Third party’s primary role
Who controls the outcome?
Best fit
Central risk




Mediation
Structure communication, clarify issues, test assumptions, and help the parties search for settlement
The parties: the mediator does not ordinarily impose a settlement
The parties still need a negotiated solution, especially when communication, trust, emotion, or option search has stalled
Power imbalance, strategic delay, pressure to settle, or no agreement


Arbitration
Hear the parties’ submissions and decide the dispute under agreed rules
The arbitrator or tribunal, to the extent specified by the agreement, rules, and governing law
The parties need finality, authoritative interpretation, or a decision after bargaining has failed
Loss of outcome control, cost, adversarial escalation, and a result neither party would have designed






Mediation is therefore not “soft arbitration,” and arbitration is not “strong mediation.” A mediator can reframe, carry proposals, surface interests, manage difficult interaction, and reality-test a package while leaving acceptance to the parties. An arbitrator receives authority to decide. The precise legal effects, confidentiality, review, and enforceability depend on the clause, institutional rules, governing law, and jurisdiction.
Evidence does not justify treating mediation as universally superior. A 2012 review of the preceding decade found diverse goals, settings, mediator strategies, and outcomes, but relatively few controlled studies comparing specific strategies or observing actual mediation behavior (Wall & Dunne, 2012). It remains a boundary on what that literature had established, not a current comparative-effect estimate. Choose the process by its task: Do the parties need help making a joint decision, or do they need someone else to make a decision?
A staged commercial clause might move from operational leads, to executive sponsors, to mediation, and finally to arbitration or litigation. It should specify the triggering dispute, decision authority, time limits, interim obligations, applicable rules, and how urgent action can be taken. Legal drafting requires advice for the relevant jurisdiction; the design principle is to make the transfer of control explicit.
Hybrid procedures such as mediation–arbitration offer a settlement opportunity plus finality and may produce perceived time or cost savings in some disputes. They also create a predictable problem when one person performs both roles: information disclosed to a mediator in confidence may appear relevant when that person later becomes the decision-maker. Parties may become less candid or doubt impartiality. Barsky (2013) analyzes these risks in family-law disputes; recent American Arbitration Association commercial-practice guidance identifies the same concerns about candor, ex parte information, informed consent, and the integrity of an eventual award (American Arbitration Association, 2025). If a hybrid is used, the parties should decide in advance whether separate neutrals will serve, what information can cross stages, and whether renewed consent is required before the role changes. Potential speed should not hide a change in authority or confidentiality.



Optional extension: search safely after agreement
A post-settlement settlement searches for a mutually preferred replacement after an initial agreement is secure. The essential condition is explicit: the existing agreement remains in force unless every required party voluntarily accepts the replacement, and either party can stop the search without penalty.
The buyer and supplier might discover that a different payment schedule releases cash or reduces risk for both. They can investigate that trade without surrendering the terms already secured. If one side uses the search to reopen settled concessions under pressure, the protection has failed.
Use the procedure only when the original agreement is secure, participants have authority, and the possible gain justifies further effort. It is an opportunity to improve the deal, not an obligation to keep negotiating after “yes.”

title: 38  Designing Better Agreements
section: Complete the minimum agreement: implementation and review
text:
Complete the minimum agreement: implementation and review

Ethics of value creation
Mutual-gain language does not establish mutual benefit. Examine whether the package makes material costs visible, preserves meaningful refusal, and assigns responsibility to someone able to carry it. A contingent bonus may encourage effort or encourage gaming; a menu may reveal priorities or hide an unattractive common term.
Ask each side to explain the agreement and its failure rules in its own words. If the explanations differ, resolve the discrepancy before relying on the signature. Legal enforceability and disclosure duties require advice for the relevant jurisdiction; operational clarity supports that work but does not replace it.


Turn the supplier package into operating rules
Return to the opening disagreement about the urgent batch. “Flexible call-offs” becomes usable when the agreement specifies the permitted volume band, forecast deadline, confirmation procedure, and surge price. A shared record then shows whether the buyer requested capacity, whether the supplier accepted it, and which clock started.
The following priority map can be used to question the proposed terms. Its entries are illustrative guesses to verify with the counterpart, rather than facts inferred from the labels “buyer” and “supplier.”
The package becomes implementable only after the parties name owners, evidence, and review. The buyer owns the rolling forecast; the supplier confirms capacity within two working days. A shared dashboard records committed volume, accepted surge orders, defects, and dependency delays. A monthly operating review handles forecasts and quality; a quarterly governance review can revise bands and investment milestones. Cure periods precede exit except for safety or fraud. Disputes escalate first to named operational leads, then commercial sponsors, then the agreed formal mechanism. The agreement records which terms survive termination and how dedicated-tooling value is recovered.
Agreement architecture therefore completes six fields: owner, measure, verification source, review date, failure rule, and exit. A deal is not complete when it looks clever on paper. It is complete when the parties can carry it out, detect failure, and adapt without inventing a new negotiation each time.

CautionEvidence Boundary



MESOs can reveal preferences only when the packages are sincere, understandable, and close in value to the offer-maker. A preference between packages need not reveal a stable priority; strategic response, culture, and context also matter. Contingent terms work only when outcomes are measurable, verifiable, sufficiently controllable, enforceable, and worth the complexity. Cultural evidence describes distributions, not individuals. Demeanor does not reliably identify deception. Mediation does not guarantee settlement or fairness, and arbitration does not guarantee a correct decision. Signing does not establish informed consent, fairness, or implementation capacity.

title: 38  Designing Better Agreements
text:
Practice Lab
Produce a one-page minimum viable agreement for the supplier obligation most likely to fail. Complete its six fields: owner, measure, verification source, review date, failure rule, and exit. Then stress-test the record against one plausible failure and revise whichever field did not provide a clear response.
Choose no more than one optional module from Table 38.3. State the diagnosed problem that justifies it and add only the information that module requires—for example, two or three sincere packages for unclear priorities, one measurable contingent term for forecast disagreement, or one explicit escalation rule for process failure. If no module is justified, record “none.” Multiple packages, full contingent-contract drafting, independent audits, detailed mediation or arbitration clauses, and multi-shock testing belong in an advanced agreement-design file, not in the minimum exercise.

Return to the term in your agreement most likely to become disputed. Can both sides tell what was promised, how fulfillment will be checked, and what happens if circumstances change? Add the provisions needed to answer those questions, then check that the extra complexity has not made the agreement harder to carry out.

title: Part VII. Designing Better Decisions
text:
Questions to carry forward
The committee knows it should hear independent judgments, yet the most senior member still speaks first. A student plans to study, yet the phone remains beside the keyboard. Knowing the problem has not changed the situation that keeps producing it.
The final part turns explanation into design. Behavior design asks what would make a useful action easier to repeat. Choice architecture examines how options are presented and how people move from intention to action. Decision hygiene considers the procedures through which a group gathers evidence, compares judgments, and learns from results.
Each intervention is a proposal to test. A new default, reminder, or review process may help, do little, or create a different problem. We need to identify whose goal it serves, what outcome would count as improvement, and how affected people can question or leave the arrangement.
We return to the hiring committee with a more useful question than whether its members are rational. How could its next decision be made easier to examine, challenge, and improve?

title: Part VII. Designing Better Decisions

Where does the intended action break down?
What small change to the conditions addresses that obstacle?
What evidence will show improvement, failure, or harm?

title: 39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier
text:
Learning goals
Give a good intention a workable next step
Imagine a student who sincerely intends to study before opening email. Each morning the laptop opens onto the inbox, the phone sits beside the keyboard, the first study task is vague, and every message offers a small unit of completion. “Care more” is not yet a design. The current environment contains a prompt, an easy action, and immediate feedback—for email.
The redesign gives the better behavior the same structural advantages. The laptop opens to the problem set. The first task is already written. The phone begins in another room. “After I place my coffee on the desk, I will solve the first visible question before opening email.” A checkmark makes the start visible. Nothing guarantees sustained study. But the desired action no longer has to defeat a complete competing system.
Behavior design is prescriptive; habit science is descriptive. Explaining a loop does not tell us whether the right response is training, cue removal, substitution, social support, treatment, a new workflow, or structural change. Design begins only after the target and competing behavior are observed precisely.
Behavior change can be difficult when stable cues, immediate consequences, and environmental constraints favor the existing behavior (Wood & Rünger, 2016). Several tools improve average outcomes in specified settings; none is a universal prescription. A useful toolkit begins with diagnosis rather than prescription.

title: 39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier
text:
Apply one five-step workflow: define the behavior, diagnose the bottleneck, redesign the decisive point, measure, and review.
Use a diagnostic or planning framework only when it clarifies a specific bottleneck.
Test whether one small redesign improves an endorsed outcome while protecting agency and recovery.

39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier

title: 39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier
text:
One primary workflow
Use the same five-step record for personal and organizational behavior:



Table 39.1: A minimum behavior-design record










Step
Required output
Governing question




1. Define the behavior
One observable target action, the competing action, and the situation in which one displaces the other
What would a camera or reliable record show?


2. Diagnose the bottleneck
The cue, immediate function or consequence, and the main constraint on the target action
Why does the current response win at this moment?


3. Redesign the decisive point
One change to the cue, action size, friction, prompt, support, or immediate feedback
What is the smallest change that directly addresses the diagnosed bottleneck?


4. Measure
Baseline, one process signal, one outcome signal, a prediction, and a time-bounded test
What observable pattern would show that the diagnosis was useful?


5. Review
A review date and a keep, revise, or stop rule, including recovery after a lapse or harm
What will change next if the prediction succeeds or fails?






Use this record to connect each change with a diagnosis, returning to earlier steps when new information changes the picture. B=MAP and COM-B can sharpen diagnosis; implementation intentions, WOOP, friction changes, temptation bundling, and precommitment can support a selected redesign. They are optional aids, not a bundle that every intervention must contain.






NoteResearch note: what the design workflow claims





Figure 39.1 is a teaching synthesis, not a published stage model. B=MAP describes motivation, ability, and a prompt converging at a behavioral moment (Fogg, 2009). COM-B treats capability, opportunity, and motivation as interacting conditions in a system that includes feedback from behavior; it does not rank them as layers (Michie et al., 2011). Research on implementation intentions, habits, and behavior-change maintenance supports planning, feedback, and preparation for obstacles, but not one universal sequence (Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006; Kwasnicka et al., 2016; Wood & Rünger, 2016). The figure therefore separates a practical design workflow from the evidence models it draws upon. The recovery note addresses a contingent response: a lapse or harm may reveal a cue, constraint, support need, or goal that needs reconsideration.

title: 39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier
section: Optional lens: diagnose the moment with B=MAP
text:
Optional lens: diagnose the moment with B=MAP
The Fogg Behavior Model offers one moment-level lens: behavior happens when motivation, ability, and a prompt converge (Fogg, 2009, 2020). Use it when Step 2 suggests that a behavior repeatedly fails at a particular moment and it is unclear whether willingness, feasibility, or the prompt is missing. For a desired repeated behavior whose motivation is volatile, making action easier can be more reliable than trying to keep motivation permanently high. Motivation often fluctuates; ability and prompts can sometimes be redesigned.






NoteResearch Lens: COM-B widens the diagnosis



COM-B asks whether capability, opportunity, and motivation converge (Michie et al., 2011). Capability includes skill, knowledge, energy, and physical ability. Opportunity includes time, tools, permission, safety, and social context. Motivation includes reflective and automatic processes. A motivational speech cannot fix a broken opportunity structure. COM-B is useful when B=MAP’s moment-level diagnosis needs a broader account of resources and institutions.



Table 39.2: COM-B and B=MAP as complementary diagnostic lenses










Diagnostic lens
Question
Inspect before prescribing




Capability
Can the person perform it?
Knowledge, skill, memory, physical capacity, emotional regulation


Opportunity
Does the environment allow and support it?
Time, access, tools, permission, safety, norms


Motivation
Do reflective and automatic motives point toward it?
Values, incentives, emotion, identity, habit, anticipated reward


Prompt
What calls for action at the right moment?
Reminder, event, place, internal state, anchor routine


Ability now
Is the action feasible in this real moment?
Time, effort, money, complexity, social risk, disruption






These models simplify a complex system. They organize questions; they do not end diagnosis. Poverty, disability, unsafe work, discrimination, addiction, and organizational power cannot be repaired by a better notification.

39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier

title: 39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier
text:
Tiny is strategic
Old behavior is practiced, cued, familiar, and usually rewarded now. A new behavior is uncertain and its benefit may arrive later. The first action should therefore be small enough to survive an ordinary low-motivation day: open the manuscript; put on the shoes; write one question; take one breath before responding. Tiny is not the destination. It is an entry point that lowers friction, reduces threat, creates data, and can grow after it begins.
Fogg’s practical recipe is: After I [reliable anchor], I will [tiny behavior]. Then I will [authentically acknowledge completion]. The anchor supplies a prompt; the tiny action lowers the ability threshold; acknowledgment makes progress detectable. The full recipe is a practitioner heuristic rather than a neurological law. Its value should be tested against the broader evidence on cues, feasibility, reinforcement, and repetition.
Motivation arrives in waves. A workshop, health result, deadline, or inspiring idea may make an ambitious plan feel easy. The plan then has to run on a tired Wednesday. Use high motivation for setup—schedule the class, prepare the tools, remove the app, arrange the partner, automate the transfer, write the first prompt—rather than as fuel the routine must consume every day.
crumbs: Part VII. Designing Better Decisions
39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier

title: 39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier
section: Optional tools for a diagnosed bottleneck
text:
Optional tools for a diagnosed bottleneck
Choose a tool only after the workflow has identified what prevents the target action. A goal that is clear but not retrieved at the critical moment may need a cue-linked plan. An action that is too difficult may need a smaller start or less friction. A delayed benefit may need immediate feedback or a carefully chosen reward. Predictable future temptation may justify precommitment. Using more tools is not evidence of a better design.
Implementation intentions turn vague goals into cue-linked behaviors. Instead of saying “I will study more,” a student says: “If I finish breakfast on weekdays, then I study for twenty-five minutes before email.” Instead of “I will be less defensive,” a manager says: “If I receive criticism, then I ask one clarifying question before explaining.” Instead of “I will save money,” a person says: “If I receive my salary, then I transfer 10 percent to savings immediately.” A complete plan makes the if/then, where, when, and how recoverable at the critical moment. Date-and-time planning prompts have improved follow-through in vaccination studies, illustrating how a valued intention can fail until it is attached to a concrete execution opportunity (Milkman et al., 2011).
WOOP adds a useful self-regulation bridge: Wish, Outcome, Obstacle, Plan. The person identifies a feasible and meaningful wish, imagines the valued outcome, identifies the real internal or contextual obstacle, and forms an if-then plan. The exercise connects a valued future with an anticipated obstacle, rather than assuming that imagining success will make action follow. Evidence on mental contrasting with implementation intentions supports modest average benefits with variation across goals and settings; it is a planning aid, not a guarantee (Oettingen, 2012; Wang et al., 2021).
Friction is a behavioral force. When friction is an important diagnosed bottleneck, reducing it can support a desired behavior; adding proportionate friction can interrupt an unwanted one. Keep the book visible and the phone away. Remove saved payment information. Put exercise clothes by the bed. Create a meeting template. Make near-miss reporting simple and nonpunitive. Require a decision question before scheduling a meeting. Many behaviors live near the margin, so small barriers or small reductions in effort can matter. They will not repair missing capability, unsafe conditions, weak incentives, or an unwanted objective.
Defaults change what happens when no active choice is made, so they belong to the choice path rather than to this moment-level behavior diagnosis. Chapter 40 examines their mechanisms, boundary conditions, and ethics. Here, keep the intervention local: change the effort required to perform the target or competing action without treating non-response as informed preference.
Temptation bundling attaches an immediate reward to a beneficial behavior whose benefits are delayed. In a field experiment, making tempting audiobooks available only at the gym initially increased visits (Milkman et al., 2014). A person might likewise reserve a favorite podcast for walking or special coffee for difficult reading. The bundle works best when the reward is exclusive enough to pull the desired behavior and does not sabotage the goal. It can be fragile when routines are disrupted or the tempting activity becomes available elsewhere.
Precommitment protects future behavior from predictable future states (Thaler & Shefrin, 1981). Examples include automatic savings, self-imposed or externally structured deadlines, app blockers, accountability partners, public commitments, cancellation penalties, locked accounts, or working with a partner. A good commitment device preserves dignity and allows recovery after failure. A bad one creates shame without changing the loop.
crumbs: Part VII. Designing Better Decisions
39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier

title: 39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier
text:
Design an attention boundary
External systems compete for the same cue and action. Notifications, autoplay, badges, saved payment, infinite feeds, and social feedback reduce the effort required to enter their loops. Even the mere presence of one’s phone can occupy cognitive capacity in some settings (Ward et al., 2017). When attention switches away from an unfinished task, part of the previous task can remain mentally active—attention residue—and reduce performance on the next task (Leroy, 2009).
A boundary makes the intended action easier to continue and the competing loop less available. It may be a device location, notification rule, website block, timebox, saved stopping point, shutdown ritual, or agreement with another person. The design question is not “How do I resist every interruption?” It is “Which boundary keeps the intended task from being asked to win the same contest repeatedly?”
Digital engagement also needs an audit:



Table 39.3: A humane digital-loop audit











Loop feature
Helpful use
Capture risk
Agency safeguard




Trigger
Timely medication or coordination prompt
Continuous interruption and anxiety cue
User-controlled timing and batching


Easy action
Removes needless access friction
One-tap entry into an endless loop
Visible stopping point and deliberate continuation


Variable feedback
Makes practice interesting
Repeated checking for uncertain social reward
Bounded sessions and honest expectations


Investment
Saves progress or supports relationships
Sunk data and streaks make exit painful
Portability, pause, easy cancellation


Measurement
Tracks a learner’s endorsed outcome
Optimizes clicks or time while welfare falls
Measure goal attainment, well-being, and opportunity cost






High engagement, variable reward, or frequent use does not by itself diagnose addiction. The ethical issue is whether a system exploits uncertainty, social anxiety, or craving against the user’s interests and whether stopping remains practicable.
crumbs: Part VII. Designing Better Decisions
39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier

title: 39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier
text:
Organizational habits
Organizations also repeat patterns, although an organizational routine is not simply an individual habit scaled up. It involves several people, roles, tools, and rules, and may be maintained by deliberate incentives or formal requirements as well as automatic responses.
A meeting that rewards confident updates and makes bad news costly can repeatedly hide useful information. Calling for openness changes little if the first person to reveal a problem is punished. Apply the workflow to an observable interaction: who does what, what follows immediately, and which part of the process could support a better response?

39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier

title: 39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier
text:
Mini-case: the defensive meeting loop
A product team says it wants psychological safety and better decisions. Yet every Monday meeting follows the same pattern. A project lead presents progress. A senior manager asks a skeptical question. The project lead hears the question as criticism and begins explaining why the team made reasonable choices. Other members go quiet. The manager interprets the defensiveness as lack of ownership and asks more pointed questions. The project lead becomes more defensive. The meeting ends with action items but little learning.
Nobody intended to create this pattern. The senior manager intended to improve the project. The project lead intended to protect the team. Other members intended to avoid conflict. But together they created a routine.
The episode suggests hypotheses to investigate. A skeptical question may cue a defensive reply, while explaining could protect the project lead’s standing in the moment. It could also reflect a genuine misunderstanding or missing context. Ask participants what they understood and inspect repeated interactions before treating status protection as the established motive or calling the routine a habit.
A redesigned routine would not begin with a motivational speech about openness. It would change the loop. Before each update, the team names one uncertainty and one assumption that could be wrong. The manager asks: “What would be most useful for us to challenge?” The project lead has an implementation intention: if a question feels like criticism, then I will first ask, “Can you say more about the risk you are seeing?” A second person is assigned to summarize the strongest concern before action items are set. The meeting ends with one learning note, not only tasks.
The revised procedure gives participants another response to practice, but the manager’s subsequent conduct will determine whether candor is actually safe. Track whether concerns appear earlier and receive useful responses, including concerns that challenge the manager’s own view.
This case illustrates the deepest practical lesson of habit science: do not rely on the self you hope will appear in the moment. Design for the self and the team that will actually be there.

title: 39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier
text:
Habit design is power
Changing cues, effort, and consequences changes what other people are likely to do. The student can endorse a study arrangement for himself; a platform designer or manager must also consider whose goals the arrangement serves.
Ask whether users can understand the design, choose otherwise, and discover its costs. A streak may encourage practice while making rest feel like failure; a reporting dashboard may improve coordination while exposing staff to surveillance. Measure the outcome people value, alongside any burden or loss of control. Increased use alone does not establish a benefit.

title: 39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier
section: Fresh starts, identity, and social context
text:
Fresh starts, identity, and social context
Stable contexts help cues retrieve practiced responses. Moving, changing jobs, or altering a recurring schedule can disrupt the cues that normally retrieve a response without necessarily erasing what was learned. A temporal landmark can also create a psychological “fresh start” (Dai et al., 2014). A transition may therefore be a useful occasion to prepare a new starting routine, though the landmark itself does not establish a lasting habit.
But contexts are not only physical. They are also social and identity-based. People repeat behaviors partly because those behaviors answer the question: What do people like us do, and who am I becoming when I do this? Identity-based motivation can make difficulty mean “this matters to people like me” or “this proves I do not belong” (Oyserman, 2009). Use identity as a flexible hypothesis—“I am becoming someone who asks one question before defending”—not a purity test. A rigid identity can turn rest into failure, a lapse into shame, and revision into betrayal.

39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier

title: 39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier
text:
Relapse, recovery, and ethics
Many behavior-change attempts include lapses, especially when old cues remain strong or circumstances change. A lapse supplies an occasion to examine which cue, state, reward, friction, social pressure, or obstacle was underestimated. When lapses are plausible, a good design specifies a recovery path before one occurs.
Recovery begins with diagnosis: What cue appeared? What state was the person in? What immediate function did the old action serve? Was the desired action too difficult, poorly prompted, socially unsafe, or no longer worth pursuing? Restarting at the next workable cue is a useful heuristic, not a demand for solitary persistence. Repeated lapses can show that the environment, support, goal, or treatment needs to change.
Behavior design can support prevention and a recovery plan, but it is not a substitute for individualized care. Addiction can involve impaired control and continued behavior despite serious harm, and some substance withdrawals can be medically dangerous. Clinical assessment and evidence-based treatment may be required; the mild routine exercises here are not a treatment protocol (Volkow et al., 2016).






CautionWillpower is not one depletable fuel



The classic ego-depletion account of willpower as a depletable resource has faced serious replication and measurement challenges (Hagger et al., 2016). Fatigue, motivation, beliefs, opportunity costs, and context still matter, but no single “willpower fuel” should be assumed.

title: 39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier
section: Measure the loop, not the story
text:
Measure the loop, not the story
Measurement begins before intervention. Record a baseline: the observable target and competing behavior, contexts, delay, and immediate consequence. Then choose the few signals that would show whether the diagnosis was right:

Behavior: Did the observable action change?
Process: Did the cue, tiny start, question, or pause occur?
Outcome: Did learning, health, judgment, cooperation, or well-being improve?
Maintenance: Does change persist after novelty and intensive support decline?
Equity and access: Who can use the design, and who bears new friction?
Unintended effects: What useful behavior, trust, autonomy, rest, or flexibility was displaced?

A streak or click is not automatically success. A learning app can increase check-ins while weakening deep learning; a negotiation script can be used frequently while eliciting no new information. Use the smallest credible reversible test: target, baseline, prediction, intervention, measure, review date, and stop or revision rule.



Table 39.4: Behavior-change tools and their best uses










Tool
Best used when…
Example




Implementation intention
The goal is clear but follow-through fails at the critical moment.
If I feel the urge to explain during feedback, then I ask one clarifying question first.


WOOP
Positive intention needs an honest obstacle and a concrete plan.
Wish: prepare earlier. Outcome: calm negotiation. Obstacle: vague starting point. Plan: if unclear, then write three interests.


Friction design
The behavior is sensitive to small barriers or ease.
Phone outside bedroom; saved card removed; document opened before leaving work.


Temptation bundling
The desired behavior has delayed benefits and needs immediate reward.
Only listen to a favorite audiobook while walking.


Precommitment
Future states predictably defeat current intentions.
Automatic savings, scheduled class, app blocker, accountability partner.


Context change
Old cues keep recruiting the old behavior.
Use a new study location, new commute, new meeting script, or new semester routine.


BRAIN observation prompts
A mild everyday impulse is present and a pause may help choice.
Use Chapter 21’s classroom mnemonic to notice the impulse; it is not a validated treatment or a guarantee that an urge will subside.


Relapse plan
A missed repetition could become identity proof.
If I miss once, then I restart at the next cue with the smallest version.












TipPractice Lab: behavior-design studio



Choose one mild, real behavior and complete the one-page record in Table 39.1:

Define: write the observable target, competing action, and recurring situation.
Diagnose: name the cue, the current action’s immediate function, and the single most important bottleneck. Use B=MAP or COM-B only if it improves this diagnosis.
Redesign: change one decisive point. Choose no more than one primary tool from Table 39.4 and state exactly what will be different in the environment or response.
Measure: record a baseline, one process signal, one outcome signal, and a directional prediction for a short reversible test.
Review: set a date and write the rule for keeping, revising, or stopping the design. Add one recovery action after a lapse and one harm or displaced value that would trigger reconsideration.

Conclude with one sentence: “If this diagnosis is useful, the mechanism should be visible as…” The completed record—not the number of frameworks used—is the output.

title: 39  Behavior Design: Make the Better Action Easier
text:
Take it forward
Choose a recurring moment when an intention loses to the easier response. Make one feasible change to that moment, observe what happens, and use the result to revise your diagnosis. A plan becomes more useful when it includes a way to resume after a lapse.






NoteOptional Media Lab



Use a short excerpt, not a copied frame. Before viewing, predict what evidence would distinguish pleasure from prediction error or motivation from ability. After viewing, identify one defensible claim, one overclaim to avoid, and one behavior-design transfer.

title: 40  Choice Architecture: The Environment Gets a Vote
text:
Opening puzzle: the form that already chose
Every choice is presented somehow. The question is whether that presentation helps people act on informed goals or quietly substitutes someone else’s goals for their own.
Imagine enrolling in a retirement plan. The contribution field already says 6 percent, a recommended fund sits first, and the opt-out link is in smaller type. You can choose another arrangement, but doing so requires more attention than accepting the form as it stands.
The prefilled contribution is both a suggested number and, if inaction implements it, a default. The highlighted fund may look like advice. Whether these features help depends on how well they fit the person’s circumstances and how easily alternatives can be understood and selected.
Now reverse the example. A subscription site makes enrollment one click and cancellation nine screens. A travel site labels an expensive option “most popular” without explaining the comparison. A checkout page adds a warranty unless the buyer notices a faint checkbox. These designs use the same behavioral mechanisms, but their objective and treatment of exit are different.
The teaching question is therefore not, “Does architecture influence choice?” Every environment does. The useful questions are: Which objective does it serve? Which mechanism does it use? What evidence says it helps? Who may be harmed? Can a person understand, refuse, and recover from it?

text:
NoteCore Idea



Menus, defaults, forms, and feedback shape how people choose. A useful design helps them understand consequences and act on informed goals; a harmful one profits from confusion or makes refusal difficult. Evaluate the whole path, including what happens when someone tries to change their mind.

title: 40  Choice Architecture: The Environment Gets a Vote
text:
Learning goals

Diagnose where a menu, default, mapping, friction, timing, social signal, or feedback changes a choice path.
Compare nudges with boosts, incentives, mandates, and structural change for the same barrier.
Design and test an intervention that protects understanding, welfare, and meaningful exit.

Choice architecture asks how an institution presents recurring choices to many people, extending the individual behavior-design tools of the previous chapter.

40  Choice Architecture: The Environment Gets a Vote

title: 40  Choice Architecture: The Environment Gets a Vote
section: From behavior design to choice architecture
text:
From behavior design to choice architecture
Behavior design often begins with a person who wants to perform a behavior but does not reliably do so. Choice architecture widens the lens to the menu, sequence, interface, institution, and rules that organize recurring choices for many people. This chapter is a synthesis: earlier chapters established option construction, framing, defaults, probability formats, mental accounts, social norms, and implementation plans. The task here is to diagnose how those mechanisms combine along one choice path, not to treat them as a new list of effects.
Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein use choice architecture for the way choices are organized and nudge for an intervention that predictably changes behavior without banning options or substantially altering economic incentives (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008). Defaults, reminders, simpler forms, social-norm messages, and rearranged menus can be nudges. A large tax, a prohibition, or a compulsory rule is not merely a nudge, although it may be justified on other grounds.
Keep three levels separate. Choice architecture is the broad environment. A nudge is one feature of that environment. Libertarian paternalism is a normative argument for some welfare-oriented nudges: preserve meaningful choice while helping people act in ways they themselves would endorse under reflection. Calling a design a nudge therefore does not establish that its objective is legitimate or that its use is ethical.
Before choosing an intervention, compare the tools available:



Table 40.1: Different tools for different barriers











Instrument
What it changes
Example
Central question




Education
Facts and explanation
Balanced guide to vaccine benefits and risks
Can the person understand and use the information at the relevant moment?


Nudge
The immediate choice environment
Put healthier food first; send a timely reminder
Does the architecture help without closing meaningful options?


Boost
The person’s competence
Teach natural frequencies or negotiation preparation
Will the skill transfer beyond this environment?


Incentive
The material payoff
Deposit refund; late fee; performance bonus
Is the reward aligned with the desired outcome and protected from gaming?


Mandate
The available actions or minimum standard
Safety requirement; disclosure rule
Is restriction proportionate to the risk and rights involved?


Structural change
The conditions producing the problem
Staffing, access, pricing, transport, or workload reform
Is individual choice really the main bottleneck?






A reminder cannot repair an unaffordable service. A literacy module cannot compensate for a deliberately deceptive contract. A default cannot create a good option that is absent from the menu. The first discipline of design is diagnosis.

title: 40  Choice Architecture: The Environment Gets a Vote
section: The plausible path: where architecture enters the loop
text:
The plausible path: where architecture enters the loop






Figure 40.1: Five questions locate possible problems in the objective, menu, understanding, action, and feedback. This author’s diagnostic map identifies places to inspect; it is not a universal sequence of psychological stages.



An intervention is plausible only when the proposed design can be connected to a barrier through a credible path:

Objective. What outcome is being improved, for whom, and according to whose values?
Menu. Which options are available, missing, grouped, ordered, or made normal?
Understanding. Can people map each option to consequences they can compare?
Action. Can intention survive attention limits, timing, friction, and competing demands?
Feedback. Can people see what happened and revise the next choice?

This sequence prevents magical thinking. “Add a reminder” is not a mechanism. A defensible claim is narrower: eligible people already intend to book; forgetting at the relevant moment is a major barrier; a timely reminder makes the action salient; the booking path is feasible; and attendance can be measured without creating new burdens.
crumbs: Part VII. Designing Better Decisions
40  Choice Architecture: The Environment Gets a Vote

title: 40  Choice Architecture: The Environment Gets a Vote
text:
Construct and explain the choice

Construct the menu: options, order, and overload
The first architecture is the option set itself. A menu can create a false binary, hide a combination, make delay invisible, or omit the option of gathering more information. Categories and order also shape comparison. People do not evaluate every item in isolation; they interpret an option relative to what appears beside it.
More options can increase fit and autonomy, but more is not automatically better. Iyengar and Lepper’s jam study made choice overload vivid: a large display attracted attention, while a smaller display produced more purchases (Iyengar & Lepper, 2000). Later reviews show that overload is not universal. It is more likely when preferences are uncertain, options are hard to compare, the task is difficult, or the chooser is trying to minimize effort (Scheibehenne et al., 2010; Chernev et al., 2015).
A useful response is to structure comparison. Offer filters or an explainable shortlist, preserve access to the fuller menu, and make a legitimate option to wait or seek advice visible. Removing an apparent duplicate is sensible only after checking whether it serves a distinct need. Disclose why a featured option is prominent, especially when sponsorship plays a role.
Choice also contains sacrifice. A well-designed menu makes opportunity cost legible: “Choosing this means giving up…” When alternatives remain invisible, the visible benefit of one option can crowd out the cost of the path displaced by it (Frederick et al., 2009).






NoteAsk, do not merely tell—but define the real choice



When it is time to leave an amusement park, I sometimes ask my daughter, “Would you like to leave now or in ten minutes?” rather than “Do you want to leave now?” At breakfast, I might ask, “Would you like one egg or two?” rather than “Do you want eggs?” These are personal illustrations, not evidence that the wording will work generally.
Both questions preserve a small area of agency, but they also make acceptance presumptive. They are therefore better understood as constrained-menu architecture than as pure equivalent-description framing. The ethical boundary depends on what is genuinely negotiable. If the family must leave, I should state that boundary honestly and offer a real choice over timing. If eggs are optional, “no egg” must remain an easy, respected answer. “Ask, do not tell” supports agency only when the offered choice is real and the response can matter.




Set the starting point: defaults and active choice
A default is what happens if a person does nothing. Defaults are powerful because doing nothing is often easier, because the default may be interpreted as advice, and because moving away from a starting point can feel like giving something up (Johnson & Goldstein, 2003; Jachimowicz et al., 2019).
Defaults can be helpful when preferences are broadly aligned, inaction is common, reversibility is high, and the default is a reasonable recommendation. They are more dangerous when preferences vary greatly, switching costs are hidden, the default benefits the designer at the chooser’s expense, or non-response is treated as meaningful consent.
Three designs should be compared rather than treating one as universally best:

Opt-in: no enrollment without an affirmative action. Appropriate when consent must be explicit or preferences are highly heterogeneous.
Opt-out: enrollment occurs unless declined. Appropriate when the default is evidence-based, low-risk, reversible, and aligned with most affected people’s considered goals.
Active choice: the person must select among clearly described options. Appropriate when preference is essential and omission should not decide, but it can become burdensome when the choice is frequent, technical, or badly timed.

A smart default uses relevant, legitimate information to improve fit—for example, a retirement contribution that responds to age and employer match. It also raises governance questions: Which data are used? Can the recommendation be explained? Does personalization create discrimination? How easily can a person choose otherwise?
The empirical examples also need their institutional boundaries. Automatic enrollment substantially increased participation in one large 401(k) plan, while active-decision designs have raised participation relative to ordinary opt-in systems (Madrian & Shea, 2001; Carroll et al., 2009). Organ-donation consent is highly sensitive to default format, but actual donation also depends on eligibility, family involvement, trust, coordination, and health-system capacity (Johnson & Goldstein, 2003). These studies show that starting points matter; they do not identify one morally or practically optimal default for every setting.


Make consequences understandable: mapping and metrics
People choose an option, but they care about its consequences. Mapping is the connection between the selectable feature and the outcome that matters. A mortgage rate must be mapped to total cost and payment risk. A medical probability must be mapped to natural frequencies and meaningful time horizons. Energy use must be mapped to money, emissions, or another metric the audience can interpret.
Make the comparison reconstructable: use the same time horizon and denominator, show total cost alongside installments, and distinguish an estimate from a guarantee. For probabilities, natural frequencies and absolute risks can help readers see quantities that relative percentages obscure. Chapter 14 develops those formats.
Metrics are frames. Chapter 12 showed why equivalent descriptions can change choice; architecture determines which description becomes the default view. “Save €40 per month” and “save €480 per year” are equivalent arithmetically but not psychologically. A fair design does not pretend framing can be eliminated; it uses symmetric, decision-relevant representations and makes important alternative frames available.
Even familiar units can map poorly. Miles per gallon is nonlinear in fuel consumed: an improvement from 10 to 20 MPG saves much more fuel over a fixed distance than an improvement from 30 to 40 MPG. Gallons per hundred miles makes that consequence easier to compare (Larrick & Soll, 2008). The design question is not which unit looks intuitive, but which one reveals the welfare-relevant difference.






Figure 40.2: Over a fixed 100-mile trip, fuel use equals 100 divided by MPG. Moving from 10 to 20 MPG lowers use from 10 to 5 US gallons, saving 5 gallons. Moving from 30 to 40 MPG lowers use from 3.33 to 2.50 gallons, saving 0.83 gallon—exactly one-sixth as much. The curve is a mathematical conversion, not an estimated behavioral effect (Larrick & Soll, 2008).



The same principle applies to mental accounting. A budget category can help someone control spending while hiding the total cost across accounts. Show both the local choice and its effect on the whole budget, as discussed in Chapter 20.

title: 40  Choice Architecture: The Environment Gets a Vote
section: Make action feasible and feedback visible
text:
Make action feasible and feedback visible

Simplification, friction, and sludge
Friction is not trivial. A form, password, waiting period, extra click, inconvenient appointment time, ambiguous instruction, or request for a document can determine whether an intention becomes behavior. Removing unjustified friction can improve access without changing anyone’s underlying preference.
But friction also protects. Confirmation screens, cooling-off periods, withdrawal limits, and deliberate pauses can reduce impulsive or irreversible harm. The right question is not “Can we remove a click?” It is “Which error does this friction prevent, and whose interest does it serve?”
Sludge is excessive or unjustified friction that makes a beneficial action difficult or an unwanted action hard to escape (Sunstein, 2021). Dark patterns reverse the ethical direction of good design: they exploit attention and effort to obtain consent, extract data, add charges, or obstruct cancellation.
A simple symmetry test is revealing:

If joining is easy, is leaving comparably easy? If consent is prominent, is refusal equally legible? If the likely benefit is vivid, are material costs and risks comparably recoverable?

Simplification must preserve meaning. Shortening a form helps only if the remaining questions still protect eligibility, safety, and informed choice. Removing text is not the same as reducing cognitive work; sometimes a comparison table or worked example adds words while making the decision easier.






Figure 40.3: Masking seldom-used controls makes the simplification problem concrete. The goal is not the fewest possible buttons, but an interface in which the controls that remain match the user’s real tasks. Hiding a necessary function can create a new error rather than remove friction.



Administrative burden has at least three components: learning what exists and whether one qualifies, complying with procedures, and bearing the stress, stigma, or loss of autonomy attached to the process (Herd & Moynihan, 2018). Field studies show why this distinction matters. Simplifying benefit notices increased take-up of an earned-income tax credit, while hands-on assistance with financial-aid forms improved aid receipt and college enrollment; information by itself was not the whole bottleneck (Bhargava & Manoli, 2015; Bettinger et al., 2012). A sludge audit should therefore count time and steps and ask who must translate, disclose, wait, travel, or absorb psychological cost.


Support action at the right moment
Information delivered at the wrong time is often inert. A reminder can close an intention–action gap when the person has already formed an intention, forgetting is plausible, and the action is feasible at the moment of contact. Reminders fail when the real barrier is cost, fear, low trust, no available appointment, or disagreement with the goal.
Forgetting is one possible barrier; planning is another. A reminder can include a concrete opportunity to act, such as choosing a date and time, while making rescheduling easy. Urgency should reflect a real constraint rather than pressure the person to decide before inspecting the terms.
Salience is selective. Making one action vivid necessarily pushes something else toward the background. Ethical design therefore asks not only what the cue reveals, but what it makes easier to forget.


An arrow that changed the action path
An input can be irrelevant to an option’s objective consequences and still be causally relevant to the decision process. In 2012, Google added a clickable right-pointing arrow while also changing font size, spacing, and text layout in advertisements on its Display Network. The hotel offer did not become better merely because an arrow appeared, but the route from noticing the offer to clicking it became more prominent. Google reported higher clicks after the bundled redesign (Land & Yuan, 2012).
The example is instructive only with its evidence boundary intact. The public report did not disclose an effect size or separately vary the arrow, so it cannot establish that the arrow alone caused the increase. Nor does a click establish profit, informed choice, or user welfare. The design lesson is narrower: action affordances belong inside the causal path, and the outcome chosen to evaluate them matters.






Figure 40.4: The same generic hotel offer is shown before and after a bundled interface redesign. The second version makes the next action prominent with a right-pointing arrow. Google reported higher clicks after a redesign that combined the arrow with typography, spacing, and layout changes; its public report did not isolate the arrow’s independent effect, disclose an effect size, or establish user welfare.



Planning evidence makes the mechanism concrete: prompting employees to write the date and time of a flu clinic increased vaccination relative to a reminder without that planning field (Milkman et al., 2011). Commitment devices solve a different problem by letting a person constrain a predictable future state; because they may impose costs, they are not always nudges in the strict sense. Save More Tomorrow illustrates a hybrid: workers committed part of future salary increases to saving, combining advance commitment, timing, and inertia (Thaler & Benartzi, 2004).


Use social information carefully
Social information can help people infer what works, what is safe, or what others approve. It can also create the behavior it reports. A message saying that many people evade taxes, waste energy, or misuse a service may normalize the very conduct it condemns. Descriptive norms tell people what others do; injunctive norms tell them what others approve.
Norm messages should use an honest reference group, avoid inventing consensus, and anticipate boomerang effects. People already performing better than the stated norm may regress toward it unless approval for the better behavior is also made clear (Schultz et al., 2007). “Most guests reuse towels” is not interchangeable with “Most guests in this room reuse towels,” and neither is defensible if the number is fabricated.
Chapter 26 distinguished dynamic norms from descriptive and injunctive norms. Here the design question is deployment: a dynamic-norm message can describe a verified trend when the desirable behavior is not yet common, and such messages have shifted sustainable choices in experiments (Sparkman & Walton, 2017). The trend, denominator, and reference group must be relevant and honest; “more people” is not a license to manufacture momentum.
Identity can make a choice meaningful, but assigning a flattering or shaming identity can become manipulation. A stronger design invites agency: “People like you do this” pressures the self; “Here is what others did, why it may matter, and how to choose” informs a decision.


Close the loop: feedback and error-proofing
Feedback is useful when it is timely, interpretable, attributable, and linked to an action the person can take. A vague annual report may arrive too late to guide a repeated behavior. A real-time warning may be ignored if it fires constantly. A progress display may motivate when the target is meaningful, but game behavior when the metric becomes the goal.
Error-proofing designs around predictable mistakes. Examples include showing the selected account before a transfer, warning about duplicate medication, previewing who will receive a message, requiring a second person for an irreversible organizational action, or making the cost of delay visible before a deadline passes.
Feedback also belongs to the designer. An intervention should generate evidence about who receives it, who acts, who benefits, who is burdened, and which unintended effects appear. Without that loop, a nudge can persist because it is elegant rather than because it works.
Home-energy reports illustrate the full learning problem. Repeated comparison and action feedback reduced electricity use, and some effects persisted after reports stopped, although they decayed over time (Allcott & Rogers, 2014). The relevant outcome is not merely whether one message moved behavior once, but whether the architecture produced useful, durable learning without making already-efficient households regress.

title: 40  Choice Architecture: The Environment Gets a Vote
section: Test and govern the whole path
text:
Test and govern the whole path

Digital architecture operates at full-path scale
Digital systems can personalize menus, defaults, ranking, timing, social evidence, and feedback simultaneously. That makes them powerful and difficult to audit. A platform does not merely host choices; its recommender system decides what becomes visible, its interface defines the next easiest action, and its metrics determine what the system learns to optimize.
Audit the platform’s metric against the user’s objective. Time on site can rise while satisfaction falls, and a successful purchase may be followed by a difficult cancellation. Personalization adds another problem: different users may encounter different terms or obstacles, making a single screenshot an inadequate audit.
Keep records of the paths shown, provide understandable controls, and examine outcomes across relevant groups. Users need a way to correct a mistaken recommendation or challenge an unwanted consequence.
Dark patterns are not only hypothetical. Design research has catalogued interfaces that obstruct, sneak, pressure, or misdirect, and a large crawl documented such patterns across shopping websites (Gray et al., 2018; Mathur et al., 2019). Continuous personalization and experimentation raise the governance burden: the same system can expose different people to different paths while leaving no shared interface for outsiders to inspect.


Treat every intervention as a hypothesis
Behavioral effects are heterogeneous. An average effect may conceal strong benefit for one group, no effect for another, and harm for a third. Context, trust, baseline behavior, implementation quality, and the availability of good options all matter. Mertens et al. (2022) reported an average behavioral effect across diverse choice-architecture studies, but its magnitude and robustness to publication bias have been disputed. A reanalysis using different publication-bias adjustments found no clear average effect (Maier et al., 2022). These aggregate disagreements do not establish that every intervention works or that none does; they make evidence for the particular design and setting essential.
Scale is a separate test. Quantitative reviews find substantial variation across nudge designs, and trials run at scale by public nudge units have produced more modest average effects than prominent academic studies might lead designers to expect (Hummel & Maedche, 2019; DellaVigna & Linos, 2022). DellaVigna and Linos found average increases in take-up of 1.4 percentage points in the nudge-unit trials and 8.7 points in the academic-journal comparison. These are averages from different collections of interventions, not a randomized test of making the same intervention larger. The response is not “nudges work” or “nudges fail,” but diagnosis, comparison, and evidence in the setting where the design will operate.
Evaluation should therefore precede celebration. Define the target outcome, mechanism, baseline, comparison, time horizon, and possible harm before launch. When feasible, pilot or randomize. Measure behavior rather than intention alone. Check persistence and spillovers. Compare the nudge with plausible alternatives, including a boost, an incentive, service redesign, or no intervention.
A null result narrows the inquiry only when the study can distinguish the explanations. Check delivery, precision, timing, and access before concluding that forgetting was unimportant. Repeating the reminder more often will not resolve a transport barrier.


Ethics and governance: helping, steering, or manipulating?
The ethical issue is not solved by saying that choices remain technically available. An option that requires exceptional attention, time, literacy, or courage may exist legally while being inaccessible in practice. Ethical architecture should be assessed on the following ten dimensions:



Table 40.2: An ethical choice-architecture audit









Test
Question




Purpose
Whose objective is being advanced?


Welfare
Would affected people endorse the objective under informed reflection?


Evidence
Is there a credible mechanism and proportionate evidence?


Transparency
Can people understand the material feature and the designer’s role?


Exit
Is refusal, switching, or correction practically easy?


Distribution
Who benefits, who bears burdens, and are vulnerable groups protected?


Plural values
Are legitimate preferences diverse enough that active choice is safer than a strong default?


Nonexploitation
Does the feature support informed action rather than use confusion, urgency, or inattention against the chooser?


Accountability
Who monitors the path, answers challenges, and removes a design that does not earn its place?


Proportionality
Is the strength of influence justified by the problem, evidence, stakes, and rights involved?






Transparency does not require a warning label so large that the intervention ceases to function. It does require that material facts, sponsorship, data use, and options are recoverable without detective work. The strongest practical standard is the one used throughout this book: Would the design remain defensible if the people affected understood how it worked, whose goal it served, and how to refuse it?
