40  Choice Architecture: The Environment Gets a Vote

title: 40  Choice Architecture: The Environment Gets a Vote
text:
Apply the plausible-path design cycle
Use a short record linking the target outcome, diagnosed barrier, proposed change, comparison, and review date. Include a competing intervention and a possible harm. The two examples below show why following the full path can change the diagnosis.

Worked example: missed appointments
Suppose a clinic wants to reduce missed appointments. “Patients forget” is a hypothesis, not a diagnosis. The team first checks whether missed visits cluster by time, transport access, language, cost, waiting time, or difficulty cancelling.
If forgetting is important, a reminder can state the time, place, preparation, and one-tap paths to confirm, reschedule, or cancel. The message arrives while action is possible. The clinic measures attendance, timely cancellation, rescheduling, staff burden, and subgroup effects. If transport or unpredictable work is the real barrier, reminders alone will disappoint; flexible scheduling or service redesign is needed.


Worked example: subscription and cancellation sludge
A digital service can be joined with one prominent button but requires a search, password re-entry, retention offers, and a telephone call to leave. The business may describe each screen as an opportunity to prevent an accidental cancellation. The full path reveals a different objective: friction is asymmetric, the expected revenue from inattention accrues to the designer, and exit exists formally while being costly in practice.
A defensible redesign makes the current plan, renewal date, total cost, data consequences, and cancellation control visible in the same account area. Leaving should require confirmation proportionate to the consequences, not endurance. A brief, freely dismissible offer to pause or change plans may be legitimate when it does not obscure cancellation. Evaluation should include successful cancellation, time and errors, unwanted renewals, complaints, and differential burden—not only retained revenue.






TipPractice Lab: architecture autopsy and redesign



In groups, document one real choice path from first cue to feedback. Mark the menu, default, mapping, friction, timing, social information, and exit. Then write a one-sentence causal claim: “Changing X should affect Y because mechanism Z.” Propose one alternative instrument and one harm measure. Exchange designs and ask: Would this remain defensible if users understood it completely?

title: 40  Choice Architecture: The Environment Gets a Vote
text:
Take it forward
Follow the choice path as the person using it would: from the first prompt to the action and its consequences. Look especially at the point where an understandable intention becomes difficult to carry out. A useful redesign makes that point easier while keeping costs, alternatives, and exit visible.

title: 41  Decision Hygiene: Build a Process That Can Learn
text:
Learning goals
Notice, test, ask, design, and learn
A hiring committee is ready to compare candidates when its chair says, “I was very impressed by the first applicant.” Several members had doubts about the work sample, but the conversation now begins with reasons to share the chair’s enthusiasm. The committee eventually agrees. Six months later, the appointee struggles, and everyone remembers having warned about the risk.
The problem spans two meetings: one in which judgments became correlated before the evidence was compared, and another in which memory rewrote the earlier uncertainty. Recognizing bias is useful, but the committee also needs a procedure that preserves independent views and a record that later events cannot silently change.
This final chapter brings the book’s tools together around that task: making consequential decisions easier to inspect and learn from.

title: 41  Decision Hygiene: Build a Process That Can Learn
text:
Build a proportionate judgment process before debating its answer.
Protect independent evidence, structured disagreement, and accountable use of models or AI.
Review forecasts, process, fairness, and outcomes without confusing luck with quality.







ImportantThe final standard



A useful intervention should remain defensible if the people affected understand how it works, whose objective it serves, what evidence supports it, and how they can refuse or revise it.

title: 41  Decision Hygiene: Build a Process That Can Learn
section: Why judgment systems fail: bias, noise, and misplaced intuition
text:
Why judgment systems fail: bias, noise, and misplaced intuition
Bias has a direction relative to a defensible target. A forecaster who is consistently too optimistic or a scale that always reads two kilograms high is biased when later outcomes or a calibrated standard supplies that target. In many value-laden decisions, however, there is no simple observable bullseye; the benchmark must be specified and defended rather than smuggled into the picture. Noise is unwanted variation among repeated, commensurable judgments that should be similar. If qualified teachers grade the same essay very differently, physicians use different thresholds for the same case, or managers rate the same candidate from 4 to 9 on a ten-point scale, the system is noisy (Kahneman et al., 2021).






Figure 41.1: Target diagrams distinguish systematic error from unwanted variability when judgments are repeated, commensurable, and compared with an observable or defensible benchmark. Level noise concerns persistent differences in judges’ average levels; pattern noise concerns different reactions to case features. Occasion noise adds within-judge variation across occasions.



The bullseye is an analogy, not a universal measurement model. It summarizes the location and spread of a set of comparable judgments when a target can be observed or normatively accepted; it cannot establish that the target is legitimate, identify why errors occurred, or decompose the spread by itself. Level noise is persistent variation in judges’ average severity or generosity. Pattern noise arises when judges react differently to features of particular cases. Occasion noise is additional within-judge variation across times or contexts. Estimating these components requires an appropriate repeated-judgment design, not one isolated decision.
Noise is easy to miss because people usually encounter one judgment, not the distribution of judgments they might have received. One candidate meets one panel. One paper receives one set of reviews. One patient sees one clinician. Yet fairness requires that similar cases receive similar treatment unless a relevant difference justifies the variation.



Table 41.1: Different sources of disagreement in a judgment system










Failure
What it looks like
First diagnostic question




Bias
Judgments are wrong in a systematic direction.
What recurring factor shifts the average?


Level noise
Some judges are generally harsher or more generous.
Does the result depend on which judge was assigned?


Pattern noise
Judges weight features idiosyncratically.
Are the criteria and their weights shared?


Occasion noise
The same judge varies with time, order, fatigue, or context.
Would this person decide the same way tomorrow?


Legitimate discretion
Variation reflects relevant information, values, or circumstances.
Can the exception be explained and documented?






The distinction matters statistically and ethically. Error increases when judgments are shifted in the wrong direction, widely dispersed, or both. Reducing dispersion around a bad target does not create a good system. Nor should consistency erase morally relevant differences. A noise audit measures variation first; responsible judgment then decides which variation is arbitrary and which is justified.
Decision hygiene is broader than teaching a catalogue of biases. The analogy is medical hygiene: handwashing can prevent infection without identifying the exact germ in advance. Independent scoring, explicit criteria, reference classes, checklists, and decision records can reduce several errors without requiring the user to diagnose the precise bias operating in the moment.
Intuition still has a place. It deserves more trust when the environment contains stable patterns and the judge receives rapid, accurate, attributable feedback. Chess and some skilled emergency work can provide such learning conditions. Long-range strategy, one-off hiring, political forecasting, and innovation often do not. Repetition can create confidence even when feedback is delayed, selective, or confounded (Kahneman & Klein, 2009).
The rule is therefore not “ignore intuition.” It is delay the global impression until the evidence has been structured. Record the first impression if it may contain expertise, but do not let it silently determine every component score. Ask not only, “How experienced is this person?” but, “Could this environment have taught the person the right lesson?”

title: 41  Decision Hygiene: Build a Process That Can Learn
text:
The structured judgment pipeline
A workflow helps connect preparation with later review. The one below is a practical synthesis to adapt to the decision:






Figure 41.2: This author’s prescriptive synthesis structures judgment by defining, decomposing, eliciting independent assessments, aggregating, recording, and reviewing. It is a design proposal whose components should be scaled and tested for the task.




Define. State the decision, prediction target, values, decision rights, affected people, and error costs.
Decompose. Evaluate distinct criteria before forming a coherent global story.
Ground. Begin with base rates, reference classes, or a transparent baseline.
Judge independently. Record estimates and reasons before discussion, hierarchy, advocacy, or AI output creates correlation.
Aggregate and compare. Examine the center, dispersion, profiles, disagreements, and model output.
Challenge. Seek disconfirming evidence, run a premortem or red team, and ask what would change the conclusion.
Decide and document. State the choice, trade-offs, authority, assumptions, exceptions, and implementation conditions.
Review and learn. Compare forecasts with outcomes, audit fairness and drift, and change the process where the evidence warrants it.

This is a proportional pipeline, not a command to make every choice slow. A low-stakes reversible decision may need only a quick check. A repeated, consequential, uncertain, contested, difficult-to-reverse, or partly automated decision deserves more structure.

title: 41  Decision Hygiene: Build a Process That Can Learn
section: Before the decision: improve the input
text:
Before the decision: improve the input
For the hiring committee, the first improvement happens before anyone advocates for a candidate. Agree on what successful work requires, what evidence can be collected comparably, and who will make the final decision. Keep alternatives visible, including reopening the search if no applicant meets an essential requirement.
Then ask where the present procedure is unreliable. More scoring forms will not help if the criteria themselves measure the wrong thing.

Diagnose before redesigning: run a noise audit
Before installing a rubric, algorithm, or extra meeting, measure the variation the system actually produces. Select representative cases from a repeated task—grading, hiring, underwriting, forecasting, peer review, or project approval. Give identical evidence to several qualified judges without discussion. Ask for anchored scores, probability estimates, confidence, and brief reasons. Examine the range and dispersion, general severity differences, and case-specific disagreement. If occasion noise matters, repeat selected cases later.
The final step is interpretive. Which disagreements reflect missing information or legitimate values? Which reflect vague criteria, different thresholds, order, mood, or irrelevant cues? Redesign the specific weak stage and repeat the audit. The question is concrete: Would we accept this decision changing merely because another equally qualified person happened to make it?






TipTen-Minute Noise-Audit Lab



Give everyone the same candidate, project, settlement proposal, essay, or risk case. Without discussion, collect one anchored score, one probability, one confidence judgment, and one brief reason. Display the distribution before revealing any preferred answer. Separate disagreement caused by different information or legitimate values from disagreement caused by vague criteria, thresholds, irrelevant cues, or occasion. Redesign one weak stage, then have the class judge a comparable second case independently.




Define and decompose before evaluating
Unstructured judgment lets charisma, familiarity, or one vivid weakness organize the whole evaluation. Decomposition asks judges to assess job-relevant or decision-relevant dimensions separately. In hiring, for example, technical skill, learning ability, teamwork, communication, and role requirements should be scored from evidence before asking, “Would I hire this person?” Comparable questions, work samples, and anchored scoring make the judgment more inspectable (Dana et al., 2013; Highhouse, 2008).
Good criteria have four properties:

they connect to the actual objective rather than a convenient proxy;
their evidence can be observed or elicited comparably;
their scale anchors describe meaning, not just numbers;
their weighting or trade-off is decided explicitly rather than smuggled in through a halo.

Structure can make the wrong value consistently influential. A perfect rubric for “cultural fit” is harmful if fit means similarity to current insiders. Decomposition improves judgment only when the target and criteria are legitimate.


Ground forecasts in the outside view
An inside view explains why this candidate, project, product, or strategy is special. An outside view begins with what happened in comparable cases and then adjusts for case-specific evidence. The reference class should be close enough to inform and broad enough to contain useful variation.
Projects make the contrast visible. Teams commonly build a detailed internal schedule and underestimate cost or delay; a reference-class forecast asks how comparable projects actually performed before accepting the case-specific story (Kahneman & Lovallo, 1993; Flyvbjerg et al., 2002). The reference class is itself a judgment and can be gamed. Record alternative classes considered, the outcome distribution in each, and the reason for every adjustment so that “our case is different” becomes an inspectable claim.
Forecasts should be probabilities or ranges, not only adjectives such as “likely” or “risky.” Over a portfolio of forecasts, calibration becomes visible: events assigned 70 percent should occur about 70 percent of the time. A Brier score can summarize probabilistic accuracy, but the deeper practice is to reward honest uncertainty and timely revision rather than confidence alone (Brier, 1950; Mellers et al., 2014).
When the choice involves a rare project with poor direct precedents, use several reference classes, analogous mechanisms, scenario ranges, and explicit assumptions. “No perfect comparison exists” is not permission to use no comparison at all.


Preserve independence, then aggregate
Discussion is valuable after information has been captured. Before discussion, it creates correlation. Early speakers anchor the range; senior people change what feels safe; repeated arguments sound more supported than they are; and private doubts disappear behind public consensus.
Use the sequence estimate first, discuss second. Ask members to record a score, forecast, strongest reason, and key uncertainty. Then display the distribution. Simple averaging can outperform immediate debate when individual errors are partly independent. Weighted aggregation can help when weights are earned through relevant calibration rather than status. Disagreement is not merely an obstacle to eliminate; it is evidence about ambiguous criteria, different information, or different models.
Aggregation is not a ritual average. It helps when judges possess relevant information and their errors are not perfectly correlated; it cannot remove a shared bias, and it can dilute a person who holds uniquely diagnostic evidence. Diverse problem-solving perspectives can improve a group’s search, but only when the process preserves and integrates them rather than producing conformity (Hong & Page, 2004; Sunstein & Hastie, 2015). Inspect the spread and reasons before deciding whether to average, weight, investigate, or escalate a decisive concern.
Senior people should normally speak after independent input is captured. Anonymous concerns can protect information in high-power settings. A facilitator should ask what evidence explains the spread, not pressure everyone toward the midpoint.







NoteResearch Lens: AI and accountable judgment



In repeated predictive tasks with measurable outcomes, simple mechanical or statistical rules often match or outperform unaided human judgment because they apply weights consistently (Meehl, 1954; Dawes et al., 1989; Grove et al., 2000). That advantage is task-specific. A model can be consistently wrong when its target, data, or deployment context is wrong.
AI is often valuable because it improves prediction, but prediction is only one task inside a decision. Building on Agrawal et al. (2019), keep four tasks separate.1



Table 41.2: Prediction is one task inside accountable decision-making









Task
Accountable question




Prediction
What state or outcome is likely, with what uncertainty, and how well is the model calibrated here?


Valuation
Which consequences matter, whose welfare and rights count, and how should error costs be traded off?


Intervention design
Which feasible action could change the outcome, under what causal assumptions and constraints?


Decision and responsibility
What should be implemented, under whose authority, with what exception, appeal, monitoring, and review?






Prediction is not responsibility. A forecast can inform a decision, but it cannot determine which consequence should count, which intervention is justified, who may authorize it, or who must answer for the result.
Suppose an AI system predicts hospital readmission accurately. The estimate does not determine whether a home visit, delayed discharge, telephone call, or no intervention would work. Nor does it decide how to weigh a missed readmission against an unnecessary intervention or how the patient’s circumstances and preferences should count. Human oversight is not a final click after the model has settled everything important. A person or institution must own the objective, causal assumptions, stakeholder costs, action, exceptions, appeal, and consequences.
The same discipline applies to different tools. Validate forecasts out of sample and inspect calibration and subgroup error. Verify facts and sources in generated summaries. Treat generated alternatives as search aids rather than complete menus. Version fixed rules and record justified exceptions. Require the accountable decision-maker to own any reasons or records produced with AI. A polished answer is not evidence of truth or completeness (Ji et al., 2023; National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2023).
Three governance failures deserve special attention. First, the target-variable problem allows technical accuracy to optimize the wrong objective or reproduce historical labels (Obermeyer et al., 2019). Second, automation bias and algorithm aversion produce over- and under-reliance rather than trust calibrated to comparative evidence (Dietvorst et al., 2015; Mosier et al., 1998). Third, fairness criteria can conflict, so no technical switch can choose among rights, error costs, history, and institutional purpose (Barocas et al., 2019). Higher stakes therefore require stronger validation, transparency, subgroup analysis, contestability, privacy protection, and real human authority to correct the system.
A practical test is: Could we explain to an affected person what the system contributed, who had power to challenge it, why that authority was legitimate, and how an error can be corrected? A reviewer without enough information or power to challenge the output cannot provide meaningful oversight and may instead be left carrying responsibility for a system they could not control (Elish, 2019).

Minimum AI-use record
When a model materially informs a consequential decision, record five fields. The purpose is not to preserve every keystroke. It is to make the contribution, verification, authority, and correction path inspectable.



Table 41.3: A minimum record for consequential AI-supported judgment









Field
Minimum record




1. Task and tool
The task delegated; tool, model, or rule used; version or access date; and why it was appropriate for this task.


2. Inputs and boundaries
Material inputs, sources, missing information, and any privacy, consent, or use restriction. Do not copy sensitive data into an unauthorized record.


3. Output and reliance
The material output, recommendation, or forecast; what the decision-maker followed, modified, or rejected; and why.


4. Independent checks
Fact and source verification, comparison with a baseline or independent human view, uncertainty and subgroup checks where relevant, and the strongest contrary evidence.


5. Authority and correction
Named decision owner, affected people, available exception or appeal, monitoring signal, review date, and who can pause or reverse the use.






For low-stakes drafting or search assistance, a brief record may be enough. As consequence, repetition, irreversibility, unequal power, or automation grows, the record and validation should grow with it. Appendix C provides a printable version.



Some choices should also be designed to learn. A pilot, diagnostic test, negotiation question, or request for supporting sources can reveal a hidden state before commitment. Ask not only which option currently looks best, but which safe action would most improve the next decision.

41  Decision Hygiene: Build a Process That Can Learn

title: 41  Decision Hygiene: Build a Process That Can Learn
text:
During the decision: structure disagreement
Separate prediction from valuation. Ask first what each person believes will happen and what evidence supports that belief. Ask separately what outcomes matter, which trade-offs are acceptable, and whose welfare or rights count. Many arguments become clearer when “too risky” is decomposed into probability and consequence.
Checklists can protect against omissions in repeated work when they are short, located at a useful pause, and tied to known failures. Haynes et al. (2009) observed lower complication and mortality rates after introducing a surgical safety checklist in eight hospitals. This was a before-and-after study, so the change cannot be attributed to the document alone; implementation and concurrent changes matter. A hiring checklist likewise needs to address an actual failure, such as scoring work samples before discussing impressions.
A premortem asks each person to imagine that the plan has failed and independently write plausible causes. The fictional certainty of failure gives doubt permission to speak (Klein, 2007). A red team goes further by constructing an adversarial test of assumptions, evidence, and execution. Red teams need genuine access, time, and protection; a ceremonial critic who cannot change the plan is not decision hygiene. A designated devil’s advocate can be dismissed as merely performing a role, so it should not replace authentic independent concern. Challenge earns its place only when someone has authority to inspect the evidence and the team records what changed in response.
Psychological safety is the social infrastructure beneath these tools. It means that people can ask, disagree, admit error, and surface risk without interpersonal punishment; it does not mean comfort, agreement, or low standards (Edmondson, 1999). Leaders create it behaviorally by inviting specific dissent, responding productively to bad news, separating a concern from the status of the person who raised it, and showing that early correction is valued more than late loyalty.
For the distinct routes by which authority, suppressed dissent, unshared information, pluralistic ignorance, and diffused responsibility can silence challenge, see Authority, Groupthink, and Shared Responsibility.
Safety and accountability are complements. High safety without evidence standards can become comfortable imprecision; high standards without safety can produce polished silence. The accountable system makes reasoning inspectable, expects preparation and correction, and protects the person who reveals a problem before it becomes a failure.

41  Decision Hygiene: Build a Process That Can Learn

title: 41  Decision Hygiene: Build a Process That Can Learn
text:
Design choices, not just advice
Advice leaves the surrounding process intact. Chapters 30–40 supplied stronger design moves: diagnose the audience model, make meaning testable, map alternatives and interests, redesign recurring cues and friction, and govern the whole choice path. Decision hygiene does not reteach those mechanisms. It asks which one repairs the diagnosed weak stage while preserving agency, challenge, and feedback.

Many organizations call a meeting before defining what must be decided. Participants hear a polished recommendation, then try to recover independent judgment from inside its frame. A better meeting separates the stages:



Table 41.4: A decision meeting organized around judgment rather than presentation










Phase
Process rule
What it protects




Before
Define the decision, criteria, evidence, authority, and affected people.
The agenda does not silently set the target.


Independent input
Collect estimates and concerns before advocacy, discussion, or AI output.
Information diversity and unanchored forecasts.


Evidence
Separate facts, assumptions, predictions, values, and recommendations.
Disagreement becomes diagnosable rather than personal.


Challenge
Use an outside view, premortem, strongest objection, and “what would change our minds?”
Doubt becomes a role, not an act of disloyalty.


Decision
State the choice, trade-offs, exceptions, owner, and implementation conditions.
Conversation becomes accountable action.


Review
Set indicators, thresholds, and a review date.
Outcomes can update the process without rewriting it.






Roles can make the process visible: one person tracks criteria, one assumptions, one risks and dissent, one unresolved questions, and one implementation. Decision rights must also be explicit. Who decides? Who advises? Who must consent? Who implements? Ambiguity here produces recurring debate and hidden vetoes.

title: 41  Decision Hygiene: Build a Process That Can Learn
section: The decision audit: from a smooth story to an inspectable process
text:
The decision audit: from a smooth story to an inspectable process
A coherent account of a decision is not the same thing as the process that produced it. Begin an audit by writing the ordinary five-sentence story: What decision did I face? What did I choose? Why did it seem right? What happened? How good was the decision? That story is useful because it captures what is currently retrievable. It is also dangerous because it tends to blend what was known then with what became known later.
Now slow the story into six inspectable components:



Table 41.5: A decision-loop diagnostic











Component
Audit question
Common failure
Process redesign




Alternatives
What options were actually on the table?
Treating the first menu as complete.
Generate, combine, negotiate, delay, or pilot.


Prediction
What was expected under each option?
Confusing confidence with evidence.
Use base rates, ranges, and disconfirming tests.


Valuation
What mattered, to whom, and why?
Treating priorities as obvious or unanimous.
Name stakeholders, trade-offs, and protected values.


Opportunity cost
What was the best feasible path forgone?
Making the unchosen future psychologically invisible.
Ask “Compared with what?” before commitment.


Context and state
What cue, emotion, norm, identity, or constraint was active?
Misattributing an incidental influence to the option.
Change timing, order, frame, role, or environment.


Feedback
What was supposed to be learned, and when?
Letting hindsight rewrite the original forecast.
Record assumptions and set a review date.






The audit does not prove that the chosen option was best, recover the road not taken, or reveal how every counterfactual future would have unfolded. It can reveal missing options, unsupported predictions, hidden values, invisible opportunity costs, contextual pressures, and feedback that was never designed. Its purpose is prospective: make the next decision more testable than the last one.






Figure 41.3: A sound or weak process can be followed by either a favorable or unfavorable outcome.

41  Decision Hygiene: Build a Process That Can Learn

title: 41  Decision Hygiene: Build a Process That Can Learn
section: After the outcome: learn without worshipping luck
text:
After the outcome: learn without worshipping luck

What a decision journal is—and is not
A decision journal is a collection of structured, time-stamped records created at two different moments. Before the outcome is known, an entry preserves what was knowable, expected, valued, and chosen. After a specified review date or trigger, a linked review records what happened and what should be learned without overwriting the original entry. Its unit is a consequential decision, not a day in the writer’s life.
The journal links two different records: what you believed before choosing and what later happened. Meeting minutes can document the choice, but usually do not preserve the alternative forecasts and learning rules needed for this comparison.
Its research basis is in components, rather than a trial of one universal journal template. Decision analysis identifies the options, consequences, and values to record (Raiffa, 1968; Keeney & Raiffa, 1976). Hindsight and outcome-bias research explains why later recollection cannot substitute for a contemporary record (Fischhoff, 1975; Baron & Hershey, 1988). Forecasting research makes predictions resolvable across repeated decisions (Brier, 1950; Mellers et al., 2014).
Writing and review also depend on the conditions. In a study of Chinese judges, reason writing before judgment reduced the influence of an induced negative feeling, but forced deliberation produced a similar effect (Liu, 2018). A meta-analysis found benefits of structured debriefing across 46 samples (\(N = 2{,}136\); average \(d = 0.67\)), not evidence that this entire journal format works for every decision (Tannenbaum & Cerasoli, 2013). Accountability can also encourage conformity when the evaluator’s preferred answer is known (Lerner & Tetlock, 1999).
The practical sequence is freeze, compare, update: preserve the original account, compare each prediction or assumption with relevant evidence, then change a rule or forecast where warranted. A record helps only if it is candid, reviewed, and protected from retrospective editing.






ImportantThe same-name rule



Every after-outcome prompt should answer the before-choosing record with the same label on the same row. If a concern appears only later, record it as “not anticipated”; do not pretend it was part of the original reasoning. The practical rhythm is freeze → compare → update.




A simplified decision journal
The table below illustrates the two-stage structure. The case and numbers are hypothetical: a university teacher is deciding whether to pilot an AI-assisted feedback tool. The point is not to fill every possible field, but to create a short record that can later contradict convenient memory.



Table 41.6: A hypothetical decision journal in which every ex-post entry answers its ex-ante counterpart










Matched learning loop
Before choosing — freeze
After the outcome — compare and update




1. Decision and execution
By 15 September, decide whether to keep the current feedback process, run a four-week pilot in one course, or adopt the tool in all courses.
The four-week pilot was implemented for 100 assignments as planned. Record any deviations before interpreting its results.


2. Alternatives and opportunity cost
The best forgone option is the current process with additional teaching-assistant time.
The teaching-assistant option was not tested, so its counterfactual result remains unknown. No clearly feasible option omitted from the original menu emerged.


3. Evidence and reference class
A local test of 20 assignments reduced average editing time from 12 to 8 minutes, but 4 drafts needed major correction. The sample is small and local; no external comparison is available.
Across 100 assignments, editing averaged 8.5 minutes, 8% needed major correction, 62% of students rated the feedback helpful, and no privacy breach was reported. This strengthens local evidence but does not establish performance elsewhere.


4. Predictions and assumptions
Pilot forecasts: 60% chance editing time is below 9 minutes; 70% chance at least 70% of students rate feedback helpful; 15% chance more than 10% of drafts need major correction. Assumptions: instructors catch material errors and opting out is meaningful.
Resolve the same forecasts: time below 9 minutes—yes; helpfulness at least 70%—no; correction above 10%—no. The recorded correction rate is below the threshold; unrecognized errors and whether opting out felt meaningful remain untested. One realized event does not by itself prove that a stated probability was well calibrated.


5. Values and stakeholders
Faster feedback matters, but accuracy, privacy, student trust, and a genuine option to decline are protected values. A privacy breach is unacceptable even if time is saved.
The observed major-correction rate met the threshold and no privacy breach was reported; this does not rule out undetected errors or breaches. Helpfulness was weaker than hoped. Trust and the experience of students who opted out were not measured, so those original values cannot yet be evaluated.


6. Context, incentives, dissent, and tools
Instructors want to reduce workload and may be unusually receptive to the tool. The strongest objection is that verification could consume the time saved. Record any model or AI advice and why it was followed or overridden.
Verification did not eliminate the time saving, but student concerns received less measurement than instructor workload. Reassess whether dissent was answered and whether reliance on the tool was calibrated to where it actually added value.


7. Choice, thresholds, and learning rule
Run the limited pilot; review after 100 assignments. Stop after a confirmed privacy breach. Do not scale if major correction exceeds 10% or helpfulness is below 70%.
The recorded implementation and review thresholds were followed, and the measured outcome was mixed. Do not scale: helpfulness missed the stated threshold. Continue only as a limited test, improve the student explanation, measure trust and opt-out experience, and set the next review before collecting more outcomes.






Review the process using what was knowable at the time. A good decision can produce a bad outcome, and a poor process can get lucky. Compare forecasts with outcomes, not stories with feelings. Ask which assumptions failed, which information was missing, which values changed, and which parts of the process should remain even though the outcome was disappointing.
Do not update from one noisy result more than the evidence warrants. Regression to the mean, random variation, and selective feedback can create false lessons. Calibrate over many predictions. Reward accurate uncertainty and timely revision, not only confident success.
The hiring committee’s later review should begin with its original scores and reasons. Without them, the chair’s enthusiasm can become a shared memory of caution. With them, members can ask which evidence was useful, which uncertainty remained, and what should change before the next appointment.


The matched fields: one name, two moments

The minimum useful entry identifies the decision, separates prediction from valuation, and defines how later evidence will be interpreted. Append the review; never edit the original entry into agreement with what occurred.



Table 41.7: A matched decision-journal template: freeze, compare, and update










Learning loop
Before choosing — freeze
After the outcome — compare




1. Decision and execution
Decision, date, owner, deadline, and scope
What was implemented, including deviations and delays


2. Alternatives and opportunity cost
Serious options and the best feasible alternative forgone
Missing options, new evidence, and counterfactuals still unknown


3. Evidence and reference class
Sources, comparable cases, missing evidence, and assumptions
Which evidence proved useful, misleading, or unresolved


4. Predictions and assumptions
Consequences, probabilities or ranges, time horizons, and resolution rules
Resolve each forecast; mark assumptions supported, failed, or untested


5. Values and stakeholders
Priorities, affected people, rights, and unacceptable trade-offs
Benefits, harms, omitted perspectives, and any later change in values


6. Context, incentives, dissent, and tools
Pressures, contrary views, and model or AI advice followed or rejected
What influence each had and whether reliance was justified


7. Choice, thresholds, and learning rule
Choice, implementation owner, review date, and continue/stop/revise rules
Whether rules were followed; process and outcome assessed separately; next test






Reflection differs from rationalization because it produces a testable change. “How can I defend what I did?” searches for coherence. “What process produced this choice?” separates evidence, values, context, and luck. “What will I do differently next time?” turns the answer into a new rule, forecast, or experiment.

Move

Typical tool

title: 41  Decision Hygiene: Build a Process That Can Learn
text:
Return to the hiring decision
Before reviewing candidates, the committee defines job-relevant outcomes, error costs, decision rights, and criteria that can be observed comparably. It records a relevant performance base rate and identifies what evidence would justify departing from it. Each member then reviews the same work sample and structured evidence, scores each dimension independently, and records a probability of success before seeing other judgments or an AI summary.
Only then does the committee compare the distribution. A spread in scores is information: perhaps the criterion is vague, members possess different evidence, or one feature has created a halo. The chair speaks after independent input. The group tests its leading account against the strongest alternative, records the choice, uncertainty, trade-offs, and reasons for any exception, and sets an implementation and review plan.
After the outcome, the committee reviews what was knowable at the time. It does not treat the selected candidate’s success or failure as proof that every earlier inference was correct. Across hires, it examines calibration, predictive validity, subgroup outcomes, exceptions, and process variation. The opening choice has become an inspectable learning system.

41  Decision Hygiene: Build a Process That Can Learn

title: 41  Decision Hygiene: Build a Process That Can Learn
text:
Ethics, governance, and proportionality
Structure is not automatically fair. A rubric can make the wrong values consistently influential. A model can turn historical discrimination into a scalable rule. A checklist can suppress professional attention. A decision journal can become surveillance. A demand for consistency can erase relevant differences.
Ask whether the criteria serve legitimate goals, whether exceptions are reasoned and reviewable, and whether affected people can challenge errors. Inspect how benefits and burdens are distributed. A model, committee, or consultant should not obscure who has authority and responsibility.
Scale the procedure to the stakes. A low-cost reversible choice may need a short note and a review date; a repeated hiring process needs stronger evidence and checks for unfair treatment. Remove a control when its burden exceeds its useful contribution.



Table 41.9: Proportionate decision hygiene










Failure mode
First-line protection
Stronger response when stakes warrant it




Inconsistent judges
Noise audit and anchored criteria
Multiple judges, calibration, model comparison


Overconfident plan
Outside view and probability ranges
Premortem, staged investment, stop criteria


Hierarchy or conformity
Independent input; senior person speaks last
Anonymous concerns, external review, red team


Hindsight learning
Decision journal and review date
Forecast scoring and portfolio-level analysis


Repeated prediction
Transparent statistical baseline
Validated model with fairness and drift audit


AI-supported judgment
Independent human view and verification
Contestability, subgroup audit, human review board


Excess bureaucracy
Short, failure-linked checklist
Remove low-value controls; preserve justified discretion












TipPractice Lab: integrated decision studio



Produce one completed, one-page judgment pipeline for a real decision:

Define: state the decision, deadline, owner, affected people, and most costly error.
Decompose: name three to five criteria and the evidence each requires before giving an overall judgment.
Ground: record one base rate, reference class, transparent baseline, or the reason none is available.
Judge independently: obtain at least two estimates, scores, or written views before discussion or AI output; if only one decision-maker is available, record an initial estimate before seeking advice.
Compare: display the estimates, disagreement, and reasons; do not average away uniquely diagnostic evidence.
Challenge: write the strongest objection, one disconfirming observation, and one safe information-gaining action.
Decide and document: state the choice, trade-offs, implementation owner, and any justified exception. If AI materially informed it, attach the minimum AI-use record.
Review and learn: specify an observable outcome, threshold or resolution rule, review date, and what will continue, stop, scale, or change.

The submitted artifact is the completed pipeline, not an essay about decision hygiene. For a low-stakes reversible choice, use only define → challenge → decide → review. For a consequential, repeated, contested, difficult-to-reverse, or partly automated decision, complete all eight stages.

title: 41  Decision Hygiene: Build a Process That Can Learn
text:
Take it forward
Return to the hiring meeting that opened the book. A better process cannot promise the best hire every time, but it can make the reasons for the choice clearer, expose disagreement before commitment, and preserve what the outcome can teach. Start with one recurring decision and build the conditions under which the next decision can improve.

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
text:
1. Feasible and consideration sets
Formal details supporting Chapters 1 and 2
Suppose you are comparing two job offers. You want to know which options are feasible, how their consequences differ, and whether another conversation with an employer could change your choice. This appendix puts the reasoning from Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 into mathematical form. Use the equations to expose an assumption or test a recommendation; the model still depends on the evidence and objectives supplied to it.
Let \(\mathcal{A}\) denote the set of actions under discussion, including options whose feasibility has not yet been checked. An action is feasible only if it satisfies the relevant constraints. Suppose the decision contains inequality constraints \(g_j(a)\leq 0\) and equality constraints \(h_\ell(a)=0\). The feasible set is
\[
A
=
\left\{
a\in\mathcal{A}:
g_j(a)\leq 0\ \text{for all }j,
\quad
h_\ell(a)=0\ \text{for all }\ell
\right\}.
\]
The constraint functions determine which actions belong to \(A\). A job that requires a licence you cannot obtain in time, for example, may be imaginable without being feasible.
This formulation also explains why prescriptive analysis tests apparent constraints. If a deadline can be negotiated, a role redesigned, or a commitment staged, the relevant constraint changes and the feasible set may expand. The best imaginable action need not be feasible, and the current visible menu need not contain every feasible action.
The consideration set \(K\) contains the alternatives a person notices, recalls, generates, or takes seriously:
\[
K(z,m)\subseteq \mathcal{A},
\]
where \(z\) represents external context and \(m\) represents internal state. Considered options can include ones that later prove infeasible, while feasible options may be overlooked. After feasibility has been checked, the available considered options are \(K(z,m)\cap A\). Comparing that intersection coherently can still miss a better option elsewhere in \(A\), which is why generating alternatives matters.
crumbs: Appendices
A  Rational Choice and Decision Analysis

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
text:
2. Preferences and the choice correspondence
Let \(\succeq\) be a weak preference relation over the feasible alternatives. The statement
\[
a\succeq b
\]
means that alternative \(a\) is at least as good as alternative \(b\) for the purposes represented by the model.
For a finite, nonempty feasible set, completeness and transitivity are sufficient for a numerical value representation \(V\) such that
\[
a\succeq b
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
V(a)\geq V(b).
\]
For infinite domains, completeness and transitivity alone need not guarantee a useful numerical representation; additional continuity, measurability, topological, or related regularity conditions are required depending on the domain. The maximization expression below also assumes that a maximum exists. With a finite, nonempty \(A\), existence is immediate. With an infinite \(A\), compactness, continuity, or another existence argument may be needed. This reduced-form distinction between a coherent benchmark and a descriptive theory has long organized decision research (Edwards, 1954).
The model’s choice correspondence returns all feasible maximizers:
\[
C(A)
=
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in A}V(a)
=
\left\{
a\in A:
V(a)\geq V(b)\ \text{for every }b\in A
\right\}.
\]
If several alternatives tie, \(C(A)\) contains several actions. Predicting a single observed choice then requires a tie-breaking rule. For the job offers, equal scores mean that the model has not yet selected one job over the other.






ImportantDo not subtract ordinal scores



A value representation of a ranking is ordinal: any strictly increasing transformation represents the same preferences. Numerical gaps such as \(V(a)-V(b)\) therefore have no substantive magnitude unless \(V\) is placed on a cardinal scale. Expected-utility indices are unique up to positive affine transformations, and multiattribute scores require explicit normalization. This appendix uses value differences only after those scale assumptions are stated.
crumbs: Appendices
A  Rational Choice and Decision Analysis

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
text:
3. Consequences, beliefs, and expected utility
The reduced-form function \(V(a)\) can be unpacked into beliefs about consequences and values over those consequences.
If action \(a\) produces a known consequence \(x(a)\), and \(u(x)\) represents the value of consequence \(x\), then
\[
V(a)=u\bigl(x(a)\bigr).
\]
Under uncertainty, let \(O\) be a finite set of possible consequences. Let \(P(o\mid a)\) be the probability assigned to consequence \(o\) if action \(a\) is taken, and let \(u(o)\) represent preferences over consequences. A standard expected-utility evaluation is
\[
V(a)
=
EU(a)
=
\sum_{o\in O}P(o\mid a)u(o),
\]
so that
\[
C(A)
=
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in A}
\sum_{o\in O}P(o\mid a)u(o).
\]
This representation separates three objects:

\(A\): feasible alternatives;
\(P(o\mid a)\): beliefs or specified probabilities over consequences; and
\(u(o)\): values or preferences over consequences.

These are probabilities for the consequences of taking each action; an observed association between an action and an outcome does not automatically supply them. The formula also requires more than completeness and transitivity. For lotteries with specified probabilities, the von Neumann–Morgenstern expected-utility representation additionally relies on continuity and independence conditions (von Neumann & Morgenstern, 1944). A subjective-probability interpretation requires further assumptions connecting choices to beliefs. Chapter 16 develops expected value, expected utility, final consequences, curvature, and the independence axiom in the setting of risky choice.
Nothing in the expression requires selfish values. A consequence may include effects on other people, fairness, identity, environmental outcomes, duties, or future generations. Some rights and obligations may instead be represented as constraints that remove impermissible actions from \(A\). Neither placement settles the normative question of whose interests count or which trade-offs are legitimate.
crumbs: Appendices
A  Rational Choice and Decision Analysis

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
text:
4. Invariance, regularity, and omitted variables
A descriptive extension allows context and internal state to shape the consideration set, beliefs, and values:
\[
V(a\mid z,m)
=
\sum_{o\in O}
P(o\mid a,z,m)\,
u(o\mid z,m),
\qquad a\in K(z,m)\cap A.
\]
After feasibility checking, and assuming at least one considered option remains feasible, observed selection can then be written as
\[
a^{\mathrm{choice}}
\in
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in K(z,m)\cap A}
V(a\mid z,m).
\]
This decomposition is not by itself a predictive psychological theory. If \(K\), \(P\), and \(u\) are adjusted only after the choice has been observed, almost any behavior can be rationalized. The representation becomes testable only when the relevant variables and their response to context are specified or measured independently of the outcome. It also represents selection, not successful execution. A model of implementation would require a separate mapping from chosen action to performed action and realized consequence.
Let \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) be two descriptions of a decision. If they leave the feasible set, consequence distributions, and values unchanged, then description invariance requires the same choice correspondence:
\[
C_{d_1}(A)=C_{d_2}(A).
\]
This condition does not require the same single action to be observed when the common correspondence contains several tied maximizers. An invariant point prediction requires either a unique maximizer or a tie-breaking rule that is itself held fixed.
The survival-versus-mortality result is informative because the descriptions were designed to express complementary versions of the same outcome information, yet preferences shifted (McNeil et al., 1982). The result challenges description invariance under that representation; it does not show that every wording change is normatively irrelevant or that all readers understand complementary descriptions identically.
In stochastic choice models satisfying regularity, adding a new alternative \(d\) cannot increase the probability of choosing an existing alternative \(a\):
\[
\Pr(a\mid A\cup\{d\})
\leq
\Pr(a\mid A).
\]
An attraction effect occurs when an asymmetrically dominated decoy raises the choice share of a target, violating regularity for that menu comparison (Huber et al., 1982). The formal condition concerns probabilities across otherwise comparable menus. It does not imply that every added option creates an attraction effect.
Defaults illustrate a different boundary. An opt-in and an opt-out design are not the same decision merely because both responses are physically available. A default may change effort, delay, perceived recommendation, responsibility, anticipated regret, or the consequence of inaction. If action costs matter, they should enter the consequences or a consistently defined net value; they should not appear as an extra primitive after \(V\) has already absorbed them. Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 use these distinctions to separate a challenge to an invariant benchmark from a variable omitted by a thin model.

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
text:
5. Opportunity cost and decision margins
Suppose \(A\) contains at least two alternatives. For a contemplated action \(a\), define a best feasible alternative forgone as
\[
b^*(a)
\in
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{b\in A\setminus\{a\}}V(b).
\]
The alternative \(b^*(a)\)—or the set of tied alternatives that satisfy the expression—is the opportunity-cost benchmark. Discovering a better feasible option can change that benchmark even when the contemplated action itself has not changed.
When \(V\) has a declared cardinal scale, including an explicit origin and unit, the opportunity cost can be reported numerically as
\[
OC(a)
=
V\bigl(b^*(a)\bigr)
=
\max_{b\in A\setminus\{a\}}V(b).
\]
A corresponding decision margin is
\[
M(a)
=
V(a)-OC(a).
\]
If \(a\) is uniquely optimal, \(M(a)>0\). If the scale is merely ordinal, however, the meaningful statement is that \(a\) ranks above or below its best forgone alternative—not that the gap is “small.” Even on a normalized cardinal scale, fragility should be assessed by varying substantive beliefs, values, and constraints rather than interpreting an arbitrary score gap in isolation.
Opportunity costs are easy to neglect when the displaced alternative is not made explicit. Experimental evidence shows that prompting consumers to consider other uses of money can change purchase decisions (Frederick et al., 2009). Chapter 2 develops the practical question: what is the best feasible path this commitment would prevent?

A  Rational Choice and Decision Analysis

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
text:
6. Multiattribute value
Suppose each alternative produces outcomes on \(J\) attributes, such as income, health, autonomy, learning, and security. Let \(x_j(a)\) be the performance of alternative \(a\) on attribute \(j\). A common additive model is
\[
V(a)
=
\sum_{j=1}^{J}w_jv_j\bigl(x_j(a)\bigr),
\]
where each \(v_j(\cdot)\) maps performance on attribute \(j\) to a common normalized scale and the weights satisfy
\[
w_j\geq 0,
\qquad
\sum_{j=1}^{J}w_j=1.
\]
A transparent normalization sets \(v_j=0\) at the least-preferred relevant level and \(v_j=1\) at the most-preferred relevant level for the decision. The resulting \(w_j\) are swing weights: they represent the importance of moving across the stated range of attribute \(j\), not a context-free claim that “health matters 30 percent.” Changing the range changes the meaning of the weight.
The additive form requires appropriate preferential-independence and scaling assumptions. It is not justified merely because a worksheet has several columns. If workload affects health, learning affects future income, or two attributes describe the same consequence, a simple sum can double-count value. The analyst should first redefine overlapping attributes. If a substantively important interaction remains, it should be modeled and elicited explicitly rather than hidden in an unexplained adjustment.
When consequences are uncertain, an additive multiattribute utility model can be nested inside expected utility:
\[
V(a)
=
\sum_{o\in O}P(o\mid a)
\left[
\sum_{j=1}^{J}
w_jv_j\bigl(x_j(a,o)\bigr)
\right].
\]
This expression keeps prediction and valuation separate. \(P(o\mid a)\) represents what is expected to happen; \(v_j\) and \(w_j\) represent how performance over defined attribute ranges is valued. Under uncertainty, the \(v_j\) terms must function as cardinal von Neumann–Morgenstern utility components on compatible scales, and the additive form requires additive independence over the relevant lotteries, which is stronger than the assumptions behind a deterministic scoring table. Without those conditions, the expression is only a pragmatic expected-score model, not an expected-utility representation. The model remains an aid to disciplined discussion, not a machine for discovering ethically correct weights (Keeney & Raiffa, 1976).

A  Rational Choice and Decision Analysis

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
text:
7. Value of information
Would a further conversation with an employer be worth your time? Information has instrumental value when its possible answers let you choose better. A question that cannot affect any relevant action has no instrumental value for that decision, even if the answer is interesting.
Let \(\theta\in\Theta\) denote an uncertain state of the world, where \(\Theta\) is finite or countable and the relevant expectations converge. Let \(p(\theta)\) be the prior probability and \(u(a,\theta)\) the value produced by action \(a\) in state \(\theta\). Without additional information, the best expected value is
\[
V_0
=
\max_{a\in A}
\sum_{\theta\in\Theta}
p(\theta)u(a,\theta).
\]
Perfect information reveals \(\theta\) before action is chosen. The expected value attainable with perfect information is
\[
V_{\mathrm{PI}}
=
\sum_{\theta\in\Theta}
p(\theta)
\max_{a\in A}u(a,\theta),
\]
and the expected value of perfect information is
\[
EVPI
=
V_{\mathrm{PI}}-V_0.
\]
Under the stated model, finite expectations, the same action set, and costless accurate revelation of the relevant state, \(EVPI\geq 0\). It is a gross upper bound on the value of any signal about that same \(\theta\) for that same decision. It is not an upper bound on information that changes the action set, reveals a different state, creates strategic consequences, or serves another objective.
Now suppose a test, pilot, interview, or study produces a finite or countable signal \(Y\), with likelihood \(p(y\mid\theta)\). A coherent joint probability model implies
\[
p(y)
=
\sum_{\theta\in\Theta}
p(y\mid\theta)p(\theta),
\]
and, whenever \(p(y)>0\), Bayes’ rule gives
\[
p(\theta\mid y)
=
\frac{p(y\mid\theta)p(\theta)}
{p(y)}.
\]
The expected value of acting after the signal is
\[
V_Y
=
\sum_y p(y)
\max_{a\in A}
\sum_{\theta\in\Theta}
p(\theta\mid y)u(a,\theta).
\]
The expected value of sample information is
\[
EVSI(Y)=V_Y-V_0.
\]
Under the same action set and payoff model, costless observation, and finite expectations,
\[
0\leq EVSI(Y)\leq EVPI.
\]
If the total cost of obtaining and using the information is \(c(Y)\), expressed in the same cardinal units as \(V\), its net value is
\[
NVSI(Y)=EVSI(Y)-c(Y).
\]
False positives, false negatives, and other ordinary signal errors belong in the likelihood \(p(y\mid\theta)\). The cost term can include money, delay, attention, privacy loss, implementation effort, and strategic disclosure. Model misspecification—such as an incorrect likelihood or an omitted state—is a separate robustness problem rather than a cost that should be added after the fact.
If every possible signal leads to the same action and the signal changes no other payoff or future decision, then the information has zero instrumental value for this decision. This is the formal counterpart of Chapter 2’s branch test: state what action follows each plausible answer before gathering more information (Raiffa, 1968).

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
text:
8. Sensitivity and robustness
A job recommendation may depend on a forecast of promotion prospects or on the weight you give flexibility. Sensitivity analysis asks how far those inputs would have to change before the recommendation changes. On a declared cardinal scale, the value difference between alternatives \(a\) and \(b\) is
\[
\Delta_{ab}=V(a)-V(b).
\]
The sign identifies the ranking: \(a\) is preferred when \(\Delta_{ab}>0\), the alternatives tie when \(\Delta_{ab}=0\), and \(b\) is preferred when \(\Delta_{ab}<0\). The magnitude has meaning only under the scale assumptions stated earlier.

Probability threshold
Suppose action \(a\) produces a high outcome \(H\) with probability \(p\) and a low outcome \(L\) otherwise, while action \(b\) produces certain outcome \(c\). Assume \(u(H)>u(L)\). Indifference requires
\[
p\,u(H)+(1-p)u(L)=u(c),
\]
which gives the threshold
\[
p^*
=
\frac{u(c)-u(L)}
{u(H)-u(L)}.
\]
An interior threshold requires \(0<p^*<1\), equivalently \(u(L)<u(c)<u(H)\). Weak inequalities allow boundary thresholds at zero or one. When \(p^*\in[0,1]\), \(a\) is preferred when \(p>p^*\). If the plausible range for \(p\) lies entirely on one side of the threshold, the ranking is robust to that uncertainty. If the range crosses the threshold, information about \(p\) may have decision value.


Weight threshold
With two normalized attributes, suppose
\[
V(a)=w\,v_1(a)+(1-w)v_2(a),
\qquad 0\leq w\leq 1.
\]
The weight at which \(a\) and \(b\) tie is
\[
w^*
=
\frac{v_2(b)-v_2(a)}
{\bigl[v_1(a)-v_1(b)\bigr]+\bigl[v_2(b)-v_2(a)\bigr]},
\]
provided the denominator is nonzero. The threshold is decision-relevant only if \(w^*\in[0,1]\); the signs of the attribute differences determine which alternative is preferred on each side. The useful question is whether reasonable stakeholders or elicitation ranges place \(w\) on different sides of the threshold, not whether an unsupported point weight equals \(0.63\) rather than \(0.61\).


Joint sensitivity
One-at-a-time sensitivity can mislead when inputs move together. A start-up’s survival, salary growth, workload, and future options may be correlated. Scenario analysis therefore varies coherent bundles of assumptions:
\[
V(a\mid s),
\qquad
s\in
\{\text{favorable},\text{central},\text{unfavorable}\}.
\]
A recommendation is robust over the declared scenario set when the same alternative remains preferred throughout it. That statement is conditional on the scenarios being substantively plausible; it does not prove global optimality or assign probabilities to scenarios that were never estimated. When rankings change, the analysis should report the conditions producing each recommendation rather than hide them inside an average score.

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
section: 9. Sequential choice, reversibility, and the cost of analysis
text:
9. Sequential choice, reversibility, and the cost of analysis
Reversibility matters because an initial action can preserve or remove future choices. Let \(a\) be an action taken now, \(y\) information observed later, and \(B(a,y)\) the set of actions available after \(a\) and \(y\). Let \(V_0(a)\) be the immediate value of the initial action and \(V_1(b;a,y)\) the continuation value of later action \(b\). Their sum requires a common cardinal, additively separable intertemporal scale; \(V_1\) must be discounted to the decision time where necessary. Under those assumptions, a two-stage evaluation is
\[
V_{\mathrm{seq}}(a)
=
V_0(a)
+
\sum_y p(y\mid a)
\max_{b\in B(a,y)}
V_1(b;a,y).
\]
Switching costs, exit costs, and implementation burdens should enter \(V_1\) or restrict \(B(a,y)\). If one initial action preserves a superset of future actions while all immediate consequences, probabilities, and costs remain the same, its continuation value is weakly higher. In practice those “all else equal” conditions often fail: a pilot may preserve flexibility while delaying benefits or imposing a setup cost.
This formulation avoids adding a free-standing “reversibility bonus” to a value function that already includes every consequence. It also clarifies why information and reversibility interact. A future signal has more instrumental value when the decision-maker retains an action that can respond to it.
Analysis itself consumes scarce resources. Let \(r\) denote one additional analysis step that may produce result \(y\), and let \(A(r,y)\) be the feasible set remaining after the step and result. Express the direct resource cost \(c(r)\), plus any delay cost not already represented through \(A(r,y)\) or \(V(a\mid y,r)\), in the same cardinal units as \(V\). The net expected gain can then be written as
\[
G(r)
=
\sum_y p(y\mid r)
\max_{a\in A(r,y)}V(a\mid y,r)
-
\max_{a\in A}V(a)
-
c(r).
\]
Under this stylized metareasoning rule, conduct the step when \(G(r)>0\). The analysis-dependent action set represents options that expire, emerge, or become infeasible during deliberation; any other consequence of delay belongs in \(V(a\mid y,r)\) or \(c(r)\), but not both. This is a normative comparison of the expected benefit and cost of one more analysis step. It is not Simon’s satisficing model itself. Bounded rationality supplies the motivation—search, attention, time, memory, and computation are scarce—while satisficing describes a different stopping strategy based on aspiration levels (Simon, 1955, 1956).
Low-stakes, familiar, reversible decisions often justify routines or simple rules. High-stakes, novel, irreversible, strategically interdependent, or low-feedback decisions often justify more structure. These are reasons to vary the depth of analysis, not proof that a particular formula should govern every decision.

title: Appendix A — Rational Choice and Decision Analysis
section: 10. What formal analysis can and cannot establish
text:
10. What formal analysis can and cannot establish
Return to the job offers. The analysis is useful if it reveals an overlooked option, a forecast that deserves checking, or a trade-off hidden inside a single score. It can tell you which assumptions support the recommendation and what would change it.
The equations cannot supply accurate forecasts or settle whose interests should count. They also do not guarantee that the chosen action will be carried out or that its outcome will be interpreted fairly. Formal analysis provides a precise account of the assumptions; behavioral evidence, practical knowledge, and ethical reasoning determine whether they are appropriate.
Chapter 16 develops risky choice further, while Chapter 20 examines how labels and mental accounts change the way consequences are compared.

title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
text:
Four questions, not one master cause
Why minds value what they do—and why origin is not obligation
A pastry can look irresistible before lunch and uninteresting afterward. Hunger helps explain the change, but it leaves other questions open: how did the person learn what tastes good, why do some tastes acquire value so readily, and why might a familiar preference work poorly in a new environment?
This appendix separates those questions. It extends Chapter 6 on valuation and Chapter 8 on useful shortcuts. Appendix A asks how a choice should relate to its stated objectives; here we ask how motives and decision processes came to take their current form.
Return to the pastry. Four questions help us separate explanations that are often compressed into the word cause.
Tinbergen (1963) distinguished these four questions to prevent one kind of explanation from displacing the others. Mechanism and ontogeny are commonly grouped as proximate explanations; function and phylogeny as ultimate or evolutionary explanations (Mayr, 1961; Scott-Phillips et al., 2011). Ultimate does not mean deepest, final, or morally superior. It identifies a kind of historical question.
The smell of the pastry, the person’s hunger, and memories of eating it contribute to an account of the present response. An evolutionary explanation asks a different question about the history of the capacities involved. Neither account replaces the other.
“Genes are the distant reason” is also too simple. Gene expression and gene–environment interaction operate during development, so genetic processes can be part of a proximate account. Evolutionary explanations concern changes in populations across generations, not a special gene located behind each behavior. Cultural transmission can recalibrate motives within a lifetime, preserve practices across generations, and alter the environments in which biological selection occurs. The useful distinction is among questions and evidence, not between genes and everything else. Modern accounts accordingly emphasize interaction among development, ecology, inheritance, and culture rather than a one-way chain from distant gene to present act (Laland et al., 2011; Richerson et al., 2010).

title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
text:
Mechanism: Which bodily, perceptual, affective, learning, and neural processes produce the attraction now?
Ontogeny: How did the response develop through maturation, individual learning, family practices, and culture?
Function: Under which past conditions, if any, did similar mechanisms affect survival or reproduction relative to alternatives?
Phylogeny: Through what evolutionary history did the relevant capacities arise?

title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
section: Evolutionary function is not a preference or a command
text:
Evolutionary function is not a preference or a command
Natural selection requires variation, some form of inheritance, and systematic differences in survival or reproduction among variants (Lewontin, 1970). It works through historical population change. It has no foresight, does not design from scratch, and cannot guarantee a globally optimal result (Gould & Lewontin, 1979).
Even “survival and reproduction” needs precision. Survival matters evolutionarily insofar as it affects genetic transmission; selection can favor reproductive benefits that carry survival costs. Fitness accounting can also include effects on relatives’ reproduction under the conditions specified by kin-selection theory (Hamilton, 1964). None of this implies that a person consciously computes genetic fitness or that reproductive success is the person’s experienced objective.
Four quantities are easily confused:



Table B.1: Fitness, preference, well-being, and moral worth are not interchangeable










Quantity
Unit of analysis
The question it answers




Subjective decision value
A person choosing in a current state and context
How much weight does the option receive now?


Experienced value or well-being
A person’s experience and evaluation over a stated horizon
What pleasure, pain, satisfaction, connection, or meaning follows?


Evolutionary fitness consequence
Relative genetic representation in a specified population and environment
How did a variant affect transmission across generations?


Normative value
Persons and institutions under an ethical or prudential argument
What ought to be pursued, protected, permitted, or prohibited?






Sweetness illustrates the distinction. A preference can have a plausible evolutionary history while producing different consequences in a setting where concentrated sugar is readily available. Explaining its origin does not decide whether eating another pastry serves this person’s present goals.
The distinction matters whenever origin and justification diverge. A status motive may once have improved access to resources and allies while making a current career choice anxious or destructive. Sweetness can retain strong appeal where concentrated sugar is abundant. People may deliberately value contraception, celibacy, adoption, scholarship, art, spiritual practice, truth, or justice. Such commitments are not errors in a hidden reproductive utility function. They are products of human capacities for learning, language, reflection, culture, and institutional life.
A recurring response also need not be an adaptation. Alternatives include a flexible learned response, cultural transmission, a by-product of another capacity, an exaptation, developmental constraint, drift, pathology, or a mismatch between a mechanism and its present environment. Several can contribute at once. Gould and Lewontin (1979) warned against treating a plausible adaptive story as sufficient evidence; Buss and colleagues (1998) later clarified distinctions among adaptations, by-products, and exaptations. The burden is to derive discriminating predictions, not merely to tell a coherent origin story.

title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
section: Needs and motives: Maslow and Kenrick
text:
Needs and motives: Maslow and Kenrick
Maslow (1943) proposed five broad classes of goal: physiological needs, safety, love and belonging, esteem, and self-actualization. He described them as a hierarchy of relative prepotency. On Maslow’s account, when several needs are seriously deprived, the relatively prepotent need is more likely to dominate attention. This is a claim about motivational priority, not a declaration that only one need can exist at a time.
The familiar pyramid makes the account look more rigid than Maslow’s text. Historical research found that Maslow did not create that diagram; later management writers turned the hierarchy into the now-standard stepped pyramid (Bridgman et al., 2019). Maslow explicitly allowed partial satisfaction, simultaneous motives, reversals, and exceptions. A meal can serve hunger, affiliation, identity, celebration, and status together.
Evidence supports the relevance of multiple needs more clearly than a universal staircase. Wahba and Bridwell’s (1976) review found limited support for the fixed ordering and little convincing support for the proposed sequence in which satisfying one level activates the next, while noting serious measurement problems. Tay and Diener (2011), using survey data from 123 countries, found that fulfillment of several kinds of need was associated with different aspects of subjective well-being. Those associations were largely independent of whether other needs had been fulfilled. The study was observational and does not establish a universal causal order, but it weighs against the claim that social connection, respect, or autonomy matter only after material needs are complete.
Kenrick and colleagues (2010) renovated the hierarchy using evolutionary, developmental, and life-history reasoning. Their proposal retains immediate physiological needs, self-protection, affiliation, and status or esteem, then distinguishes mate acquisition, mate retention, and parenting. Later-developing systems overlap rather than replace earlier ones, and current cues can activate any system that has developed.



Table B.2: Three representations that should not be treated as equivalent










Maslow’s original proposal
Popular simplification
Kenrick et al.’s proposal




Several partly satisfied needs; relative priority, reversals, and multiple motivation
A fixed staircase completed one level at a time
Overlapping, cue-sensitive systems linked to development and proposed evolutionary problems


Physiological, safety, belonging, esteem, and self-actualization
The same labels presented as a universal ranked pyramid
Physiological, self-protection, affiliation, status, mate acquisition, mate retention, and parenting


Useful taxonomy with limited direct testing in the original paper
Memorable teaching icon
Integrative, hypothesis-generating theory rather than a validated universal ordering






Keep three questions separate when using this framework: when a motive develops, what activates it now, and what historical function is proposed for it. Those are different claims even when they concern the same behavior.
Parenting can arise later in development without becoming every parent’s dominant motive, producing the most pleasure, or possessing greater moral worth. Kenrick and colleagues also removed self-actualization as a separate fundamental motive; they proposed that activities commonly described as self-actualizing could be largely subsumed under status or esteem and mating-related motives. Commentators argued that this reduction underweights culture, meaning, and distinctively human symbolic goals, and that discarding self-actualization was premature (Kesebir et al., 2010; Peterson & Park, 2010). Showing that creativity can carry status does not show that status exhausts its causes or meaning.
Maslow offered a taxonomy of recurring needs; Kenrick and colleagues proposed an evolutionary reorganization. Both can suggest questions about an active motive, but their inventories and ordering should not be treated as established laws. The meal remains a useful reminder that hunger, belonging, and social meaning can matter at the same time.
