title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
section: Rationality has more than one benchmark
text:
Rationality has more than one benchmark
A quick choice of food might be consistent with a person’s preference, sensible given limited time, and unhelpful for a long-term health goal. Different standards can therefore produce different assessments of the same choice. Appendix A develops the formal benchmark. Here the task is to keep its purpose distinct from ecological and evolutionary questions.



Table B.3: Different standards and an evolutionary lens can produce different assessments of one behavior










Lens or standard
Central question
A possible failure or limit




Coherence rationality
Do beliefs and preferences satisfy stated logical, probabilistic, and consistency relations?
Intransitive choice or a probability judgment that violates the named rule


Epistemic rationality
Are beliefs and confidence appropriately responsive to the available evidence?
Confidence can exceed what the evidence warrants.


Instrumental rationality
Given the person’s beliefs and endorsed ends, is the chosen means expected to advance those ends?
The chosen means may not be expected to advance the endorsed end. An instrumentally rational action can also fail because a reasonable belief was false or bad luck intervened.


Procedural rationality under bounds
Is the process appropriate to the stakes and the limits of information, time, attention, and computation?
A feasible process can still spend far too much or too little effort for the decision.


Ecological rationality
How well does this strategy exploit the structure of this environment?
A reliable cue in one ecology can become misleading in another.


Resource rationality
Does the procedure use limited computational resources efficiently for the modeled objective and costs?
The conclusion changes when the assumed resource, prior, objective, or cost changes.


Evolutionary explanation—not a rationality criterion
What historical fitness consequences could have favored this mechanism over variants?
Historical success need not produce present coherence, welfare, or moral value.






Simon (1955, 1956) made limits and environmental structure central to theories of choice. The heuristics-and-biases program then documented systematic departures from specified benchmarks (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974), while the adaptive-toolbox program formalized simple procedures and asked when they succeed (Gigerenzer & Goldstein, 1996; Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier, 2011). These are not mutually exclusive questions. A judgment can violate a coherence rule, arise from an identifiable heuristic, and perform well under one environment but badly under another.
Ecological rationality is strategy–environment fit. Recognition, for example, can help when exposure genuinely covaries with the target, and mislead when publicity is manufactured (Goldstein & Gigerenzer, 2002). Resource-rational analysis goes further by modeling the value of improved performance against the costs of computation (Lieder & Griffiths, 2020). It can turn an apparent imperfection into an efficient approximation under stated constraints. But “optimal” belongs to the model, not automatically to the human. Critics note that a useful modeling method does not by itself establish that people are generally resource-rational (Rahnev, 2020).

Optimally irrational?
Lionel Page’s Optimally Irrational (2023) develops the productive thesis that some behavioral anomalies become intelligible when evolution, cognition, strategic interaction, and omitted constraints are brought into the analysis. The title is best treated as a question, not a verdict.
Before calling a behavior optimally irrational, specify:

The benchmark it violates. Logic, Bayesian updating, expected utility, consistency, or something else?
The objective being optimized. Accuracy, current payoff, time, computational cost, experienced welfare, strategic commitment, or fitness?
The information and constraints. What could the decision-maker actually know and compute?
The environment. Which cue–outcome relations and feedback conditions make the rule succeed?
The comparator. Better than which feasible alternative procedure?
The evidence. Does the model predict new variation, or merely rationalize an observed error after the fact?

Sometimes the richer model will vindicate a simple rule. Sometimes it will reveal a mismatch. Sometimes the original benchmark remains appropriate and the person made a consequential error. “Evolution produced it” cannot decide among these possibilities.

title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
section: Heuristics can be tools and sources of bias
text:
Heuristics can be tools and sources of bias
A familiar cue can make a good shortcut when it tracks the outcome we care about. If the relationship changes, the same shortcut can mislead. To evaluate it, we need to specify the information available, the cost of mistakes, and the feedback through which the person could learn.



Table B.4: Conditional success does not turn a heuristic into a universal rule











Process
Why it can work
When it can fail
What the evidence does not show automatically




Recognition
Exposure may covary with prominence, size, quality, or another target.
Advertising or unequal exposure breaks the relation.
That ignorance is generally beneficial or recognition is used exclusively


Skilled intuition
Repeated valid patterns and sufficiently clear feedback can compress learning into rapid recognition.
Rare, unstable, strategically manipulated, or delayed-feedback environments do not calibrate confidence.
That experience alone creates expertise


Sensitive threat threshold
If a missed danger is much costlier than a false alarm, many cheap false positives can minimize expected loss.
Error costs, base rates, or cues differ from those assumed.
That a particular fear, anxiety, or social judgment evolved for this function


Availability
Ease of retrieval can track frequency or recency in a representative sample of experience.
Vivid news, selective memory, and engineered exposure distort what is retrievable.
That every availability effect is adaptive or genetically inherited






Kahneman and Klein (2009) provide a useful bridge: intuitive expertise deserves trust when an environment contains learnable regularities and the decision-maker has substantial practice with sufficiently clear feedback. Confidence is not one of those conditions.
Error-management theory makes the evolutionary logic precise in a different way. If the fitness costs of false negatives and false positives were systematically asymmetric, selection could favor a decision threshold that produces many errors of the cheaper kind (Haselton & Buss, 2000). Nesse’s (2005) smoke-detector model applies the same signal-detection logic to defensive responses. The model shows that apparently excessive alarms can be optimal under specified costs and base rates. It does not establish that any observed human bias is an adaptation. Historical ecology, heritable variation, mechanism, and distinctive predictions still require evidence.
Three empirical claims must remain separate:

A strategy can outperform an alternative in a modeled environment.
People actually use that strategy under the stated conditions.
The strategy or its selection mechanism evolved because of that performance.

Evidence for the first does not prove the second or third. This separation prevents ecological rationality from becoming an all-purpose defense of behavior.

title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
section: Mismatch is a testable hypothesis, not a slogan
text:
Mismatch is a testable hypothesis, not a slogan
A mechanism whose performance or fitness consequences depended on a recurrent cue–outcome relation can perform poorly when the distribution, intensity, or meaning of cues changes. This evolutionary mismatch is one bridge from adaptation to contemporary bias (Li et al., 2018). But “Stone Age mind in a modern world” is too vague to explain an observation.
A useful mismatch claim identifies four elements:

Cue: What feature does the mechanism detect?
Past relation: What outcome did that cue reliably predict in the relevant historical ecology?
Environmental change: How has the cue–outcome relation, intensity, or timing changed?
Predicted consequence: When and for whom should the response now become excessive, insufficient, or misdirected?

Sweetness offers a plausible structure: a cue related to energy availability can remain attractive when food production concentrates it beyond earlier ranges. A digital notification offers a more tentative hypothesis: cues of socially relevant information may capture attention even when platforms generate far more cues with weaker informational value. The second account needs direct evidence about the cue, mechanism, learning history, and comparison environment; “technology hijacks evolution” is not evidence.
Ancestral environments were diverse, and human learning and culture can change quickly. A response that looks mismatched may instead reflect current incentives, habit, social learning, measurement error, or deliberate choice. A good mismatch hypothesis predicts when the behavior should strengthen, weaken, or disappear as the cue–outcome structure changes.

title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
section: How to evaluate an evolutionary explanation
text:
How to evaluate an evolutionary explanation
An evolutionary account earns confidence by surviving alternatives and generating evidence beyond the observation it was invented to explain.



Table B.5: Different evidence answers different parts of an evolutionary claim










Evidence
What it can contribute
Persistent limitation




Formal model
Makes variants, objectives, constraints, and trade-offs explicit
A result follows only from its assumptions.


Comparative evidence
Tests whether variation across species or populations matches the proposed ecology
Similarity and difference can have several historical causes.


Developmental evidence
Reveals timing, plasticity, sensitive periods, and learning pathways
Early emergence alone does not prove genetic adaptation.


Cross-cultural evidence
Tests universality and predicted ecological variation
Sampling, translation, institutions, and shared history complicate inference.


Experiment or natural experiment
Tests cues, mechanisms, and environmental contingencies
Present causal effects do not by themselves identify evolutionary origin.


Genetic or historical evidence
Connects heritable variation or change across time to selection hypotheses
Complex behavior is polygenic, developmentally mediated, and culturally embedded.






Before accepting an adaptation claim, identify the mechanism, the proposed historical problem, and the alternative variants or explanations. Then ask what the account predicts across environments, development, cultures, or species. The strongest test is an observation that the proposed account and a plausible rival predict differently.
Without such a test, the account remains a possibility rather than an established explanation. The optional population-model note below shows why specifying an update rule is also essential when the claim comes from a simulation.

section: What the evolutionary lens changes in a decision
text:
What the evolutionary lens changes in a decision
Return to the invitation to give a prestigious talk from Chapter 6. An evolutionary lens does not produce a hidden correct answer. It improves the diagnosis.



Table B.6: Evolution adds diagnostic questions; it does not choose the objective









Lens
Question for the invitation




Proximate mechanism
Which feelings, bodily states, memories, and anticipated rewards make the invitation attractive or aversive now?


Development and culture
How did professional identity, family obligations, institutional norms, and prior experience shape those signals?


Evolutionary hypothesis
Are status, affiliation, threat, or opportunity motives plausible parts of the explanation, and what evidence would distinguish them?


Ecological fit
Does prestige predict the outcomes the person cares about in this professional environment, or is it a noisy cue?


Resource fit
Would further analysis improve the choice enough to justify its time and attention costs?


Normative judgment
After forecasting consequences for self and others, which values and obligations does the person endorse?






The invitation may now look different because we have examined what prestige predicts, how the response developed, and which present commitments matter. An evolutionary explanation can contribute to that understanding; the person must still decide which consequences to pursue.

title: Appendix B — Evolutionary Explanations of Value, Choice, and Rationality
text:
Optional research notes






NoteCauses across timescales





Sapolsky’s backward clock
Robert Sapolsky’s Behave (2017) starts with an action and works backward: from immediate neural activity to the preceding situation, bodily state, development, and evolutionary history. The method makes a useful demand on an explanation. Naming what happened in the brain just before a choice leaves open how that system came to respond as it did.
Determined (Sapolsky, 2023) opens with the old anecdote of a world resting on a turtle, which rests on another turtle, and so on. Sapolsky reverses the usual joke. A final turtle floating without support would resemble a choice with no antecedent cause. He uses the phrase “turtles all the way down” for the claim that intentions, neural events, development, social conditions, culture, and evolution form an unbroken causal history. He uses that history to argue that there is no causally independent chooser outside biology and environment, and then asks how punishment, praise, inequality, and compassion should change if free will is rejected.
Two distinctions matter for the argument. Showing that an event has antecedent causes does not by itself establish causal determinism. Determinism is not perfect prediction: even a causally deterministic system can remain practically unpredictable because it is complex, sensitive to initial conditions, or imperfectly observed. Randomness is not agency: an undetermined event would not, merely by being random, become an authored or controlled choice. These distinctions explain why Determined examines chaos, emergence, and quantum mechanics rather than treating unpredictability as evidence of free will.
The useful scientific lesson is narrower than Sapolsky’s conclusion about free will. Tinbergen’s framework distinguishes kinds of explanation; it does not by itself settle the metaphysics of agency or the ethics of responsibility. Nor is the causal structure literally a vertical stack. Current states, development, institutions, and culture interact through feedback, and causes at one level can alter conditions at another. This book therefore adopts Sapolsky’s demand for causal depth—do not stop at the reported reason or nearest mechanism—without presenting his rejection of free will as an empirical consensus. Compatibilism offers a live alternative: it holds that free will can be compatible with determinism, and some compatibilist accounts locate relevant control in causally realized capacities such as responsiveness to reasons rather than in an exception to causal history (McKenna & Coates, 2024).









NoteA proposed history of cognitive capacities





Bennett’s five proposed breakthroughs
Max Bennett works forward from simpler nervous systems toward human cognitive capacities. In A Brief History of Intelligence, drawing on an earlier hypothesis-and-theory article, Bennett proposes five cumulative “breakthroughs” in the lineage leading to humans (Bennett, 2021, 2023).



Table B.7: Bennett’s proposed breakthroughs provide a first-approximation map, not five settled dates or discrete inventions





Proposed breakthrough
Lineage used in Bennett’s model
Decision-relevant capacity
Connection in this book




Steering
Early bilaterians
Integrate internal state with external cues to approach or avoid
Valuation


Reinforcing
Early vertebrates
Learn action values from experienced consequences
Habits and reinforcement


Simulating
Early mammals
Represent possible actions and outcomes before acting
Internal models and goal-directed control


Mentalizing
Early primates
Represent one’s own and others’ knowledge, intentions, and future states
Strategic interdependence and communication


Speaking
Early humans
Use semantic, rhythmic communication, including language and music
Communication






The sequence suggests an expansion in the sources from which choice can learn: inherited valence, the consequences of one’s own actions, internally simulated futures, observed agents and inferred minds, and culturally communicated experience. Later capacities do not replace earlier ones. Human deliberation still depends on approach and avoidance, reinforcement, and embodied action; language and culture can redirect those systems rather than float above them.
Bennett explicitly calls the five-stage sequence a simplified, anthropocentric first approximation. It follows one lineage toward humans; it does not rank living species on a ladder, imply that extant animals are frozen ancestors, or rule out convergent evolution. The number, boundaries, neural implementations, and historical timing of the breakthroughs remain hypotheses. Its value here is organizational: it connects phylogeny to distinct capacities for valuing, learning, imagining, understanding other agents, and sharing models.









NotePopulation and spatial models





Population and spatial models
Classical game theory asks what a deliberate player should choose against another strategy. Evolutionary game theory instead asks which strategies become more common under a declared process linking payoff to replication, survival, or imitation (Maynard Smith & Price, 1973). The vocabulary can describe genes, cultural transmission, or organizational routines only when the transmission mechanism is named. A frequency change is not evidence of natural selection merely because an evolutionary equation can reproduce it.
For two strategies, let \(x\) be the share using strategy 1. Let \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) be nonnegative reproductive or imitation weights derived from their payoffs, with \(xf_1+(1-x)f_2>0\). A discrete replicator-style rule is
\[
x' = \frac{xf_1}{xf_1+(1-x)f_2}.
\]
These restrictions keep the updated share between zero and one. Arbitrary game payoffs, especially negative ones, cannot be inserted without a stated mapping to admissible weights. The equation specifies a process to investigate rather than a claim that people literally use it. Any conclusion remains conditional on the payoff function, initial shares, population mixing, horizon, omitted costs, and choice of update rule. An evolutionarily stable strategy is resistant to invasion by any sufficiently rare alternative strategy in the model’s strategy space. It is not automatically a consciously chosen strategy, a welfare optimum, or a moral recommendation. A stable population mixture is also different from each person deliberately randomizing.
Spatial models add another dependency: who interacts with whom. Cooperative clusters, conditional helping, or aggregate segregation can arise under particular neighborhoods and update rules. A model pattern does not identify human intent, innateness, or the historical cause of a real city or institution. Before interpreting a formal or simulated population result, preserve this minimum record:



Table B.8: A minimum provenance record for population and spatial models









Model component
Minimum provenance




Frequency update
Payoffs, initial shares, update rule, and horizon


Spatial interaction
Topology, neighborhood, timing, mobility, vacancies, and tie-breaking


Stochastic simulation
Pseudorandom generator, seed, replications, and outcome distribution—not only one attractive run


Transport claim
The real-world observation that could distinguish the modeled process from learning, imitation, institutional change, or selection






Figure B.1 applies that standard. In one seeded Schelling-style teaching run, agents move only when fewer than one-third of their occupied neighbours share their group and choose a vacancy satisfying that threshold. The average same-group-neighbour share rises from 0.48 to 0.68. The pattern shows what these declared rules can generate; it does not show that the same threshold, motive, or process caused segregation in a real neighbourhood.






Figure B.1: Local moves produce more same-group clustering in one seeded teaching simulation. The model illustrates a possible process; it is not evidence about the cause of segregation in a real neighborhood.



The retained generator, scripts/build_schelling_sequence.py, uses Python’s random.Random(20260830) on a bounded 18 × 14 grid, with 107 agents per group and 38 vacancies. Neighbors are the eight surrounding cells, excluding vacancies from the same-group share. An agent with no occupied neighbors is treated as satisfied and assigned a same-group share of one. Each sweep shuffles occupied cells; an unsatisfied agent moves uniformly among currently acceptable vacancies. The run stops after a sweep with no moves or after 25 sweeps. Here it stops after four sweeps and 44 moves.
Reproducible teaching implementations include Schelling-style segregation (Schelling, 1969; Wilensky, 1997), evolutionary prisoner’s-dilemma dynamics (Wilensky, 2002), and one specified ethnocentrism model (Hammond & Axelrod, 2006; Wilensky, 2003). Tournament success, repeated-game equilibrium, and evolutionary stability answer different questions: tit-for-tat’s success in one tournament and its vulnerability under another mutation–selection process are not contradictory findings (Axelrod, 1984; Imhof et al., 2007). The correct inference is always conditional on the declared process.

title: Appendix C — Portable Tools
text:
Individual judgment and decision process
Preserve a decision before its outcome with the journal, or examine an earlier decision with the audit. The shorter tools below focus on evidence, disagreement, and intuitive judgment.








NoteOne-Page Decision Journal



Use one entry for a consequential, uncertain, repeated, contested, or difficult-to-reverse decision. Complete Before choosing before the result is knowable. At the review trigger, append After the outcome without rewriting the original. Definitions and evidence are in Chapter 41.
Use the same seven labels at both moments. The right-hand entry must answer the left-hand entry on the same row.








Learning loop
Before choosing — freeze
After the outcome — append; do not overwrite




1. Decision and execution
Entry ID, time stamp, owner, deadline, scope, and exact decision.
What was implemented, when, and with what deviations or delayed effects?


2. Alternatives and opportunity cost
Serious options, best feasible alternative forgone, and excluded options.
Was an important option missing? What is known—and still unknowable—about the forgone paths?


3. Evidence and reference class
Sources, base rate or comparable cases, missing evidence, and fact–estimate–assumption labels.
Which evidence proved diagnostic, weak, misleading, missing, or unresolved? What new evidence arrived?


4. Predictions and assumptions
Resolvable forecasts with horizons, probabilities or ranges, and load-bearing assumptions and causal rationale.
Resolve the same forecasts. Which assumptions were supported, failed, or remain untested? Score calibration across comparable entries where useful.


5. Values and stakeholders
Criteria, priorities, affected people, protected constraints, and trade-offs.
Evaluate the same criteria and people. What was misweighted, neglected, or legitimately changed?


6. Context, incentives, dissent, and tools
Affect, pressure, incentives, roles, conflicts, strongest contrary view, and model or AI advice with follow-or-override reasons.
Which influence, dissenting concern, or tool output mattered? Was reliance or override calibrated to demonstrated value?


7. Choice, thresholds, and learning rule
Choice and reason, implementation owner, review trigger, evidence to collect, and continue–stop–scale–revise thresholds.
Were the process and thresholds followed? Rate process and outcome separately. State what should change, what should not, and the next test or review.



Remember the rhythm: freeze → compare → update. A concern noticed only afterward is useful evidence, but label it “not anticipated” rather than rewriting the original reasoning.
Keep access and retention proportionate to the stakes. The journal is a learning aid, not a substitute for required minutes, approvals, professional records, or privacy safeguards.









NoteDecision Audit Studio



Part 1 — capture the story. In five sentences, state the decision, choice, why it seemed right at the time, what happened, and how good the decision now seems on a 1–7 scale.
Part 2 — expose the process. Reconstruct alternatives, predictions, valuation, opportunity cost, context or state, and intended feedback. Identify the weakest link. Rate process quality and outcome quality separately. Finish: “The weakest link was ___ because . Process quality: /7. Outcome quality: /7. Next time I will improve it by .”
The audit cannot prove that the chosen road was best or recover the counterfactual road not taken. It can make missing options, weak evidence, hidden values, social influence, and unresolved uncertainty visible.









NoteAttention Audit



Write down what received attention and what was overlooked. Identify a feature of the situation that could explain the difference—for example, a vivid story, the order of information, or time pressure. Propose one change that would make the missing evidence easier to notice.









NotePrediction–Valuation Split



Write the disputed claim twice. Under Prediction, state what each person believes will happen, with probability or range and the evidence that could change it. Under Valuation, state what matters, to whom, the consequence if the prediction is wrong, and the trade-off each person is willing to accept. Finish with one sentence: “We disagree mainly about , so the next useful step is .”








NoteExpectation Loop Map



Choose one expectation and draw a possible path through which it could help change an outcome. The links might involve attention, interpretation, action, another person’s response, or physiology where relevant. Mark which links are observed and which are conjectures. Identify one comparison that could distinguish an expectation’s causal influence from an accurate forecast.








NoteBias Redesign Studio



Choose one process—hiring, investing, exam preparation, project planning, purchasing, or negotiation. Name a likely trigger such as an early anchor, vivid anecdote, identity threat, global impression, or time pressure. Redesign the process before the trigger appears: specify who does what, when, using which independent evidence. Prefer a changed environment to a promise of willpower.









NoteHeuristic Detector




What question needs an answer?
Which cue or rule appears to guide the judgment? If an easier question was substituted, name it.
When would that cue or rule give a useful answer?
What comparison or missing evidence could reveal a mistake here?

Finish with one change to the judgment process that addresses the identified weakness.

title: Appendix C — Portable Tools
text:
Probability, risk, time, and well-being
Start with the Probability Judgment Audit for a forecast or the Risky-Choice Audit for a choice among uncertain outcomes. The remaining tools address the specific problems named in their titles.







NoteProbability Judgment Audit



Define the event, population, time horizon, and the condition on which the probability depends. Translate percentages into counts within a shared population, keeping clear which subgroup each conditional rate refers to. For a conjunction, check that it is no more likely than either component; when adding probabilities, account for overlap. Record the forecast and a rule for resolving it. After resolution, score the same event—for a binary outcome, the Brier score is \((p-y)^2\), where \(p\) is the forecast probability between 0 and 1 and \(y\) is 1 if the event occurred and 0 otherwise.









NoteRisky-Choice Audit



List outcomes, probabilities or ambiguity, expected value, utility-relevant consequences, and the maximum affordable loss. Elicit the certainty equivalent before naming a risk attitude. State the reference point and whether the same prospect was described as a gain or a loss. Ask how insurance or diversification changes the possible payoffs. Separately, ask whether new information would change the probability estimates or the chosen action enough to justify its cost. Finish by naming what expected utility explains, what prospect theory describes, and what neither model identifies from one choice.








NoteExperience-Sample Audit



What outcomes were encountered, how many times, and through which sampling policy? Which rare outcomes could easily be absent? What caused sampling to stop? Are recent, vivid, or similar cases overrepresented? Did earlier choices remove opportunities for corrective learning? Add the best available description—base rates, denominators, time horizon, and uncertainty—then explain why description and experience agree or conflict.








NoteIntertemporal MOST Audit



Write the full stream of outcomes for each option. Use MOST to check magnitude, opportunity cost (including hidden zeros), sign, and time frame. Then ask whether cash needs, trust in future payment, inflation, or transaction costs explain the choice before attributing it to impatience. If you propose a commitment, specify the goal it protects and what happens after a missed step.








NoteMental-Accounting Audit



Name the label, reference point, budget boundary, opening and closing date, and payment–consumption link. Separate acquisition utility from transaction utility and sunk costs from future consequences. Reconstruct the choice once inside the current account and once across the full balance sheet or portfolio. Preserve a boundary when it protects a valued goal; relax it when the label, rather than future value, drives the decision.








NoteMarket Claim Audit



State the information set and expected-return model behind an efficiency claim. For an anomaly, ask about risk, mispricing, data mining, transaction costs, financing, short-sale constraints, and post-publication decay. For a bubble claim, separate uncertain fundamental value from evidence of feedback, resale motives, leverage, liquidity, and arbitrage limits. Historical patterns are evidence to diagnose, not trading instructions.








NoteWell-Being Measurement Audit



Specify whether the claim concerns experienced affect, remembered experience, life evaluation, meaning, or behavior. State the question wording, time window, scale, sample, comparison, and uncertainty. Separate income level from changes and adaptation; correlation from intervention; average effects from distribution and subgroup differences. Use forecasts from comparable lives or episodes before trusting a focusing intuition about what will make life go well.

title: Appendix C — Portable Tools
text:
Behavior and self-regulation
Use the Behavior Redesign Canvas to change a repeated action. The short urge-observation exercise is useful when a noticeable impulse is part of the episode.







NoteBehavior Redesign Canvas



Choose one mild, repeated behavior. Reconstruct cue → impulse → action → outcome, using impulse to mean readiness to act even when it was not consciously noticed. Record what the action accomplished in the moment.
Specify one feasible replacement and one change to the setting that would help it occur. Decide what you will record for a week, when you will review it, and how you will resume after a lapse. The output is the old routine, the proposed change, and a measure of whether it helped the person’s own goal.








NoteOne-Minute Urge Observation



Choose a mild everyday impulse. Pause, breathe, and notice what the urge feels like without requiring it to disappear. After about a minute, record what changed and choose the next action. This is an observation exercise; a minute is a practical interval, not a prediction of how quickly an urge should fade. It is not treatment for addiction or a crisis.

title: Appendix C — Portable Tools
text:
Persuasion, communication, and connection
Use the Verified Understanding Loop when people may be interpreting the same words differently. The message and listening tools help you prepare what to say or ask.






NoteModel-Updating Message



Before drafting, state who the audience is, what they currently believe, what concerns them, and what evidence could reasonably change their view. Name the desired response and the strongest objection to it.
For a short message, use AND–BUT–THEREFORE: establish shared reality, explain the problem, and propose the next step. For a fuller message, STORY means Shared reality, Trouble, Opportunity, Reasons to believe, and Yes to a specific decision. Make the action feasible and the uncertainty visible. Both are writing prompts; neither guarantees persuasion.








NoteLayered Listening



Begin with what happened, then ask what it meant to the speaker. Explore feelings, history, or relationships when they are relevant and the person welcomes the question. Check what is wanted from the conversation: understanding, advice, a decision, repair, or a commitment. The layers guide curiosity; they are not a required interrogation sequence.









NoteVerified Understanding Loop



Ask, listen, and restate the meaning in your own words. Invite the speaker to correct what you missed, then check again. The aim is an account the speaker recognizes as accurate. You can understand a position while continuing to disagree with it.

title: Appendix C — Portable Tools
text:
Negotiation
Begin with Negotiation Preparation. Use the later tools when an offer, tactic, disagreement, or implementation problem needs closer attention.







NoteNegotiation Preparation




State your best alternative to a negotiated agreement (BATNA) and how you could improve it. Use it to determine the least acceptable agreement, allowing for risk and implementation costs.
List the issues, priorities, target, proposed opening, and supporting standards.
Record what you know about the other side’s interests and alternatives, and what you need to ask.
Prepare possible packages, a concession plan, and terms for implementation and review.









NoteTactic Diagnostic



Treat a tactic as a possible signal, not proof of the counterpart’s constraint. Diagnose it before reacting.



Table C.3: A diagnostic response to common bargaining tactics.










Move
What it may be trying to signal or produce
Disciplined response




Flinch or visible shock
Your proposal is unreasonable
Return to standards and ask for the basis of the reaction; visible emotion alone does not establish that the offer is unreasonable.


Nibble
A late, small request will be conceded because both sides want closure
Reopen the package and link any addition to a reciprocal change.


Limited authority
An absent approver prevents movement
Verify the mandate and make any proposal conditional on approval of the whole package.


Good cop / bad cop
Pressure followed by relief should accelerate concession
Treat the roles as one process; slow down and ask for constraints and proposals in writing.


Exploding offer or deadline
Delay will destroy the opportunity
Verify what changes at the deadline, compare the BATNA, and request enough time for informed review.


Take it or leave it
The stated term is final
Test credibility without bargaining against yourself; compare the complete offer with the BATNA.


Bogey—falsely presenting a low-priority issue as crucial—false scarcity, or a fake bottom line
A priority or constraint is more important or fixed than it is
Ask for evidence, use conditional packages, and verify claims where possible. Deliberate deception remains unethical even when tactically common.














NoteMediation and Arbitration Are Different Choices



A mediator helps parties seek a voluntary agreement and ordinarily does not impose the result. An arbitrator hears the dispute and issues a decision under the applicable procedure. In final-offer arbitration, the arbitrator chooses between submitted final offers; whether that choice concerns a whole package or individual issues depends on the rules. Before choosing a process, establish the neutral’s authority, costs, confidentiality, and whether the decision is binding or reviewable.








NotePackage and Contingency Worksheet



List the negotiable issues and estimate what matters to each side. Prepare several packages of approximately equal value to you that trade differently across issues; these are multiple equivalent simultaneous offers (MESOs). Use the response to learn about priorities.
If the disagreement concerns a future event, consider a contingent term with a clear measure and verification process. Check whether either side could manipulate the measure or bear a risk it cannot manage. A signed agreement can remain the fallback while the parties voluntarily search for an improvement.

title: Appendix C — Portable Tools
text:
Organizational choice and decision systems
Use the Structured Judgment Pipeline to organize a group decision. Add the choice-architecture or AI-use record when the design involves those features, and use the ethical audit to examine who is affected.






NoteChoice-Architecture Audit



Trace one real path: objective → menu → understanding → action → feedback. Mark the options, order, categories, default, mapping, friction, timing, social information, and exit. Write the mechanism as a testable sentence: “Changing ___ should affect ___ because ___.” Compare a nudge with a boost, incentive, mandate, or structural change. Check purpose, welfare, evidence, transparency, exit, and distribution of burden.









NoteStructured Judgment Pipeline



Define the decision, its owner, and the people affected. Break the judgment into relevant criteria and establish a comparison or reference class. Have members record estimates independently before hearing the group or an AI recommendation.
Compare estimates and the reasons behind them, then examine the strongest objection. Record the decision, trade-offs, implementation responsibility, and conditions for reconsidering it. Set a review date and an outcome that can be checked. Use fewer steps when the stakes and complexity are low.









NoteMinimum AI-Use Record



Use this extension when a model materially informs a consequential decision:

Task and tool: task delegated; tool, model, or rule; version or access date; and reason for use.
Inputs and boundaries: material inputs and sources, missing information, and privacy, consent, or use restrictions.
Output and reliance: material output; what was followed, modified, or rejected; and why.
Independent checks: fact and source verification, baseline or independent human comparison, uncertainty and subgroup checks where relevant, and strongest contrary evidence.
Authority and correction: decision owner, affected people, exception or appeal, monitoring signal, review date, and who can pause or reverse the use.

Scale the record and validation with consequence, repetition, irreversibility, unequal power, and automation. Do not place sensitive data in an unauthorized record. Chapter 41 explains the distinction between prediction, valuation, intervention, and responsibility.









NoteEthical Audit



Answer six questions before implementation and again at review:

Whose objective is being optimized?
Who receives the benefit, and who bears the cost or tail risk?
Would affected people understand and endorse the mechanism under informed reflection?
Is refusal, correction, appeal, or exit genuinely available?
Does unequal power change the meaning of apparent consent?
What evidence will reveal harm or failure after implementation?

Add the domain-specific risk—deception, stigma, distribution, coercion, privacy, automation, or another foreseeable harm—and name who has authority to pause, correct, compensate, or end the intervention.

title: Appendix C — Portable Tools
text:
Classroom extensions
These activities are teaching protocols, not additional decision tools. Assign one only when it serves a stated learning objective.






NoteCase, Video, and Conversation Practice



Case or video debrief. Before viewing or reading, predict the central difficulty. During the case, record observable behavior rather than inferred motive. Afterward, identify the proposed mechanism, a plausible alternative explanation, information learned or lost, economic or relational cost, one boundary condition, and one better action to test. A clip or case illustrates behavior; it does not establish effectiveness outside its context. Linked videos remain with their rights holders.
Message production. Create a 3–5 minute message for a real audience and attach a design note of no more than 200 words: current audience model; meaningful contradiction; proposed update; strongest evidence; protected value or identity; specific action; uncertainty; and ethical safeguard. Peer feedback diagnoses the message rather than the presenter.
Connection prediction. Before a four-minute paired conversation, privately predict enjoyment, awkwardness, and connection. Compare forecast with experience. Participation and depth must be voluntary.
Depth and responsiveness. Begin naturally, then ask permission to follow one answer a level deeper—from fact to experience, meaning, emotion, or value. Debrief the difference between curiosity and intrusion.
Warm honesty. In triads, practice care + observable behavior + owned impact + invitation to the other person’s view + one testable request. Unsafe or high-power conflicts may require documentation, representation, or formal support rather than a classroom script.

title: Appendix E — Running an Experimental Study: From Question to Credible Evidence
text:
The experimental workflow
A practical workflow for designing, implementing, analyzing, and reporting behavioral experiments
A clinic introduces a shorter appointment reminder, and attendance rises. The staff would like to keep it, but attendance might also have risen because the season changed or a different group of patients received appointments. What would let them attribute the improvement to the reminder?
This appendix follows an imagined study from that question to a report another researcher could examine. The final worked example uses generated data, so you can reproduce its calculations without mistaking them for evidence about real patients. Read the appendix as a methods chapter or return to the relevant phase while planning your own study.
The work has five phases. Each leaves a record needed to interpret what follows.
The design card collects the decisions to make before data collection. The sections below explain why each matters.

title: Appendix E — Running an Experimental Study: From Question to Credible Evidence
section: Start with the claim you want to earn
text:
Start with the claim you want to earn
The reminder example allows four different questions:

Description: By how much did attendance rise?
Prediction: Which patients are likely to miss a future appointment?
Causation: What would attendance have been without the new reminder?
Mechanism: Did the reminder work by improving comprehension, attracting attention, or changing something else?

A before–after count could answer the descriptive question while leaving the others unresolved. To estimate the reminder’s effect, we need a credible comparison; to explain its mechanism, we need evidence that separates the possible pathways.






Figure E.1: Five questions connect an experimental design to the claim it can support. Revisit earlier steps when the evidence exposes a weakness.



The figure helps locate a weakness before it becomes a confident conclusion. If the attendance record is incomplete, for example, a sound assignment procedure alone will not rescue the final estimate.

E  Running an Experimental Study: From Question to Credible Evidence

title: Appendix E — Running an Experimental Study: From Question to Credible Evidence
text:
Define the question

1. Turn a topic into a question and hypothesis
“Anchoring,” “happiness,” and “AI advice” are topics. A research question specifies what would count as an answer.
For an empirical study, write:

For population P, what is the effect or association of intervention/exposure X, relative to comparison C, on outcome Y, over time T, and through which proposed mechanism M?

Not every question needs every element in its title. The design does.
A hypothesis should specify a prediction that could be contradicted. For the clinic, that might be: assignment to the shorter reminder increases recorded attendance within thirty days relative to assignment to the standard reminder. The outcome and comparison make the proposal testable.
Three distinctions prevent later confusion:

Confirmatory analysis evaluates a claim and analysis plan specified without using the outcome pattern.
Exploratory analysis uses the data to discover patterns and generate explanations.
Post hoc prediction can be valuable, but it must not be narrated as if it was specified in advance.



Research question check

Can another researcher name the population, comparison, outcome, and horizon?
Is the question descriptive, predictive, causal, mechanistic, or a synthesis question?
What result would count against the hypothesis?
Is the study feasible with the available sample, ethics, time, access, and measurement?
Would the answer change theory, a decision, a design, or a boundary condition?



2. Define the construct before choosing the instrument
A construct is the theoretical object: trust, impatience, fairness, experienced affect, cooperation. An operationalization is how the study makes that object observable: an item, scale, choice, response time, transfer, physiological signal, or coded behavior.
Similar labels can hide different constructs. A one-shot transfer, a self-report of generosity, and repeated helping behavior are not interchangeable measures of “prosociality.” Different labels can also hide near-identical measures. Name the construct first, then justify why the operation captures it in this population and setting.
Reliability concerns the consistency or precision of a measurement for its intended use. Validity concerns whether the interpretation of the score is warranted. A measure can be reliable and invalid: a scale can reproduce the same number while measuring the wrong object. High internal consistency does not establish construct validity. A correlation with brain activity does not certify a questionnaire as the true measure of a mental state.
Before data collection, record:

exact items, task, instructions, response scale, timing, scoring, exclusions, and version;
why the measure fits the construct and decision context;
evidence about reliability and validity in a relevant population;
whether the treatment changes the measure itself rather than the underlying construct;
whether comparison across languages or groups assumes comparable scale use;
which outcome is primary and which are secondary, manipulation checks, mediators, or exploratory.

Manipulation checks need care. A post-treatment check can be a useful diagnostic, but conditioning the main analysis on passing it can break randomization. If the treatment changes how people interpret the check, the check is also an outcome.
Measurement is not clerical work after theory. It is the bridge between theory and data (Flake & Fried, 2020).


3. Separate description, prediction, causation, and mechanism



Table E.2: Claim families require different evidence











Claim family
Target question
Design requirement
Common overreach




Description
What happened, to whom, and how variable was it?
Defined population, measure, sampling, missingness
Generalizing beyond the observed population


Association
How do measured variables co-vary?
Transparent adjustment and measurement
Calling an adjusted coefficient an effect


Prediction
How well does a model forecast new observations?
Honest out-of-sample evaluation and distribution-shift checks
Treating predictive importance as a causal lever


Causation
What would change under an intervention?
Credible counterfactual and identification assumptions
Treating before–after change as treatment effect


Mechanism
Through which pathway did the effect arise?
Variation or evidence that separates pathways
Relabeling a mediator correlation as a process






Prediction and causation can point in different directions. An excellent predictor may be impossible or unethical to intervene on. A weak predictor can still be a useful treatment if its manipulated change affects the outcome. “The model predicts who defaults” does not answer “What policy reduces default?”
Mechanism is harder still. Showing that treatment changes a proposed mediator and the mediator correlates with the outcome is not, by itself, a causal mechanism test. The mediator is post-treatment and can be confounded with unmeasured responses. Mechanism evidence becomes stronger when designs manipulate or otherwise identify the pathway, rule out alternatives, and predict boundary conditions.

title: Appendix E — Running an Experimental Study: From Question to Credible Evidence
text:
Design the comparison

4. Make the counterfactual and confounding visible
For person \(i\), let \(Y_i(1)\) denote the outcome under treatment and \(Y_i(0)\) the outcome under control. The individual causal effect is:
\[
Y_i(1)-Y_i(0).
\]
Only one potential outcome is observed. The missing one is the counterfactual problem. A comparison group is useful when its observed outcome represents what would have happened to the treated units without treatment.
Confounding occurs when the treatment comparison also reflects other causes of the outcome. If staff send the new reminder only to patients who are easier to contact, contactability may help explain an attendance difference. Statistical adjustment addresses that problem only under assumptions about the measured causes, the model, and what remains unmeasured.
Ask of every causal claim:

Why is the comparison group a credible counterfactual?
Which common causes of treatment and outcome are blocked by design?
Which remain possible?
Did treatment affect observation, attrition, reporting, or exposure to the outcome?
Could one unit’s treatment change another unit’s outcome?



5. Choose the design that identifies the contrast



Table E.3: Designs answer different questions under different assumptions











Design
What creates the comparison?
Strong use
Central assumption or limit




Randomized experiment
Known random assignment
Average effects of assignment in the study population
Implementation, attrition, interference, and sampling still matter


Laboratory experiment
Randomization in a controlled task
Mechanisms and comparative statics
Task, stakes, participants, and institution bound transport


Field experiment
Randomization in a natural setting
Causal effects under field implementation
Less control; treatment delivery and spillovers may vary


Natural or quasi-experiment
Rule, threshold, shock, timing, or instrument
Causal effects when the assignment process is credible
Each design has specific untestable assumptions


Observational study
Naturally occurring differences
Description, prediction, hypothesis generation; sometimes causal analysis with strong assumptions
Unmeasured confounding and selection


Simulation
Outcomes generated by an explicit model
Logic, mechanisms, sensitivity, boundary results
A result about the model is not automatically evidence about people






“Quasi-experiment” is not a stamp of causality. A regression discontinuity design needs continuity near the threshold and limited manipulation. Difference-in-differences needs a credible counterfactual trend and attention to timing and heterogeneous treatment effects. An instrumental-variable design needs instrument relevance plus independence, exclusion, and—for the usual LATE interpretation—monotonicity. A natural event is useful only if the process generating exposure supports the comparison.
No design dominates on every dimension. Control can improve internal validity and narrow realism. Field context can increase realism and add uncontrolled pathways. Build a body of evidence whose weaknesses do not all point in the same direction.


6. Random sampling and random assignment solve different problems
Random sampling selects units from a population and supports population description under the sampling design. Random assignment allocates eligible units to conditions and supports causal comparison within the experimental sample.
A convenience sample can support an internally valid randomized comparison but not a population prevalence estimate. A representative survey can estimate population characteristics yet fail to identify a causal effect. Keep the two random processes separate.






Figure E.2: Sampling connects observed people to a population; assignment creates a comparison within the study. Both inferences depend on the design and its implementation.



Figure E.2 keeps the direction of inference visible. Sampling asks how observed units connect to a defined population. Assignment asks whether outcomes differ because units were allocated to different conditions. A study can do either, both, or neither.

Random assignment balances in expectation
Random assignment does not guarantee that realized groups are identical. With a common assignment probability, it makes assignment independent of baseline potential outcomes and covariates. Stratified designs provide the corresponding independence within strata; unequal assignment probabilities require the appropriate weighting or adjustment. Across repeated allocations under a balanced design, baseline differences average to zero; in one realized sample, chance imbalance can occur (Imbens & Rubin, 2015).
This changes how balance should be used.

Verify the assignment code, unit, probabilities, strata, clusters, and allocation concealment.
Report important baseline covariates by group and inspect standardized differences or design-relevant summaries.
Do not run dozens of baseline significance tests and treat one p < .05 as proof that randomization failed. Under valid randomization, some chance differences are expected; p-values mainly restate that fact (Senn, 1994).
Pre-specify adjustment for strong predictors to improve precision; do not select controls by whether their baseline test is significant.
Investigate patterns that suggest coding errors, differential recruitment after assignment, or implementation failure.



Rerandomization is a design, not a rescue
Discarding an allocation after viewing an inconvenient imbalance can invalidate the stated assignment mechanism. But the rule “never rerandomize” is also wrong. Rerandomization can be valid when the acceptable-balance criterion, variables, and procedure are specified before treatment assignment and the analysis accounts for that restricted randomization (Morgan & Rubin, 2012).
Stratification and pair matching can improve balance or precision; cluster assignment may be needed when treatment is delivered to groups or spills across individuals. Record the procedure and use an analysis appropriate to it.



7. Plan precision before collecting outcomes
Power is the probability that a specified analysis will meet its decision criterion under a specified effect and data-generating process. It is not a property of sample size alone.
A defensible design calculation declares:

primary outcome and estimator;
smallest effect of substantive interest and plausible effect range;
outcome variance, baseline correlation, and repeated-measure structure;
assignment ratio, clusters, intraclass correlation, and strata;
expected noncompliance, attrition, missingness, and multiple testing;
significance or interval criterion and analysis model.

Do not take the largest published estimate from a small study, insert it into a calculator, and call the resulting sample adequate. Selective publication and sampling variation tend to make early significant effects too large.
Low power causes more than missed significance. Conditional on passing a significance filter, estimates can have the wrong sign (Type S error) or a seriously exaggerated magnitude (Type M error). Design analysis should therefore examine plausible estimates and uncertainty, not only a binary rejection probability (Gelman & Carlin, 2014).
After data collection, observed power computed from the observed effect adds little. Report the estimate, compatible interval, design assumptions, and what effect sizes the study could or could not distinguish.

title: Appendix E — Running an Experimental Study: From Question to Credible Evidence
text:
Run the study

8. Protect the assignment during implementation
A randomized design can lose its meaning after allocation. Track a participant or unit flow from eligibility through assignment, delivery, outcome observation, and analysis.






Figure E.3: Assignment, treatment receipt, and outcome observation are different events. An intention-to-treat comparison keeps the original assignment groups while addressing missing outcomes and interference.



Figure E.3 prevents several losses from being collapsed into “dropout.” Noncompliance separates assignment from treatment receipt. Missingness or attrition separates assignment from outcome observation. Interference means that one unit’s assignment or treatment changes another unit’s exposure or outcome. Each changes the estimand or the assumptions needed for interpretation.

Attrition and missing outcomes
Attrition is dangerous when missingness differs by assignment or relates to potential outcomes. Equal attrition rates do not guarantee equal selection, and a low percentage is not automatically harmless.
Report rates and reasons by arm, timing, baseline predictors of missingness, and sensitivity analyses under plausible missing-data assumptions. Do not silently replace the randomized sample with complete cases and retain the original causal language.


Noncompliance: assignment is not receipt
Let \(Z\) be assignment and \(D\) treatment received.
With randomized assignment at a common probability, complete outcome observation, and a treatment contrast defined appropriately for interference, the intention-to-treat (ITT) effect is estimated by comparing outcomes in the assigned groups:
\[
ITT = E[Y\mid Z=1]-E[Y\mid Z=0].
\]
ITT answers the effect of offering, assigning, or implementing the treatment under observed compliance. It preserves the randomized comparison and is often the policy-relevant estimand.
The effect among those who actually received treatment is not obtained by simply comparing receivers with nonreceivers; receipt is selected. With binary assignment and treatment receipt, consistently defined treatment versions, and no interference between units, assignment can identify a local average treatment effect (LATE) for compliers. The standard interpretation also requires:

relevance: assignment changes treatment receipt;
independence: assignment is as good as random relative to potential outcomes and compliance types;
exclusion: assignment affects the outcome only through treatment receipt;
monotonicity: assignment never makes a unit less likely to receive treatment; in the binary potential-receipt model, \(D_i(1)\geq D_i(0)\) for every unit.

Then the Wald ratio is:
\[
LATE = \frac{E[Y\mid Z=1]-E[Y\mid Z=0]}{E[D\mid Z=1]-E[D\mid Z=0]}.
\]
LATE concerns the compliers whose receipt changes with this instrument, rather than everyone offered treatment (Angrist et al., 1996). With a positive first stage no greater than one, the ratio has the same sign as ITT and at least its absolute magnitude. That rescaling does not make LATE the population-wide effect or establish that it will travel to another implementation.


Spillovers, interference, and displacement
The usual no-interference assumption says one unit’s outcome does not depend on other units’ assignments. Social information, contagion, peer effects, congestion, and markets often violate it.
Spillovers can make the standard difference too small, too large, or simply answer the wrong question. A job-placement program can help treated workers while displacing untreated workers from a fixed number of jobs. The direct effect and the total labor-market effect are different estimands.
Possible responses include randomizing at a higher level, varying treatment saturation, measuring networks, defining exposure mappings, and using pure control markets. None is automatic. State whose outcome depends on whose treatment.


Evaluation can change behavior
Participants may change behavior because they know they are being studied or because they infer what the researcher expects. The clinic should therefore consider whether the two reminder groups receive different attention beyond the intended message. These responses are possibilities to investigate, with no guaranteed direction.
Reduce avoidable salience, blind participants or staff where ethical and feasible, use unobtrusive or administrative measures with appropriate consent and privacy, standardize contact, and design diagnostics. Deception or undisclosed observation requires independent ethical justification; methodological convenience does not override respect for persons.

title: Appendix E — Running an Experimental Study: From Question to Credible Evidence
text:
Report, reproduce, and extend

10. Replication is estimation under a declared protocol
A replication is not a ritual in which an effect “works” or “fails.” It asks whether an estimate appears under a specified protocol, sample, setting, measure, and analysis—and how the new estimate changes cumulative uncertainty.

Direct replication holds key procedures close to the original to test repeatability under a defined protocol.
Conceptual replication tests a theory with a different operation; a difference can reflect the theory, the new measure, or an unrecognized moderator.
Multi-site replication estimates average effects and heterogeneity across implementations, populations, and settings.
Reanalysis or reproduction checks whether reported results follow from the declared data and code; it is not the same as collecting new data.

Large replication projects in psychology and experimental economics found both replicated effects and substantial attenuation or heterogeneity (Camerer et al., 2016; Open Science Collaboration, 2015). The lesson is not that an entire field is false. It is that single studies—especially small, flexible, selected ones—provide less certainty than clean narratives imply.
For a useful replication, document fidelity and departures, compare effect estimates with intervals, analyze protocol heterogeneity, and update the cumulative claim. A statistically significant original and nonsignificant replication can still have compatible estimates. A binary verdict discards that information.


11. Build an open and reproducible workflow
Transparency is not “put everything online.” Human-subject data can contain confidential or re-identifiable information. The target is as open as possible and as protected as necessary.
A minimum project structure preserves:

immutable raw inputs with provenance and checksums;
a data dictionary, consent and access conditions, and de-identification decisions;
versioned materials, assignment code, and implementation logs;
scripted transformations from raw to analytic data;
an environment or dependency record plus random seeds where relevant;
a machine-readable analysis that regenerates tables and figures;
a README with exact commands and expected outputs;
a deviation log connecting preregistration, implementation, and final analysis;
disclosure of inaccessible data, proprietary materials, or manual steps.

Run the pipeline in a clean environment before release. Check that figures and tables match the manuscript, the sample flow adds up, and the public package contains no direct or inferable identifiers. The FAIR principles—findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable—do not imply that every dataset is public; “accessible” can mean a governed access process (Wilkinson et al., 2016).
Preregistration, open materials, open code, and registered reports change different incentives. They should be evaluated and improved rather than treated as badges of truth (Munafò et al., 2017; Nosek et al., 2018).


12. Transport the result only as far as the evidence travels
Internal validity concerns whether the comparison supports the causal claim in the studied setting. External validity concerns where the result travels: to which people, tasks, institutions, treatments, outcomes, and times.
“The laboratory is artificial” is not a complete criticism. Every design abstracts. A lab can identify a mechanism that is hidden in the field. A field experiment can be realistic and highly local. A representative sample can improve population description but not guarantee that an intervention effect transports across institutions.
Build a transport argument:

Name the target population and setting.
Compare the study and target on effect modifiers, treatment delivery, outcome measurement, incentives, and equilibrium conditions.
Explain why the mechanism should remain or change.
Test heterogeneity with enough precision and without converting exploratory subgroups into facts.
Seek replications whose contexts vary on the proposed boundary condition.

External validity is not a yes/no property of a study. It is an argument supported by design, theory, and accumulated evidence.


13. Match the final sentence to the design



Table E.4: Claim-to-design matching










Evidence obtained
Defensible sentence
Sentence to avoid




Cross-sectional association
“X and Y were associated in this sample.”
“X changed Y.”


Out-of-sample predictive accuracy
“The model predicted Y in the held-out sample under this data environment.”
“The important predictors are causal levers.”


Randomized ITT estimate
“Assignment to the offer changed Y by … in the study sample.”
“Receiving treatment has this effect for everyone.”


Valid IV estimate
“For compliers induced by this instrument, treatment changed Y under the stated assumptions.”
“This is the universal treatment effect.”


Laboratory treatment effect
“Under this task, institution, stakes, and sample, treatment changed behavior.”
“Humans always behave this way.”


Simulation result
“Under these model rules and parameters, the mechanism can produce the pattern.”
“The simulation proves the human mechanism.”


Mediator correlation
“The pattern is consistent with the proposed pathway.”
“The mediator caused the effect.”






Scientific writing becomes clearer when it states the estimand and scope before the interpretation.

title: Appendix E — Running an Experimental Study: From Question to Credible Evidence
section: Worked study: from question to report
text:
Worked study: from question to report
Here is the complete calculation for the imagined clinic. This simulated teaching study connects the design record to generated outcomes and an estimate; it supplies no evidence about a real reminder programme.
Question. Among patients already eligible for a routine appointment, what is the intention-to-treat effect of assignment to a shorter, plain-language reminder, relative to the standard reminder, on attending within thirty days?
Design specified for this teaching example. Randomly assign 1,200 eligible patients in equal numbers after eligibility is fixed. The primary outcome is an administrative indicator for attendance within thirty days. The primary estimator is the difference in mean attendance by assignment, with an unpooled standard error and 95% confidence interval. Analyze every assigned patient in the assigned arm; report missing administrative outcomes rather than excluding them silently. Secondary outcomes, subgroup comparisons, and mechanism measures are exploratory unless separately declared.



Table E.6: Planned design for the simulated reminder study









Design-card field
Declared choice




Population
Patients eligible for the appointment under the clinic’s existing rule


Treatment and comparison
Plain-language reminder versus standard reminder


Unit and assignment
Individual patient; exactly 600 assignments per arm


Primary outcome
Attendance recorded within thirty days


Estimand
ITT risk difference: assignment to new reminder minus assignment to standard reminder


Main threats
Delivery failure, wrong contact information, spillovers within households, missing administrative records, and outcome-definition errors


Mechanism boundary
The contrast tests the reminder package; it does not separately identify comprehension, fear reduction, salience, or lower friction


Decision rule
Report estimate and interval; the clinic evaluates operational cost, distribution across patient groups, and implementation errors before scaling






The data below are generated with a declared seed and fixed probabilities solely to make the workflow reproducible:
import math
import random

rng = random.Random(20260830)
n_control = n_treatment = 600
control = [int(rng.random() < 0.65) for _ in range(n_control)]
treatment = [int(rng.random() < 0.70) for _ in range(n_treatment)]

p_control = sum(control) / n_control
p_treatment = sum(treatment) / n_treatment
effect = p_treatment - p_control
se = math.sqrt(
    p_control * (1 - p_control) / n_control
    + p_treatment * (1 - p_treatment) / n_treatment
)
ci = (effect - 1.96 * se, effect + 1.96 * se)
The generated data contain 380 attendances among 600 control assignments and 417 among 600 treatment assignments. Attendance was therefore 63.3% under the standard reminder and 69.5% under the plain-language reminder. The estimated ITT difference is 6.2 percentage points, with an approximate 95% confidence interval from 0.8 to 11.5 percentage points.
Design-matched interpretation. In this simulated study, assignment to the plain-language reminder increased recorded attendance by 6.2 percentage points relative to assignment to the standard reminder. The interval remains compatible with effects from about 0.8 to 11.5 points under the stated standard-error approximation. The result estimates the reminder package in the simulated study population. It does not establish which component caused the difference, whether the effect would persist in another clinic, or whether the redesign is ethically and operationally preferable for every patient group.
What the simulation leaves out. The code follows the declared generation and estimation procedure, but it bypasses recruitment, delivery, missing outcomes, and spillovers. A real study would need records of eligibility, assignment, message delivery, outcome collection, and every protocol deviation, alongside the analysis code and access conditions. Reproducing the calculation checks the calculation; it does not verify real-world treatment delivery.

title: Appendix E — Running an Experimental Study: From Question to Credible Evidence
text:
Ethics is part of identification
The Belmont principles remain a useful starting point: respect for persons, beneficence, and justice. Respect requires meaningful information and voluntary participation where consent applies. Beneficence requires risks to be minimized and justified by potential value. Justice asks who bears research burdens and who can benefit.
Ethics also affects evidence. Coercive recruitment selects participants. Privacy fears change answers. An intervention that cannot be implemented ethically may have little policy relevance. Excluding affected groups for convenience can make the sample uninformative about those who bear the decision.
Institutional review, data-protection law, registration, and local procedures change over time. Check current requirements with the relevant institution before collecting data; a historical lecture link is not approval.

A useful experimental question names the comparison, outcome, population, and period.

Study and practice

Design a comparison for the clinic that would separate the reminder package’s effect from a seasonal change.
Explain what you would record if some messages were not delivered or some attendance outcomes were missing.
Propose a further comparison that could distinguish comprehension from attention as a mechanism.







TipActivity: break and repair the evidence chain



Choose one claim from the book or current media. Place it in Figure E.1. State the question, construct, measure, comparison, estimand, and final sentence. Mark the weakest arrow. Then propose the smallest feasible redesign that would strengthen that link. If the redesign cannot support the original claim, narrow the claim.
Submit the completed pipeline, one explicit assumption, the revised design, and a final sentence whose strength matches the evidence the redesign could earn.

title: Appendix F — When Evidence Breaks: The Replication Crisis and Research Integrity
text:
When a striking result becomes less convincing
Publication bias, underpowered studies, data fabrication, and the systems that can correct them
Evidence map updated: 10 September 2026. Replication findings and journal notices are dated below so that later evidence can revise the account.
Imagine that one hundred teams test promising interventions. You hear about the studies with striking positive results, while inconclusive studies attract little attention. Years later, larger replications produce a less impressive picture. Some effects recur, some become smaller, and others disappear.
The published studies may all have followed recognizable scientific procedures. Why, then, did the picture change so much?
To answer, follow a result from the original question to the article you read. Sampling variation matters, but so do decisions about what to measure, which analysis to report, and which results become visible. The same trail helps distinguish an uncertain effect from a flawed record; a failed replication alone cannot tell you that someone fabricated data.
Each stage in Figure F.1 changes what readers can know. Preregistration records a plan; open code lets others check the calculation; replication collects new evidence. Their usefulness depends on the problem at that stage.
Behavioral science uses the phrase replication crisis for accumulating evidence that some influential findings are less stable, smaller, or more context-dependent than the published literature initially suggested. “Crisis” captures the seriousness of the credibility problem. It can also mislead if it implies that all findings failed at once or that one replication determines truth.
Large coordinated projects provide important evidence, not a census of an entire field. The Open Science Collaboration attempted replications of 100 studies published in three psychology journals. Ninety-seven percent of the original studies reported statistically significant results, compared with 36% of the replications; the replication effects were, on average, about half the magnitude of the originals (Open Science Collaboration, 2015). Those numbers revealed substantial attenuation and uncertainty within the sampled literature. They did not establish that “only 36% of psychology is true.”
In experimental economics, Camerer et al. (2016) replicated 18 laboratory studies from the American Economic Review and the Quarterly Journal of Economics using prespecified designs with at least 90% power to detect the original effect size. Eleven of the 18 replications found a significant effect in the original direction, and the average replicated effect was 66% of the original. Again, the proper conclusion is bounded: this selected set contained both recurrence and attenuation.
“Statistically significant again” depends on sample size, noise, analysis, and threshold. An original and replication can fall on opposite sides of .05 while having compatible effect estimates. Two significant estimates can also disagree sharply in magnitude. Compare estimates and uncertainty, protocol fidelity, and context; a replication rate is not the proportion of a field that is true.

title: Appendix F — When Evidence Breaks: The Replication Crisis and Research Integrity
text:
A concrete update: watched eyes and the honesty box
Bateson, Nettle, and Roberts (2006) alternated pictures of eyes and flowers above the price list beside an honesty box in a university coffee room. Contributions relative to consumption were higher during the eye-image weeks. The result suggested that even a minimal cue of observation might activate reputational concern.
The memorable image travelled further than the cumulative evidence justified. Northover et al. (2017) later reported two meta-analyses that found no reliable overall effect of artificial surveillance cues on generosity. That result does not prove that observation cues can never matter. It narrows the defensible claim: an eye image is not a dependable behavioral remote control, and any effect may depend on the task, outcome, population, or setting. An organization considering such a poster should test the relevant behavior in its own setting, rather than assume that the image creates accountability.
This is how scientific updating should work. Retain the original observation, widen the evidence base, revise the general claim, and identify the boundary conditions that future studies must test.
